story: Newton has no single downtown. It is a city of thirteen villages, among them Auburndale, Chestnut Hill, Newton Centre, Newton Corner, Newton Highlands, Newton Lower Falls, Newton Upper Falls, Newtonville, Nonantum, Oak Hill, Thompsonville, Waban and West Newton, laid out over hills such as Nonantum, Waban, Chestnut and Oak Hill, with the Charles River along the north and west. Mills came first: Upper Falls had a mill on the river by 1688, and its National Register district holds Greek Revival, Gothic Revival and Late Victorian houses. Nonantum's worsted mills drew Irish, French Canadian, Italian and Jewish workers. When the Boston and Worcester railroad reached West Newton in 1834, Newton became one of the country's earliest commuter suburbs.

Each village grew in its own era. Around Farlow and Kenrick Parks in Newton Corner, Greek Revival and Italianate houses from the 1840s sit among Queen Anne and Colonial Revival homes built from about 1870 to 1910. Newton Highlands was platted after the Charles River Railroad arrived in 1852, with Mansard, Italianate and Colonial Revival houses, and Waban took off after the Highland Branch station opened in 1886. Auburndale's local historic district covers about 275 properties, including a house from 1730. Oak Hill, by contrast, was market-garden farmland until the 1950s.

Census figures show how old the stock is: a median build year around 1942, nearly half of the city's roughly 34,000 homes built before 1940, and about 80 percent before 1980. About 21 percent of units are in two-to-four-unit buildings and about 70 percent are owner-occupied. That means plenty of two-families, close lot lines and painted wood, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules on almost every pre-1978 exterior.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is most often considered for Newton's two-family houses and for postwar homes in places like Oak Hill, which stayed farmland until the 1950s. On a two-family, it can cut repainting costs for owners who share the building, but the details matter: corner posts, window trim and the junction with porches are where vinyl jobs on older houses usually look wrong. On Victorian houses in Newton Corner, Newton Highlands or Upper Falls, much of the character is in the trim, so it is worth deciding what will be kept, wrapped or replaced before choosing vinyl at all.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: So much of Newton was built before 1940 that clapboard is often the original wall surface, from 1840s Greek Revival houses near Farlow Park to Colonial Revival homes of the early 1900s. When re-cladding, match the existing exposure and keep corner boards, frieze boards and casings at their original depth. Back-primed cedar or pine and smooth engineered clapboard both work; the choice depends on budget and how much original material is staying. On houses this old, lead-safe practices are a standard part of removing painted boards.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits many Newton houses where owners want painted lap siding without wood's upkeep, especially the Colonial Revival and early twentieth-century houses found in villages like Newton Highlands and Newton Corner. It needs proper clearances at roofs and grade, and on tight lots its weight and cutting dust call for careful planning of staging and cleanup with neighbors close by. A smooth face with matching trim usually looks more appropriate on an older house than a deeply textured wood-grain board.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingled walls appear across Newton's late Victorian and Colonial Revival houses, and Queen Anne designs, of which the Farlow and Kenrick Parks district has many, often combine shingles in gables with clapboard below. Replacing shingles on these houses means matching exposure and any patterned courses, then stain or paint to suit. Cedar lasts longest with an underlayment that allows drying and with careful flashing at the many intersections these roofs and walls have. Fiber-cement shingle panels are an alternative for plainer walls.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: On a Newton house that is eighty or more years old, a full replacement often uncovers several eras of work: original clapboard, an asbestos or aluminum layer added mid-century, and patched sheathing around later additions. Stripping to the frame lets those problems be fixed and windows be properly flashed. In dense villages such as Nonantum, Newtonville or West Newton, staging between houses and protecting the neighbor's property are part of planning the job. Because about four of five homes predate 1980, lead-safe practices will apply to most tear-offs. Any older layer suspected of containing asbestos should be tested before removal.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Newton's houses span Federal, Greek Revival, Italianate, Gothic Revival, Mansard, Queen Anne and Colonial Revival styles, so trim work here often means reproducing a specific profile rather than installing stock boards. Italianate brackets, Gothic Revival bargeboards and Colonial Revival cornices can be remade in wood or cellular PVC milled to match. On two-family houses, porches and their columns, rails and ceilings are often where rot starts and are worth inspecting during any exterior project.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Hills shape drainage in Newton. A house on a slope near Waban Hill or Chestnut Hill sheds water quickly toward the downhill side, while lots near the Charles in Auburndale or the Lower Falls collect it. Seamless aluminum gutters with downspouts directed away from foundations, and away from the neighbor's lot where houses are close, cover most needs. Older houses may still have wooden or built-in gutters; those should be evaluated for restoration or replacement together with the roof edge.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With half the housing older than 1940, Newton roofs vary widely: steep Victorian roofs with turrets and dormers, Mansard roofs in places like Newton Highlands, gable roofs on two-families, and low-slope sections over porches and additions. Each needs a different approach, and some steep or Mansard slopes may carry slate worth repairing rather than replacing. For asphalt reroofs, a full tear-off, deck repair, ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, and good attic ventilation are the basics. Tight lots also affect how debris is handled.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Old houses often need targeted repairs rather than full replacement: a few rotted clapboards under a window, a damaged shingle panel, or siding pulled loose by a falling branch. Repairs should match the existing profile and finish and address the source of water. In pre-1978 homes, which are most of the city, lead-safe practices apply even to small repairs on painted surfaces.

story: Lexington was settled around 1642 as the farming edge of Cambridge, became a separate parish in 1691 and was incorporated in 1713. Its best-known buildings stand near the Battle Green in Lexington Centre: Munroe Tavern from about 1695, Buckman Tavern from about 1710 and the Hancock-Clarke House of 1737. Neighborhoods such as Meriam Hill, Loring Hill, Munroe Hill and East Lexington, which residents call East Village, grew up around that older core, and Vine Brook once powered mills before irrigating farms.

What sets Lexington apart is what happened after the Second World War. Population jumped about 60 percent in the 1950s, and by the 1970s many farms had become subdivisions as the Route 128 technology economy grew. Alongside conventional houses, the town gained a series of modernist neighborhoods: Six Moon Hill (1947-1953) by members of The Architects Collaborative, with flat, low-pitched or butterfly roofs, narrow vertical siding and walls of glass; Five Fields, begun in 1951 on a former dairy farm, with 68 half-acre lots built from three standard plans; Peacock Farm, mostly 1953-1960, split-levels in vertical cedar by Compton and Pierce; and Turning Mill and Middle Ridge by Carl Koch. Six Moon Hill and Peacock Farm are both on the National Register.

Census estimates put Lexington's median build year around 1965, with about 21 percent of homes built before 1940 and roughly 65 percent before 1980. About 80 percent of the roughly 12,750 units are owner-occupied, and under 5 percent are in two-to-four-unit buildings. Exterior work here ranges from colonial-era detail to mid-century houses whose wood siding and low roofs need their own approach, with EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules applying to painted surfaces on pre-1978 homes.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical option on the conventional houses that went up in Lexington as farms were subdivided in the 1950s and 1960s. It is a poor match for the modernist neighborhoods, where narrow vertical wood siding is part of the design, and for houses near the Battle Green whose value lies in their period detail. Where vinyl does fit, choose a profile and exposure close to the original siding and keep trim widths generous so the house does not look stripped down.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard belongs on Lexington's older houses, from the colonial-era buildings around Lexington Centre to the nineteenth- and early twentieth-century homes on Meriam Hill and in East Village. Re-cladding one of these houses well comes down to copying the existing exposure, corner details and casing depth, and using back-primed cedar or pine, or a smooth engineered board where the owner prefers lower maintenance. Most of these houses predate 1978, so removing old painted boards is done under lead-safe procedures.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: For Lexington's many homes from the 1950s through the 1970s, fiber cement offers painted lap siding that does not rot and holds paint longer than wood. It also comes in vertical panel and board-and-batten formats, which can suit owners of contemporary houses who want a lower-maintenance alternative, although in Six Moon Hill or Peacock Farm it is worth considering how far a substitute departs from the original wood. Fiber cement is heavy, must be cut with dust control and needs proper clearances at grade and roof lines.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar has an unusual place in Lexington: Peacock Farm's houses were clad in vertical cedar boards, and much of the town's mid-century modern housing relied on natural wood siding. Replacing or repairing that cladding usually means matching board width and orientation rather than switching to shingles. On traditional houses, cedar shingles remain a good choice for gables and full walls. In either case, cedar lasts longest when it can dry from behind and is kept clear of soil and roof runoff.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a Lexington house from the postwar subdivision years is the time to check sheathing, add housewrap and flashing that many original installations lacked, and consider insulation board while walls are open. For mid-century modern houses with large expanses of glass, the junction between siding and window walls needs particular care. Older houses closer to Lexington Centre deserve a look at which original features should be kept before tear-off starts, and lead-safe practices apply to painted siding on homes built before 1978.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim in Lexington ranges from the cornices and door surrounds of eighteenth-century houses to the thin, minimal edges of TAC-designed modern homes, where trim is barely visible by design. Replacing rotted pieces means respecting whichever approach the house was built with: profiled casings and corner boards on traditional houses, or flush, simple detailing on contemporary ones. Cellular PVC and composite boards can be milled to suit either style and resist rot at sills, fascia and rake boards.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lexington's modernist neighborhoods were laid out to follow the land, with houses at varied angles and preserved oak trees at Five Fields, so leaves and uneven grades are part of the gutter question there. Low-pitched or flat roofs on mid-century houses often drain differently than steep roofs, sometimes through scuppers or internal drains, and should be evaluated as such. On conventional homes, seamless aluminum gutters sized to the roof, with guards under heavy tree cover and downspouts carried away from foundations, cover most needs.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Roofing in Lexington depends heavily on the neighborhood. Conventional pitched-roof houses from the 1950s and 1960s usually take asphalt shingles with ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and valleys and good attic ventilation. The flat, low-pitched and butterfly roofs found in Six Moon Hill and similar developments need membrane systems and careful flashing at walls and skylights, not shingles. Older houses near the Battle Green may have steep slopes, dormers and chimneys that need re-flashing during any reroof.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Many problems can be handled with a repair: a few split vertical boards on a mid-century house, rotted clapboards beneath a window, or shingles lifted by wind. The repair should match the existing material, width and finish and fix the source of water, which on low-pitched roofs is often an overflowing edge or a failed flashing at a wall. On homes built before 1978, lead-safe practices apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.

story: Peabody began as the South Parish of Danvers in 1752, broke away as South Danvers in 1855, took the name Peabody in 1868 and became a city in 1916. For generations it was the Leather City: tanneries drew immigrants from many countries, and Turkish and Kurdish workers filled boarding houses on Walnut Street. The prosperity of that era shows in two National Register districts. The Washington Street Historic District (1985), running south from Main Street toward Aborn Street along Washington, Holten and Sewall Streets, holds two- and three-story wood-frame houses in Federal, Greek Revival and Italianate styles, including the 1810 Gen. Gideon Foster House and tannery owner Abel Proctor's house of about 1830. The Civic Center district (1980) pairs the Second Empire city hall with mid-nineteenth-century houses on Chestnut and Franklin Streets.

Most of the city is newer. West Peabody was largely farmland until the 1950s, and Peabody's population grew more than 40 percent in the 1950s and nearly 50 percent in the 1960s. Census estimates put the median build year around 1966, with about 22 percent of homes built before 1940 and about 64 percent before 1980. Around 14 percent of the roughly 23,000 units are in two-to-four-unit buildings, and about two-thirds are owner-occupied, so multi-family buildings are a real part of the local mix.

The landscape adds variety: the Ipswich River on the northwestern border, Suntaug Lake, Crystal Lake, Spring Pond and the 275-acre Brooksby Farm. The Peabody Historical Commission's guide on re-siding historic homes advises against vinyl and aluminum on those houses, and pre-1978 homes fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is widely used on Peabody's postwar houses, especially in West Peabody, which was mostly farmland until the 1950s, and on multi-family buildings where owners want to cut maintenance. It is a different story on the city's historic homes: the Peabody Historical Commission's guide to re-siding historic houses advises against vinyl and aluminum there. Owners of older houses near downtown should read that guidance first. Where vinyl fits, a good profile, solid flashing and proper trim widths make the difference in how it looks.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Federal, Greek Revival and Italianate houses of the Washington Street and Civic Center districts were built with wood clapboard, and the Historical Commission's re-siding guide steers owners of historic homes away from vinyl and aluminum. Re-cladding one of those houses means matching exposure, corner boards and casing depth so the facade keeps its proportions. Back-primed cedar or pine holds paint longer than face-primed boards. Nearly all of these houses predate 1978, so removing painted boards falls under lead-safe rules.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable choice for Peabody's many mid-century homes and for two- and three-family buildings where owners want a painted look with less upkeep than wood. Its weight and the dust from cutting call for careful planning on tight urban lots near downtown, and it needs proper clearances at the ground and roof lines. On a house of historic character, it is worth checking the Historical Commission's guidance first, since it addresses which replacement materials are appropriate on historic homes.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit older Peabody houses whose design originally included them, and they are an alternative to clapboard on the gables and dormers of early twentieth-century homes. In wetter spots, such as lots near the Ipswich River, Crystal Lake or Spring Pond, the key is letting shingles dry from behind and keeping the bottom course well above the ground. Natural cedar weathers to gray unless stained, and pre-finished shingles reduce maintenance.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Peabody's housing stock includes many homes built during the 1950s and 1960s boom and a substantial share of two-to-four-unit buildings, about 14 percent. On a multi-family house, full replacement means coordinating with tenants and planning staging around porches and entries. Stripping to the sheathing allows window flashing and insulation upgrades. Before replacing siding on a historic home, it makes sense to check with the Historical Commission and Inspectional Services about permits and guidance. Lead-safe procedures apply on pre-1978 homes.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim gives Peabody's older houses much of their character: Italianate brackets on Washington Street, Greek Revival cornices and door surrounds on Chestnut Street, and the porches and casings of later houses. Replacing rotted trim with matching profiles in wood or cellular PVC keeps the look intact. On mid-century homes, sills, fascia and rake boards are the usual problem spots. Where trim is wrapped in metal or plastic, the original profile is lost, which is one more reason to read the Historical Commission's re-siding guide before a project.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Peabody's rivers and ponds shape drainage. Homes near the Ipswich River, the Waters River, Suntaug Lake or Spring Pond need downspouts directed well away from foundations, and lots near Brooksby Farm and other wooded or open land can collect leaves. Seamless aluminum gutters sized to the roof, with guards under heavy tree cover, suit most houses. On multi-family buildings, gutter capacity and downspout placement near shared walkways need careful thought.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With a median build year around 1966, many Peabody roofs cover mid-century homes, and asphalt shingles with ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys and good attic ventilation are the standard approach. Older houses in the historic districts may have steeper roofs, dormers and chimneys that need re-flashing, and any mansard or other complex roof form needs a closer inspection before pricing. Multi-family buildings often have low-slope sections over porches that call for membrane roofing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small problems, such as a few rotted clapboards, cracked vinyl or loose shingles after a storm, can often be fixed without a full re-side. A good repair matches the profile and color and fixes the cause, which is often a clogged gutter, a missing kick-out flashing or a downspout emptying against the wall. For historic homes, the Historical Commission's guidance on materials is worth checking, and lead-safe practices apply on pre-1978 houses.

story: Northborough started out as the north part of Westborough. It was set off as a district in 1766 and became its own town in 1775, and its early industry gathered along the Assabet River. The Northborough Historical Society's newsletter traces that waterside history: a fulling mill driven by the river a little north of Main Street in the late 1700s, comb factories from 1839 into the twentieth century, and Thomas Blair's camera business near the river and on Winn Street in the 1890s. On Hudson Street, the Chapin Mill and David F. Wood's mills made woolen cloth and shoddy after the Civil War. Caleb Chapin rebuilt his mill in brick after it burned in 1869.

Most houses in town are much younger than that history. Census figures count about 6,100 homes with a median construction year of 1980. Roughly half were built before 1980, and about one in nine predates 1940. More than four in five are owner-occupied, and only around 8 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so most exterior projects here involve a single-family house, one owner and one set of decisions.

The town's Historic District Commission works mostly through signs, cemetery projects and encouragement. Its June 2021 minutes record that attempts in the late 1970s to create a local historic district near the town center failed. They also note that areas on Summer Street and School Street had once been recommended for the National Register, and that the commission sent letters to owners on Howard, South, Church and Crawford streets thanking them for keeping up their properties. If you own one of those older houses, it is worth calling the town before you change the look of the front. For the large stock of 1970s and 1980s houses, the work is mostly about replacing materials that are reaching the end of their first life.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With half the town's housing built in or after 1980, many Northborough homes are on their original siding, or on a first replacement put on decades ago. Vinyl is a practical choice for a house of that age, but the panels should not go up until the wall underneath has been checked. Window heads, deck ledgers and the base of the wall are where water damage tends to hide on houses from this period. Ask that the estimate spell out the house wrap, the flashing at each window and the trim system, so you know what you are paying for before work begins.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: For the roughly 11 percent of Northborough houses built before 1940, clapboard is the material most likely to fit the house. Matching the exposure, meaning the visible width of each course, matters more than the species of board when you patch an old wall. Any house built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules once painted surfaces are disturbed. Expect the plan to include containment and cleanup. If the house is on one of the streets the Historic District Commission has noted, call the town before you change materials.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners of 1970s and 1980s houses who want a painted lap look without the upkeep of wood. The boards are heavy and are cut with dust control, so a crew needs room to stage them. Most Northborough lots are single-family and owner-occupied, which usually makes that easy to arrange. Fiber cement needs specific clearances above the roof and the ground, and it needs flashing at butt joints. Those details belong in the written estimate, not just the brand name.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a reasonable choice for an antique house near the center or a house that already wears them, and they also work on gable ends and dormers. In a town where the Historic District Commission has sent letters praising owners who keep up old houses on Howard and Church streets, natural materials fit the setting. Shingles want airflow behind them, a decision about whether to leave them to weather or to stain them, and attention at the bottom courses, where splashback from the ground keeps the wood damp.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement is a good time to fix the problems a 1980-era wall may hide: missing flashing, thin sheathing and poorly sealed windows. Because only about 8 percent of Northborough homes are in two- to four-unit buildings, most projects here involve one owner, which makes it simpler to add insulation board or upgrade windows at the same time. For houses built before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when old paint is disturbed during tear-off. Get the scope, materials and disposal in writing at the free on-site assessment.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is often where Northborough's late-20th-century houses show their age first: rotted sill noses, split corner boards and soft fascia behind the gutters. Replacing trim in PVC or primed composite is common when the siding is still sound. On older houses near the town center, matching the original profiles of the casings, frieze boards and returns keeps the house looking right. Ask what is being replaced and what is being wrapped. Covering rot with aluminum or vinyl only hides it.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Northborough sits around 300 feet above sea level, with the Assabet running through town. Snowfall and leaf drop from street and yard trees, more than elevation, decide how hard gutters work here. Seamless aluminum in a 5- or 6-inch profile fits most single-family houses. The key questions are downspout placement, so water clears the foundation, and whether to add guards under big trees. On older houses with wood gutters or rotted fascia, the fascia repair has to come first.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Much of the town's housing dates from around 1980, so a large number of roofs are well past their first replacement, and some have two layers of shingles. A tear-off lets the deck be inspected and re-nailed and lets ice-and-water membrane go in at the eaves and valleys. On older houses near the center, check whether the existing roof boards are spaced planks, which may need a new deck before new shingles. Ventilation at the ridge and soffits should be part of the quote.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Not every problem needs a new wall. A cracked vinyl panel, a few rotted clapboards or a damaged corner can usually be repaired if matching material is available. A repair visit should also look for the cause, such as a missing kickout flashing or a leaking gutter, so the same spot does not fail again. On a house built before 1978, even a small repair that disturbs paint falls under lead-safe rules.

story: Westborough was settled around 1675 near Lake Chauncy, in what was then the west part of Marlborough, and was incorporated in 1717. The commercial center later shifted downtown after the railroad arrived. Two National Register districts show what grew up after that. The West Main Street Historic District, roughly bounded by Milk, Main, Blake and Fay streets, is listed for Greek Revival and Late Victorian architecture. East of the center, the Vintonville Historic District covers about 80 properties on Cottage, Elm, Spruce, Green, Pine, Brigham, Cedar, South and Beach streets. Most are modest houses on small lots, built between 1860 and 1890 on streets laid out by Otis Vinton.

Census data puts the town at about 8,300 homes, with a median year built of 1976. A little more than half went up before 1980, and about 13 percent predate 1940. The mix is more varied than in neighboring Northborough. Only about 62 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and roughly one in ten is in a two- to four-unit building. The town also sits at a highway crossroads: the Mass Pike and I-495 meet on its west side, and Route 9 runs nearby.

Water shapes the landscape. The Sudbury and Assabet rivers both start here, and the town holds Lake Chauncy, Hocomonco Pond, Cedar Swamp Pond, the Westboro Reservoir and the George H. Nichols Reservoir. Fay Mountain is the high point. For exterior work, that means a 19th-century wood house in Vintonville and a 1970s house on a wooded lot near a pond can need very different plans.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: About half of Westborough's housing dates from after the mid-1970s, and vinyl is a common replacement on those houses. On the smaller lots of Vintonville or around West Main Street, vinyl over old clapboard can flatten the trim details that make a 19th-century house look the way it does. If you go that route, keep or rebuild the window casings and corner boards rather than burying them in J-channel. On newer houses, the wall underneath matters most: check the sheathing at window corners before the panels go on.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The West Main Street district is listed for Greek Revival and Late Victorian buildings, and Vintonville's houses mostly date from 1860 to 1890. Those styles were built to be seen in painted wood. Replacing clapboard on houses of that era means matching board width and exposure, and saving original trim where it can be saved. Every house built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when old paint is cut or scraped, and with about 13 percent of the town's homes older than 1940, that comes up often.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits a painted lap look on a house where wood would be hard to keep up, such as a 1970s or 1980s house in a shaded neighborhood near one of the town's ponds or reservoirs. The boards hold paint well but need correct clearances at the ground and roof, flashed butt joints and careful handling during installation. In a two- to four-unit building, which makes up about one in ten Westborough homes, plan the staging and the schedule with every occupant, because the walls are shared.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit an older Westborough house, especially on Late Victorian buildings, which often used decorative shingles on gables and upper walls. Replacing those patterns course for course, rather than switching to plain lap siding, keeps the house's character. On wooded lots near Lake Chauncy or Hocomonco Pond, shingles that stay damp and shaded need room to dry. A rainscreen gap behind them and good gutters help, and so does trimming back plants that touch the wall.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Westborough's housing is more mixed than its neighbors': about 38 percent of homes are rented, and roughly one in ten is in a two- to four-unit building. A full replacement on a multi-family house affects tenants as well as the owner, so plan access, debris removal and how the work is divided up. On single-family homes from the 1970s, the main value of a full replacement is the chance to inspect sheathing and redo window flashing. For houses built before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply during tear-off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is what tells a Greek Revival house on West Main Street from a Late Victorian one: wide corner pilasters and frieze boards on one, brackets and turned porch parts on the other. Replacing rotted pieces with the same profiles keeps that difference. On the more modest 1860s-1890s houses in Vintonville, the trim may be simpler but is still worth matching. On newer houses, PVC trim at the sills and the base of the walls cuts down on repainting.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With so many ponds, swamps and reservoirs in town, many Westborough lots are wooded or low-lying, and both affect gutters. Leaves and needles call for guards or regular cleaning. Water at the downspouts needs to be carried well away from foundations on wet ground. Seamless aluminum suits most houses. On older houses with built-in or wood gutters, repair the fascia and roof edge first. Ask where each downspout will discharge before the job starts.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: A median build year of 1976 means many Westborough roofs are on a second or third set of shingles, and the deck under them should be checked during tear-off. Ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and valleys, balanced intake and ridge venting, and new flashing at chimneys and sidewalls should all be in the quote. On the town's multi-family buildings, larger roof areas and porches make staging and debris protection worth planning ahead.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small problems are often worth fixing on their own: a few split clapboards, a cracked vinyl panel, or rot where a deck meets the house. On older houses the repair should match the existing board size and exposure. Whatever the material, find out why the spot failed, whether from flashing, a gutter or splashback, so the fix holds. On a rental or multi-family building, tell tenants before the work starts.

story: Shrewsbury was laid out on the north side of what early records called the Rocky Plain, along the road from Boston to Connecticut that later became the Boston Post Road. That ground is now the Shrewsbury Historic District around the town common. Its 1976 National Register nomination describes a small group of buildings, most from the 18th and early 19th centuries. They include the white clapboard First Congregational Church of 1766, the Reverend Joseph Sumner House of 1797, and the Federal-style Samuel Haven, Philo Slocum and Jonas Stone houses, all with clapboard walls and multi-pane sash. The nomination also notes that the area has been a local historic district since October 1972.

Most of the town came later. Streetcar lines in the 19th century spurred single-family building, the population doubled between 1915 and 1940, and summer residents put up cottages along Lake Quinsigamond. Today Census figures show about 15,400 homes, a median build year of 1979, about half built before 1980 and roughly 11 percent before 1940. Around 72 percent are owner-occupied, and only about 6 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings.

The terrain is the other factor. Its terrain is described as hilly and uneven, cut by small streams, and it sits at about 670 feet, noticeably higher than the towns to the east. Houses on hillsides, steep driveways and lake lots with little room between the water and the wall are a different job from a flat suburban lot.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Shrewsbury's postwar and 1970s houses make up much of the town, and many are ready for new siding. Vinyl works on them when it is installed loose enough to move with temperature and when the window and door flashing behind it is done properly. On a hillside lot, the downhill wall is often a full story taller than the uphill one. Ask how that elevation will be staged and whether the starter course will clear the grade everywhere.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The buildings around the Shrewsbury common are described in their National Register nomination as white clapboard, from the 1766 church to the Federal houses of the early 1800s. If your house is in the local historic district, which has existed since October 1972, visible exterior changes may need review first, so talk to the town before ordering material. Elsewhere, clapboard is a natural fit for the streetcar-era houses built between 1915 and 1940. For any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives a painted clapboard look with less upkeep, which suits Shrewsbury's mid-century and 1970s houses and some lakefront houses where wood paint fails quickly. The planks are heavy and need careful handling. On the town's hills and steep lots, staging and material storage take some planning. Correct clearances at the ground, decks and roof lines, and flashed joints, make the difference between a wall that lasts and one that swells at the edges.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: The lakeside cottages that summer residents built on Lake Quinsigamond are the kind of house where cedar shingles often look right. Shingles near water get more moisture and less sun on the shaded side, so a rainscreen gap and a clear finish plan, whether stained or left to weather, matter. On the higher, windier parts of town, fasteners and underlayment deserve as much attention as the shingles themselves.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: About 72 percent of Shrewsbury homes are owner-occupied single-family houses, and half were built before 1980, so many owners are now weighing a full re-side. Tear-off is the chance to see the sheathing, add insulation board and redo window flashing. Houses built before 1978 require lead-safe (RRP) practices once old paint is disturbed. Inside the Town Common local historic district, find out what approvals are needed before choosing materials.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Federal houses on the common, such as the Samuel Haven House with its fanlight and sidelights, show how much trim defines an older facade. Similar detail is worth preserving on any early house in town. On newer houses, the trim that fails first tends to be the water table, the window sills and the fascia boards behind the gutters. PVC or composite replacements cut down on repainting, provided they are flashed and fastened properly.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: At about 670 feet and with hilly terrain, Shrewsbury gets runoff that moves fast across lots and down driveways. Gutters and downspouts should be sized for the roof area and should send water away from foundations, especially on the uphill side of a house built into a slope. Near Lake Quinsigamond and in wooded neighborhoods, guards cut down on clogs. Seamless aluminum suits most houses. Wood gutters on older homes need fascia repairs first.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Higher ground means more snow load and ice at the eaves than on lower towns to the east, so ice-and-water membrane along the eaves and in valleys matters here. Many of the town's roughly 15,400 homes date from the 1970s and are on their second or third roof. A full tear-off allows the deck to be checked. Balanced intake and ridge venting helps limit ice dams, and on lake houses, wind exposure affects the shingle and nailing choice.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A storm-damaged section, a cracked vinyl panel or a few rotted boards at the base of a wall can often be repaired without re-siding the whole house. The repair should use matching material and fix whatever let the water in. In the Town Common local historic district, ask the town before replacing visible original material. A photo of the damage helps when you schedule the on-site look.

story: Marlborough was settled in 1657 by families from Sudbury and incorporated in 1660, but its housing reflects the shoe industry more than its colonial founding. Samuel Boyd and his brother Joseph opened the first shoe factory in 1836. By 1890 the town was a major shoe center of about 14,000 people and became a city that year. Rice & Hutchins ran factories from 1875 to 1929, and Frye boots were made here into the 1970s. The Marlborough Center Historic District along Main Street, between Mechanic Street and Route 85, holds the commercial center of that era. Most of its buildings are brick and stone and date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, alongside Queen Anne houses such as one on Prospect Street.

The housing numbers show that history. About 21 percent of the city's roughly 17,200 homes were built before 1940. About 17 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, and just 56 percent are owner-occupied. After that came a second boom. The population grew by almost half in the 1960s, and I-495, I-290 and the Mass Pike brought high-tech employers and office parks to areas such as the Southwest Quadrant. The median home was built in 1974.

The city sits at about 450 feet, with Lake Williams, Millham Reservoir and Fort Meadow Reservoir inside its limits and the Assabet crossing the northwest corner. French Hill, near the center, is one of the older named neighborhoods. A house in Marlborough may be a 19th-century multi-family near Main Street or a house from the 1960s boom, and the exterior work differs a lot between the two.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Much of Marlborough's housing went up during the 1960s growth spurt and the decades after, and vinyl is a common choice on those houses. In the city's two- to four-unit buildings, about 17 percent of all homes, vinyl can cover large walls economically. Porches, bays and stairways need careful detailing so water does not get behind the panels. Before installing, check the existing sheathing and flashing. Burying problems under new panels only postpones them.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: With about one in five homes built before 1940, Marlborough has more prewar wood houses than most of its neighbors. Many are close to the downtown shaped by the shoe factories. On those houses, new clapboard can match the original exposure and keep the corner boards and window casings in proportion. Any house built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules once painted surfaces are disturbed, and on multi-family buildings that includes protecting tenants during the work.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a good fit for Marlborough's older multi-family houses near the center, where owners want a painted wood look with less repainting. It also suits newer single-family houses in the outer neighborhoods. On tall walls and tight lots, the heavy boards need solid staging and dust-controlled cutting. Ask that clearances, butt-joint flashing and the paint system be written into the estimate. Those details decide how the siding holds up.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit gable ends, porches and upper stories on Marlborough's Queen Anne-era houses, which often mixed shingles with clapboard. Matching the original pattern when replacing sections, whether straight, staggered or fancy-cut, keeps the house's character. On a whole wall, shingles work best with a rainscreen gap and a decision up front about staining versus natural weathering. That matters more on shaded lots near the reservoirs.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full re-side on a Marlborough two- or three-family house means planning around tenants, porches and shared driveways as well as the walls. With only about 56 percent of homes owner-occupied, many of these jobs involve rental property. Tear-off reveals the condition of sheathing that may be a century old. On houses from before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply. Get the scope, debris handling and schedule in writing before work begins.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Late Victorian and Queen Anne houses around Marlborough Center depend on their trim: brackets, porch columns, window hoods and decorative boards. Rot in those parts can often be repaired by rebuilding the profile in wood or cellular PVC, rather than wrapping it in aluminum. On postwar houses, fascia, rakes and window sills are the usual failure points. Fixing them with the siding work saves a second round of staging.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Large multi-family roofs near downtown, sloped lots, and wooded areas around Lake Williams and the reservoirs each put different demands on gutters. Size the gutters and downspouts for the roof area, especially on big gable roofs, and make sure discharge does not flow onto a neighbor's lot or a shared driveway. Seamless aluminum suits most houses. Guards help where trees overhang.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Marlborough's roofs range from the steep, complex roofs of 19th-century houses to the lower-pitch roofs common on many postwar houses. Older roofs may have plank decking that needs sheathing before new shingles go on. Low slopes need extra underlayment. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys is standard practice. On multi-family buildings, the roof plan should cover porch roofs and dormers too.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A section of damaged siding, a rotted corner or a failing porch skirt can usually be fixed without re-siding the whole house. On older buildings, matching the existing material and exposure matters. Any repair should also deal with the source of the water, such as a gutter, flashing or splashback. On rental property, fixing small problems early usually costs less than a full re-side later.

story: Worcester grew fast after the Blackstone Canal opened in 1828 and the railroad to Boston arrived in 1835. The population rose from about 17,000 in 1850 to more than 195,000 by 1930. Much of that growth was housed in wood-frame three-deckers, a building type Worcester is considered the likely birthplace of. Three-deckers were mostly built between about 1870 and 1920, typically balloon-framed, with one apartment per floor, bay windows facing the street and stacked porches at the back. Worcester's sewer charges, based on street frontage, pushed builders toward narrow lots, which is why so many of them stand close together.

The numbers make Worcester different from the suburbs around it. Of about 85,900 housing units, roughly 41 percent were built before 1940, three in four before 1980, and the median year built is 1951. About a third are in two- to four-unit buildings, and only around 43 percent are owner-occupied. Neighborhoods such as Main South, Vernon Hill, Union Hill, Quinsigamond Village, Kelley Square and Shrewsbury Street were traditionally home to the immigrant communities that worked in the city's industries. The Worcester Historical Commission reviews changes in the local historic districts at Crown Hill, Massachusetts Avenue and Montvale.

The city is also hilly and snowy. It sits at about 480 feet, Tatnuck Hill is its highest point, and it averages around 64 inches of snow a season, with nor'easters a regular risk. For owners on a fixed income, the city's CDBG Elder Home Repair program offers grants to homeowners 62 and older with incomes at or below 80 percent of area median, for major systems including roofs, siding and windows, on owner-occupied one- to four-unit houses.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Re-siding a Worcester three-decker means three stories of wall, bays on every floor and porches to work around. On a narrow lot with a house a few feet away, staging and debris control take as much planning as the siding itself. Before new panels go on, check the sheathing at the bay windows and at porch connections, where water usually gets in. If the house is in a local historic district such as Crown Hill or Montvale, ask the Historical Commission first.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: With about 41 percent of its homes built before 1940, Worcester has a large stock of houses that started out in wood clapboard. On houses in the Crown Hill, Massachusetts Avenue or Montvale local historic districts, exterior changes are reviewed by the Worcester Historical Commission, so check before you change materials. For pre-1978 houses, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply whenever painted surfaces are disturbed. The city also runs a lead abatement program for qualifying owner-occupied homes with young children.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can give a three-decker or an older single-family house a painted lap look without the repainting schedule of wood. It is also less flammable than some older siding. Fire officials have pointed to petroleum-based shingle siding as one risk factor on older three-deckers. The boards are heavy, and three-story walls on tight lots need solid staging. Butt-joint flashing and clearances at porches and roof lines should be specified in the estimate.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles show up on Worcester's Victorian and early 20th-century houses in gables, porch walls and upper stories. When sections fail, matching the original course height and pattern keeps the facade consistent. On a full wall, shingles need a dry backing and good gutters above them. On a three-decker's tall, exposed walls, a rainscreen gap helps them dry after wind-driven rain.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full re-side on a Worcester multi-family building affects every apartment: windows, porches, utility lines and the yard all come into it. About a third of the city's homes are in two- to four-unit buildings. Owners 62 and older who live in a one- to four-unit house and meet the income limit may qualify for the city's CDBG Elder Home Repair grants, which cover siding, roofing and windows. Under that program, the city bids the job out and pays the contractor directly. For pre-1978 buildings, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The trim on a three-decker does a lot of work: the bay windows, the cornice, the porch columns and rails on every level. Rot tends to start where porch floors meet the wall and at the bottoms of bay window panels. Rebuilding those parts in wood or cellular PVC, with proper flashing, often matters more than the siding choice. In local historic districts, keep the original profiles.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Worcester averages around 64 inches of snow a season, and many of its houses are on hills, which makes heavy-duty gutters and solid fascia important. Three-deckers with flat or low-slope roofs may drain through internal drains or scuppers rather than standard gutters, and those need to be checked before replacing anything. On narrow lots, run downspouts so the water does not spill onto a neighbor's house or a shared driveway.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Heavy snow and nor'easters make the roof the first line of defense on a Worcester house. On the city's many three-deckers, flat or low-slope roofs call for membrane roofing rather than shingles. Gabled and hipped roofs need full ice-and-water protection at the eaves. Older houses may have plank decking or several layers to remove. Income-eligible owners 62 and older can look into the city's Elder Home Repair grants, which list roofs among the covered systems.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: On older Worcester houses, a few failed boards, a damaged corner or a loose section of vinyl can often be fixed without re-siding. Repairs on houses built before 1978 involve lead-safe work rules. Fixing the cause, such as a leaking porch roof or gutter, keeps the problem from coming back. On a three-decker, upper-story repairs may need ladders or staging even for a small patch, so ask about access when you schedule.

story: Fitchburg grew up along the Nashua River as a water-powered mill city. Through the 19th century its mills turned out machines, tools, clothing, paper and firearms, and in the early 20th century paper mills lined the riverbanks and drew workers from across Europe. Much of the city's housing dates from those decades: Census figures put the median year built at about 1950, with roughly 43 percent of homes built before 1940 and close to 80 percent before 1980. The city is known for Victorian architecture built at the height of that mill-town prosperity, and the Monument Park Historic District, about 10 acres beside Main Street, still holds a concentrated group of 19th- and early 20th-century buildings.

This is also a city of shared buildings. About 31 percent of its roughly 17,700 housing units sit in two- to four-unit structures, and only about 54 percent are owner-occupied, so a typical exterior project here may involve several households, a landlord and tenants, and a narrow side yard against the next lot. Neighborhoods such as Cleghorn, Crockerville, The Patch, Tar Hill, Upper Common, South Fitchburg and West Fitchburg each have their own street pattern, and the terrain is far from flat: the city averages about 470 feet in elevation and rises to roughly 1,210 feet at Brown Hill near the northwest corner.

For an older Fitchburg house, the work usually starts with what is under the current siding. Decades of layering, repainting and patching are common on buildings this age, and because the large majority predate 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices apply whenever painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With so many two- to four-unit buildings and rental properties in the city, vinyl is often chosen because it takes painting off the maintenance schedule. On a tall multi-family wall, the details that matter are a flat, sound substrate, enough room in the nailing slots for expansion on long runs, and properly flashed J-channel around every window. A building of that age may carry more than one earlier layer of siding underneath; it is worth deciding before ordering material whether to strip to the sheathing or install over, because that choice affects trim depth and window returns.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard was a standard cladding in the decades when much of Fitchburg was built. Where original clapboard survives in decent shape, replacing only the failed courses and matching the exposure keeps the wall consistent. When a full wall needs new clapboard, back-primed boards, a rain-screen gap behind them and careful corner and casing details give paint a better chance of lasting. Plan for RRP lead-safe practices on any pre-1978 painted wall before scraping or removing boards.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners who want a painted-wood look on an older Fitchburg house without wood's upkeep. It is heavier than vinyl, so on tall walls with tight side yards, staging and material handling need planning before the first board goes up. Cut edges should be sealed, clearances above roofs and grade kept per the manufacturer, and the trim plan settled early, since fiber cement on a Victorian facade looks right only when the corner boards, frieze and window casings are sized to match the building's proportions.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Queen Anne design, a style represented in the Monument Park district, often used cedar shingles in decorative bands or gable ends above clapboard lower floors. Replacing patterned shingle sections means matching the exposure and cut (fishscale, diamond, straight) so the repair reads as original. On a full shingle wall, a breathable underlayment and stainless or hot-dipped nails help the shingles weather evenly. Gables on tall Victorian buildings can sit high off the ground, so safe access is part of the plan.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a Fitchburg two- or three-family building is a larger job than on a single-family house: more wall area, more windows and doors, and often tenants who need access throughout. Taking siding off usually reveals the real condition of sills, sheathing and window framing, and on buildings from the early 1900s some rot repair should be budgeted. A written estimate that separates siding, trim and contingency carpentry makes it easier to compare bids. Pre-1978 painted surfaces fall under EPA RRP rules.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is where Fitchburg's mill-era houses carry their character: deep cornices, porch columns and railings, window hoods and brackets. These parts take the most weather and are often the first to rot. Where original profiles can be saved, repairing with matching milled stock is usually better than wrapping in flat aluminum, which hides decay and flattens the detail. Cellular PVC can replace rotted sections where they stay painted. Porch floors and stair stringers on multi-unit buildings deserve close inspection whenever trim work is done.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Many older Fitchburg buildings have wide eaves, porches stacked on multiple floors and roofs that drain toward a shared side yard or driveway. Gutters and downspouts should carry water away from foundations and walkways, not dump it onto a neighbor's lot or a lower porch roof. On hillside streets, downspout placement needs to account for grade so water does not run back toward the house. Older built-in or wood gutters, where present, should be checked for leaks into the cornice before deciding to replace or line them.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With the city rising from the Nashua River valley to about 1,210 feet at Brown Hill, homes on higher streets can see more snow and wind than those near downtown. Ice-and-water membrane at the eaves and valleys, solid ventilation and attention to porch-roof tie-ins all matter on older multi-story buildings. Tall, steep roofs on Victorian-era houses also make staging and fall protection a real part of the cost. Removing old layers lets the decking be inspected rather than assumed sound.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repair makes sense when damage is limited: a few split clapboards, a loose vinyl course, or rot around one window. The goal is to match the existing material and exposure and to find and fix the water source so the patch does not fail again. On pre-1978 painted wood, lead-safe practices apply. On a multi-unit building, check the walls next to porches and stairs as well, since those are where splash and snow sit longest.

story: Douglas is a hill town on the Rhode Island and Connecticut line, sitting about 580 feet above sea level, and a large share of its land is woods and water. Douglas State Forest covers about 5,525 acres in the southwest corner and includes Wallum Lake. Whitin Reservoir, at about 400 acres, lies to the west, with Badluck Pond nearby and Manchaug Pond to the north. Outside the old centers, much of the town is woodland.

Two older centers anchor the town. The Old Douglas Center Historic District, listed on the National Register in 2001, takes in about 192 acres around the common and Center Cemetery, with houses mostly in the Federal and Greek Revival styles alongside the 1834 First Congregational Church. About a mile east, East Douglas grew along Main Street and the Mumford River and became the town's economic center in the 1830s. The Hayward Mill there, a woolen mill whose present building dates from 1880, has been converted to housing.

Most of the town is much newer than those centers. Douglas had fewer than 3,000 residents in 1970 and nearly doubled by 1990, and Census data puts the median home at about 1986, with only around 22 percent of homes built before 1940. About 84 percent of the roughly 3,500 housing units are owner-occupied, and few are in multi-family buildings. In practice that means many homes approaching their first or second siding and roof replacement, often on wooded lots where shade, leaf litter and pine needles shape how the exterior wears.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A lot of Douglas housing went up during the 1970s-to-1990s growth period, and many of those homes are now on their original siding. When re-siding them, check the sheathing under the old material, especially on shaded north walls near the forest where moisture lingers. Choose a vinyl profile and color that holds up to strong summer sun on open lots, and plan the mildew-prone shady sides with good drainage behind the panels. Insulated vinyl is an option where walls were built with minimal insulation.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard fits the older houses around the town common, where the historic district is made up largely of Federal and Greek Revival buildings, and the older streets of East Douglas. Matching the original reveal and corner treatment keeps a repair or new wall in character. On new or newer homes in wooded settings, wood clapboard should be back-primed and installed over a drainage gap, since walls that see little direct sun stay damp longer and paint can fail early. Plan RRP lead-safe practices on any pre-1978 painted surface.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement handles shaded, damp walls better than bare wood and does not rot or attract insects the way wood can on wooded lots. It is a good fit for owners of 1980s and 1990s homes who want a painted look without wood maintenance. Installation details matter: keep the bottom course clear of soil and mulch, maintain clearance above roof lines, and flash windows carefully. Factory-finished boards cut down on the repainting cycle.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit lakeside and wooded homes around Wallum Lake, Whitin Reservoir and Manchaug Pond, where a natural finish fits the setting. Shade and lake moisture can encourage moss and mildew, so a breathable underlayment, good spacing between shingles and trimming back overhanging branches help them dry out. Stainless fasteners are worth the cost. Expect shingles on shaded walls to weather differently from sunny sides; a bleaching oil or semi-transparent stain can even out the look.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement often comes up on Douglas houses from the 1970s through the early 1990s, when original siding, trim and windows tend to wear out together. Stripping to the sheathing allows a look at framing, adding a weather-resistive barrier and fixing window flashing that may not meet current practice. On older houses in the historic center or East Douglas, replacement is a bigger decision: original materials and profiles carry the character of the building, and pre-1978 paint brings RRP rules into play.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On Federal and Greek Revival houses near the old common, trim is the defining feature: wide corner boards, entablatures and doorway surrounds. Repairs should match those profiles. On newer homes, rot most often shows at the bottom of corner boards, around garage door jambs and along fascia under gutters that overflow with leaves. Cellular PVC trim resists moisture on shaded walls, and keeping the bottom edge of trim above grade and mulch beds helps it last.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With a state forest of about 5,525 acres and wooded land across town, homes near the forest or along the ponds deal with leaves, pine needles and seed pods for much of the year. Gutter guards matched to the type of debris, larger downspouts and downspout outlets that move water away from foundations on sloped lots all help. On shaded roofs, snow and ice linger longer at the eaves, so gutters should be firmly hung with hidden hangers spaced closely enough to carry that weight.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: At around 580 feet with hills over 700 feet, Douglas gets plenty of snow, and tree cover keeps many roofs shaded and slow to dry. Moss and algae on north slopes are common in wooded settings, so algae-resistant shingles and good attic ventilation are worth considering. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys is standard practice here. Before installation, overhanging limbs should be trimmed back to cut down on debris and damage from falling branches.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repair is the right call for limited damage such as a cracked panel, a section hit by a falling branch or a localized soft spot. Match the existing material, find where the water got in, and fix that first. For pre-1978 painted wood, follow lead-safe practices. If the damage came from a tree, it is a good moment to look at other limbs hanging over the house and the roof edge above the repair.

story: Groton was settled in 1655, burned in the raids of King Philip's War and rebuilt with garrisons, and its town center still gathers around the common, First Parish Church and Gibbet Hill. Main Street holds older civic and residential buildings such as the Gov. George S. Boutwell House and the former Groton High School at 145 Main Street, which later housed Prescott Elementary. The Groton School, founded in 1884, sits on Farmers Row, and Lawrence Academy dates to 1793. In West Groton the Hollingsworth family acquired a paper mill in the early 1800s, and the former Groton Leatherboard Company building at 6 West Main Street is now senior living.

Much of today's housing is more recent. Groton's population nearly quadrupled between 1950 and 2020, with the biggest jumps around 1960 and 2000, and Census data puts the median home at about 1988. Only around 17 percent of homes predate 1940, about 89 percent of the roughly 3,800 units are owner-occupied, and few are in multi-family buildings. The Nashua and Squannacook rivers drain the town, and a large share of its land is protected open space, so many newer homes sit on wooded lots.

Exterior work in the town center has an extra step. Groton has a Historic Districts Commission set up under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40C, and its minutes show it reviewing visible projects on Main Street and Farmers Row, from a new barn's roofing and trim to porch lattice on a Main Street house, while setting aside work that cannot be seen. Owners near the center should check with the commission before planning visible exterior changes.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl fits many of Groton's homes built during the late-20th-century growth, especially on wooded lots away from the center. On those houses, the main questions are the condition of the sheathing, how windows were flashed originally, and whether to add insulation board while the walls are open. For houses inside the historic districts along Main Street or Farmers Row, talk with the Historic Districts Commission before choosing vinyl, since it reviews visible changes to building exteriors there.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Older houses on Main Street, Farmers Row and in West Groton were typically clad in wood clapboard, and on visible walls in the historic districts, matching original materials carries weight with the commission. Commission minutes record one Main Street owner uncovering an original gable detail while removing siding, a reminder that stripping an old wall can reveal features worth keeping. Back-primed boards, matching exposure and careful corner work help new clapboard blend with old. RRP lead-safe practices apply to pre-1978 paint.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a practical choice for Groton's newer homes on wooded, shaded lots where wood siding stays damp and paint wears quickly. It holds paint well and resists rot and insects. Keep the bottom courses clear of grade and mulch, flash every penetration, and seal cut ends. On houses in the historic districts, ask the commission early whether fiber cement is acceptable on visible walls, since material and profile both affect how a facade reads from the street.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Groton's wooded setting and homes near Lost Lake or the river corridors, where a natural weathered finish fits. Shaded walls can grow mildew or moss, so a breathable underlayment, stainless fasteners and some pruning of overhanging trees help the wall dry. Expect north and south sides to weather at different rates unless a finish is applied. Leaving a gap between the lowest course and the ground keeps splash-back off the bottom row.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Many homes from Groton's growth decades are now reaching the age where original siding, trim and windows tend to be replaced together. Removing everything to the sheathing allows a real inspection of the framing, a proper weather barrier and current window flashing. For older houses in the center, full replacement is a bigger decision, both because original materials carry historic value and because visible changes in the districts are reviewed by the commission. Pre-1978 painted surfaces fall under EPA RRP rules.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is often the focus of historic district review in Groton: commission minutes show members asking for window trim and roof trim details on a new barn on Farmers Row. On older houses, porch columns, cornices and window casings should be repaired to match the original profiles where possible. On newer homes, fascia and rake boards under overflowing gutters and corner boards near the ground are the usual problem spots, and cellular PVC holds up well on shaded walls.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With much of Groton wooded and a large share of land kept as open space, most homes deal with leaf fall and pine needles. Gutter guards matched to the debris, wide downspouts and outlets that move water away from foundations are worth the effort. Homes near Lost Lake or the Nashua and Squannacook rivers should also watch where roof water ends up on the lot. Downspouts should not discharge onto walkways or driveways where the water can freeze.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Wooded lots keep many Groton roofs shaded, so moss, algae and slow snowmelt at the eaves are common. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, balanced attic ventilation and algae-resistant shingles all fit these conditions. For homes in the historic districts, roofing material is a visible feature; commission minutes show it reviewing a roofing material choice on Farmers Row. Trimming limbs back from the roof before installation helps protect a new roof from debris.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repair suits limited damage: a split board, a panel cracked by a falling branch, or rot near one window or door. Match the existing material and reveal, and fix the source of water. Pre-1978 painted wood needs lead-safe practices. On houses in the town center's historic districts, keeping a repair to matching material and profile also keeps it in line with what is already on the building.
