story: Ayer is a railroad town. Before it was incorporated in 1871, this corner of Groton was called Groton Junction and later Ayer Junction, the spot where the Fitchburg Railroad (1844) crossed lines built in 1848, including the Worcester and Nashua and the Peterborough and Shirley. The downtown shows it. The Ayer Main Street Historic District, which runs between Park and Columbia streets, was built mostly between 1872 and 1898, after an 1872 fire cleared away many earlier structures. Its buildings are nearly all brick and stone, with only three in wood frame, and its Italianate and Second Empire storefronts lead east to a Victorian Gothic town hall paid for by Dr. James Cook Ayer.

The other force behind local building was the Army. Camp Devens opened in 1917, became Fort Devens, and shaped the town's commerce until the base closed in 1996. The Fort Devens Historic District extends into Ayer and Harvard. Its core is a group of Georgian Revival buildings from 1929 to 1939 set around a parade ground, with rows of single-family housing toward Auman Avenue. Water is never far off: the Nashua River, Nonacoicus Brook, where a mill hamlet stood in 1667, and Sandy and Long ponds.

Census figures put Ayer at about 3,900 housing units with a median build year of 1977. About 21 percent of homes predate 1940 and about 54 percent predate 1980. One home in five sits in a building with two to four units, and roughly 69 percent are owner-occupied. That means a fair number of rental and small multi-family buildings, where coordinating with tenants and planning work around several entrances is part of any exterior job.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With about a fifth of Ayer's homes in two-to-four-unit buildings, vinyl often comes up on rental and small multi-family houses, where whoever pays for upkeep wants less of it. On those buildings the weak points are usually the many window and door openings and the joints where porches meet the wall, so flashing at each opening deserves the closest attention in an estimate. Just over half the town's homes predate 1980, and for houses built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply once old painted surfaces are disturbed during tear-off.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard is the in-kind choice for wood-frame houses dating from the decades after the junction took off in the 1870s. Before material is ordered, the existing reveal, meaning the exposed width of each board, should be measured so new boards line up with any sections that stay. Boards should be primed on all sides, including cut ends, and finish-painted soon after they go up. Leaving new clapboard unpainted for a season is one of the most common reasons it cups and checks early.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement fits the later part of Ayer's housing, where the median home dates to the late 1970s, for owners who want a painted-board look with longer repaint intervals. The boards are heavy and are cut with dust control, so staging room on tight in-town lots should be sorted out at the assessment. The manufacturer's clearances from roof lines, decks and finished grade should be kept, and that matters most on low, damp ground near the Nashua River or the ponds, where the bottom course takes splash and standing snow.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles have no place on the brick and stone blocks of Main Street, but they can suit a wood-frame house in a leafy setting near Sandy or Long Pond. Shaded, damp walls are where shingles struggle, so an airspace or rainscreen mat behind them helps them dry. The finish should be decided up front: stain, primer and paint, or bare wood left to weather. When new shingles patch into old, expect a visible color difference for a few seasons before the new wood catches up.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement is the chance to see what the old cladding has been hiding. On the roughly one in five Ayer homes built before 1940, that may mean board sheathing with gaps, missing insulation, or window frames that have shifted over the years. On houses from the 1970s, damaged sheathing edges around openings are more typical. Once siding comes off, the sheathing should be checked, and any repairs should appear as separate line items in the written estimate so the owner knows what was found and why it was fixed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Ayer's downtown grew up in the Italianate and Second Empire years, styles that rely on cornices, brackets and window hoods. On older wood-frame houses with that kind of detail, rotted pieces are best rebuilt to the same profile rather than replaced with flat boards, and an unusual molding can often be assembled from stock pieces. Cellular PVC is a sensible substitute at the spots that rot first, such as the bottoms of door casings and corner boards, where rain splashes back off steps and the ground.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lots near Sandy Pond, Long Pond and the river corridors that carry heavy tree cover drop leaves and needles that fill gutters quickly. Larger downspouts, or guards suited to the kind of debris, cut down on overflow. Downspouts should discharge well away from the foundation, especially on low ground near the Nashua River or Nonacoicus Brook. On multi-unit buildings with several doors and stairs, the gutter layout should keep roof water off steps and walkways, where it can freeze into ice in winter.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Roofs vary across Ayer's mix of late-1800s buildings near the old junction and houses from the 1970s and later, and an older roof may carry more than one layer of shingles. A full tear-off shows the deck's condition, and soft or delaminated boards should be replaced before the new roof goes on. Ice-and-water membrane belongs at eaves and valleys. Multi-family houses often carry several dormers, chimneys and porch roofs, and each one is a flashing detail that should be renewed rather than reused.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repair makes sense when a wall is mostly sound and the damage is local: a cracked vinyl panel, a split clapboard, a bumped corner. The main difficulty is matching an older or discontinued profile and color, and the free on-site assessment is the time to find out whether a match exists or whether the whole wall should be redone. When damage keeps returning to the same spot, the cause, often a leaking gutter or missing kick-out flashing, should be fixed first.

story: Oxford sits in a valley, and much of the town lies in the flood plain of the French River. The river is named for the French Protestants (Huguenots) who settled here in 1687, and the remains of the fort they built in 1694 survive near Huguenot Road. The town was incorporated in 1713. North and west of Oxford Center, a large tract is held by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for flood control. The Hodges Village Dam on the French River, finished in 1959 after the 1936 floods, anchors that land, which also serves as the Greenbriar nature preserve. The river passes through Hodges Village, and North Oxford, along Route 20, has its own ZIP code.

The town center is the Oxford Main Street Historic District, listed on the National Register in 2011. It covers 95 acres along Main Street from Huguenot Street to Front Street. Its houses are Federal and Greek Revival, with Greek Revival the most common. They share the street with the John Wetherell Store of about 1817, the 1793 Universalist church, the 1829 First Congregational Church and the 1903 Charles Larned Memorial Library. On a street like this, siding and trim choices are easy to see from the sidewalk.

Census estimates count about 5,200 housing units, with a median build year of 1972. About 19 percent predate 1940 and about 61 percent predate 1980, so roughly four homes in ten date from the 1940s through the 1970s. About 83 percent are owner-occupied, and about 12 percent are in two-to-four-unit buildings. Much of the housing now needs its first or second round of exterior replacement.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: For the mid-century houses that make up a large share of Oxford's stock, vinyl is often the practical replacement for worn wood or older aluminum siding. Window and door openings need new flashing tied into the housewrap, not old trim reused as a nailing base. Around 61 percent of homes here predate 1980, and for those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when old painted siding or trim is disturbed. On Main Street's older facades, the profile and the width of the corner boards make the biggest difference to how vinyl looks.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Federal and Greek Revival houses on Main Street were built for painted wood clapboard, and it remains the in-kind material for them. Greek Revival houses often have wide corner boards and a deep frieze under the eaves, and new clapboard should keep those proportions instead of crowding them. Boards should be back-primed and installed over a drainage layer. Where an old wall has only a few failed boards, selective replacement can keep most of the original wood in place.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits Oxford owners who want the lines of painted clapboard on a 1950s through 1970s house with less frequent repainting. The material needs clearance above finished grade and above roof surfaces, and on low lots in the French River valley that bottom clearance is worth checking carefully. Cutting produces silica dust, so it should be done outdoors with dust control. Factory-primed or prefinished boards should have cut ends sealed so moisture does not wick in.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are less typical in a center dominated by Greek Revival clapboard, but they can work on a gable, an addition or a house in a wooded part of town. On damp, low ground in the river valley, a rainscreen behind the shingles helps the wood dry from both sides. A stain or treatment applied before installation protects the back faces. The finish choice should be settled at the start, because an opaque stain, a semi-transparent stain and natural weathering each lead to a different maintenance schedule.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Oxford's stock spans from early-1800s houses on Main Street to the postwar decades, and a full replacement uncovers very different conditions depending on age. Older walls may have plank sheathing and no insulation, while mid-century houses may have fiberboard sheathing that has softened around openings. Every exposed wall should be inspected before new material goes on, and rotted sills or sheathing should be repaired then, not covered. The written estimate should spell out how that hidden repair work will be priced.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Greek Revival houses carry much of their character in the trim: wide pilasters at the corners, a broad frieze board, and door surrounds with sidelights. On the houses that line Main Street, rotted trim should be rebuilt to the original dimensions rather than narrowed to standard lumber sizes. Where the trim sits near grade or under a dripping eave, cellular PVC or a primed, rot-resistant wood is a sensible choice. Fresh caulk and paint at every joint keep water out of the end grain.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Because much of Oxford lies in the French River's flood plain, getting roof water away from the house matters more here than in hillier towns. Downspouts should run to extensions, splash blocks or a drainage system that carries water away from the foundation, not let it pool by basement walls. Gutters should be sized for the roof area they drain. Wooded lots will need guards or regular cleaning, and seamless aluminum cuts down on the joints that leak.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Oxford's mix of 19th-century houses in the center and the many homes built from the 1940s through the 1970s means roofs vary widely in age and pitch. On lower-pitched roofs, ice-and-water membrane should be carried well up from the eaves. A tear-off is the time to check the deck, replace soft boards and confirm the attic is properly vented. Chimneys and dormers on older houses need new step and counter flashing rather than reused metal.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A repair is worth considering when the damage is confined to one area: a few boards, a damaged corner, or panels cracked by a branch. Finding a matching profile and color for older vinyl or wood siding is often the hardest part, and the free on-site assessment can establish whether a clean match is possible. If moisture caused the damage, the source should be found and corrected before patching, or the new material will fail the same way.

story: Concord was settled in 1635 as the first inland colonial settlement in New England, and Monument Square was laid out that same year. The Concord Monument Square-Lexington Road Historic District extends from the square to the southeast and northwest. It contains well-preserved houses in Georgian, Federal and mid-19th-century revival styles, along with Wright's Tavern and the Ralph Waldo Emerson House. Lexington Road also has several historic houses of its own, and the town keeps Orchard House, home of the Alcotts from 1858, and The Wayside. Minute Man National Historical Park follows Route 2A toward Lexington. In parts of town like these, an exterior job is judged as much by what it keeps as by what it adds.

Water and open land shape the rest of town. The Sudbury and Assabet rivers meet near the center to form the Concord River, and there are kettle holes and low marshes as well as Walden Pond, Great Meadows National Wildlife Refuge and Estabrook Woods. West Concord, a village of its own, sits on the Assabet with Route 62 as its Main Street, Warners Pond to the north and Kennedys Pond to the southwest. Its railroad depot, Union Station on Commonwealth Avenue, is on the National Register. From 1835 to 1940, gunpowder was made at the American Powder Mills along the Assabet.

Census estimates count about 7,000 homes, with a median build year of 1969. Roughly 23 percent predate 1940 and about 65 percent predate 1980. About 76 percent are owner-occupied, and only about 8 percent are in two-to-four-unit buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is most at home on Concord's postwar and later houses, which make up a large part of a stock whose median home dates to 1969. In the historic districts along Lexington Road and around Monument Square, the look of a facade carries more weight, and any change in material should be checked with the town first. About two-thirds of homes predate 1980; on those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted wood is disturbed. A wider-profile panel and real-wood-sized trim keep vinyl from looking thin.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Georgian and Federal houses like those around Monument Square were built with painted wood clapboard, and replacing in kind keeps their proportions intact. Original boards are often narrower than modern stock, so the reveal should be measured and matched, especially where new and old boards meet on the same wall. Quartersawn or vertical-grain clapboard holds paint longer than flat-sawn boards. Each board should be primed on all faces and laid over a drainage plane so the wall can dry.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives the look of painted clapboard on mid-century homes, and on additions where an owner wants long paint life. Choose a lap width that matches the main house so an addition does not stand out. In historic districts, any substitute material should be cleared with the town before it is specified. The boards need clearance from grade, decks and roofs, and on wet lots near the rivers or the Great Meadows marshes, that bottom gap helps keep the lowest course dry.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit wooded settings, such as houses near Estabrook Woods or Walden Pond, and older outbuildings and additions where a natural finish fits. Shaded walls under heavy tree cover stay damp longer, so shingles there benefit from an airspace behind them and from stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails that will not streak. Before work starts, decide whether to stain, paint or let them weather. Where a historic house already has shingles, the exposure and the coursing of the old shingles should be copied exactly.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: About a quarter of Concord's homes date from before 1940, and on those a full replacement usually exposes board sheathing, gaps around old window frames and little or no insulation in the walls. Postwar homes bring their own issues, such as soft sheathing at corners and under windows. Every opening should be re-flashed while the walls are open. For houses in or near the historic districts, it is wise to document the original trim and siding details before removal so they can be reproduced.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On a Georgian or Federal house, the trim carries much of the design: cornices, pedimented doorways, corner boards and window casings. Replacing rotted pieces with profiles milled to match keeps a house in line with the character of streets like Lexington Road. Damage tends to cluster where water collects: sills, the lower ends of corner boards and the tops of window heads. Repairing those with durable wood or cellular PVC and re-sealing joints extends the life of the paint.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Big trees and open woodland are part of Concord's landscape, and lots near Walden Pond, Estabrook Woods or the river corridors can fill gutters quickly. Guards matched to the debris, and downspouts large enough to keep up, reduce overflow. On low ground near the Sudbury, Assabet and Concord rivers, downspouts should carry water well clear of the foundation. On older houses with built-in or wood gutters, repairing or relining in place can preserve the original appearance.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Concord's housing includes colonial-era houses in the historic districts and a large number of homes from the 1950s through the 1970s, so roofs differ widely in pitch, complexity and age. On historic houses, the roofing color and texture is part of the streetscape and deserves careful selection. Any re-roof should include ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, new flashing at chimneys and dormers, and a check of attic ventilation. Overhanging branches should be trimmed back before new shingles go down.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A targeted repair can be the right choice when a wall is sound and the problem is local: a few split boards, a damaged corner or rot under a window sill. The challenge is matching an older profile, exposure or color. On historic houses, repairing original material is often better than replacing it. The free on-site assessment can determine whether a matching repair is practical, and any underlying cause, such as a leaky gutter or poor flashing, should be corrected first.

story: Weston's rocky ground never suited large-scale farming, and it had few sites for water power. From the 1860s, wealthy families built country estates here, and by 1900 the town was being described as a country town of first-class residences. That era left the fieldstone First Parish Church of 1888, the first library of 1899, the 1914 central fire station and the 1917 town hall. After World War II, construction of Route 128 and the Massachusetts Turnpike led to the subdivision of former estates and farms, and a 1950s zoning bylaw raised the minimum amount of land needed to build. Many of those postwar single-family houses are now being replaced by much larger ones.

The older town survives in its historic districts. The Boston Post Road Historic District follows Route 20 for about three and a half miles past the Golden Ball Tavern of 1763 and Josiah Smith's tavern of 1757, with widely spaced properties at either end. Along North Avenue, the Kendal Green Historic District includes the Whitney Tavern of about 1707, houses built by the Hobbs tanning family, and houses built by the Hook and Hastings organ company for its factory workers. Other National Register districts include Case's Corner, Silver Hill and Glen Road, and the town also has a local historic district. More than 2,000 acres are parks, fields, wetlands and forest, and the town has 37 designated scenic roads.

Census estimates count about 4,000 homes, with a median build year of 1964. About 23 percent predate 1940 and about 65 percent predate 1980. Roughly 88 percent are owner-occupied, and only about 2 or 3 percent sit in two-to-four-unit buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl can make sense on garages, outbuildings or postwar houses where an owner wants minimal upkeep. Premium thicker panels, real-wood-width trim and careful color selection keep it from looking out of place on streets with wood-sided neighbors. About two-thirds of Weston's homes predate 1980; on those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed. In historic districts, any change in material should be checked with the town first.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Painted clapboard ties together much of Weston's older housing, from the taverns on Boston Post Road to the Hobbs family and organ-worker houses along North Avenue in Kendal Green. When boards are replaced, the new ones should copy the old exposure and thickness so the coursing lines up across a wall. Vertical-grain wood takes and keeps paint best. Back-priming and an air gap or drainage mat behind the boards help them stay flat on shaded walls under mature trees.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits Weston owners who want the look of painted clapboard with longer repaint intervals. On a large house, the weight and length of the boards make careful staging and handling part of the plan. Lap width and trim proportions should be chosen to suit the style of the house. The boards need clearance from grade, roofs and decks, and cut ends should be sealed with the manufacturer's recommended primer or paint.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Weston's wooded lots and estate-era houses, where natural materials fit the semi-rural setting of its scenic roads. Shaded walls under mature trees stay damp longer, so a rainscreen gap and stainless or hot-dipped galvanized fasteners help shingles last. Settle early on whether they will be stained, painted or left to weather. On houses with original shingle work, such as decorative courses or flared bottoms, those details should be reproduced rather than simplified.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Weston's stock ranges from 18th-century houses to postwar homes built after Route 128 opened, and a full replacement exposes different problems in each. Older walls may have plank sheathing and no insulation; houses from the 1950s through the 1970s may have softened sheathing around windows and at corners. All exposed sheathing should be inspected and repaired before new siding goes on. On larger houses, the work should be sequenced elevation by elevation so walls are not left open to weather.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim does a great deal of the work on a Georgian or Federal facade: cornices, door surrounds, corner boards and window casings. On houses in the Boston Post Road or Kendal Green districts, rotted pieces should be replaced with matching profiles rather than flat stock. Water damage tends to start at window sills, the bottoms of corner boards and porch posts. Durable wood species or cellular PVC at those points, with joints sealed and painted, reduce repeat repairs.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With more than 2,000 acres of forest, fields and wetland and many wooded lots, leaves and needles are a major gutter issue in Weston. Guards suited to the trees overhead and larger downspouts help, and downspouts should carry water well away from foundations. On large houses with complex roofs, valleys concentrate water at certain corners, and gutter size should reflect that. Older houses with wood or built-in gutters may be better served by repairing and relining them than by switching to aluminum.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: The much larger houses now replacing many of Weston's postwar homes tend to bring bigger roofs, and every valley, dormer and chimney on a roof like that is a flashing detail that needs care. On older houses in the historic districts, roofing color and texture matter to the streetscape. Ice-and-water membrane belongs at eaves, valleys and around penetrations, and attic ventilation should be checked during any re-roof. Overhanging branches on wooded lots should be cut back to reduce debris and abrasion.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: On a house with a few rotted boards beside an otherwise healthy wall, such as an early house along North Avenue or a 1960s home off a scenic road, patching is usually cheaper and keeps more original fabric than re-siding. Success depends on finding stock that matches the old exposure and thickness, then feathering paint so the patch disappears. The free on-site assessment is where that match gets checked. Water that caused the rot, from a sill, a gutter end or a missing flashing, has to be stopped before the new boards go in.

story: Millis was East Medway until 1885, when Lansing Millis, a railroad entrepreneur, led the push to incorporate it as its own town. The Great Black Swamp had always divided it from Medway, and the railroad made the split practical. The Millis Center Historic District, listed in 2007, covers 110 acres along Curve, Daniels, Exchange, Irving, Lavender, Main and Union streets. Most of its buildings date from after 1850, in Late Victorian and later revival styles, and only four houses are older. The oldest is the John Richardson House at 191 Curve Street, a mid-18th-century Georgian colonial. The district also includes two 19th-century industrial complexes and a residential area north of Main Street, which began as the Hartford and Dedham Turnpike.

Industry left its own place names. The Clicquot Club, on Main Street, gave its name to the village of Clicquot. In the west of town, Causeway Street was a center for clay and sand digging, and its brickyards supplied bricks for large estates in the area. Heather's Pond is a former clay pit. The Charles River runs through town, and Bogastow Brook flows into South End Pond. Older survivors include Richardson's Tavern, built about 1720, and the Ellice School, a Greek Revival building from about 1849.

Census estimates count about 3,500 homes. Only about 13 percent predate 1940, but about 61 percent predate 1980, which means much of Millis was built in the decades after World War II. The median build year is 1974. About 83 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and about 14 percent are in two-to-four-unit buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Much of Millis was built between the 1940s and the 1970s, and on houses from those decades vinyl is a common replacement for worn wood, cedar or aluminum siding. The key details are new flashing at windows and doors and trim that is sized to look like real wood, so the house does not look flat. About 61 percent of homes predate 1980, and for those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed during removal.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Painted wood clapboard is the in-kind material for the Late Victorian houses around Exchange, Curve and Union streets in the historic center. New boards should match the original exposure, and decorative details such as corner boards and frieze should keep their original size. Boards should be primed on all faces and installed over a drainage layer, then painted promptly. Where only a few boards have failed, selective replacement can keep most of an old wall intact.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits Millis's many postwar and 1970s houses when an owner wants painted-board looks with longer repaint intervals. The boards need clearance from grade and roofs, and on low lots near the Charles River, Bogastow Brook or the Great Black Swamp, keeping that bottom gap helps prevent moisture problems. Cutting must be done with dust control. The heavier boards and longer lengths should be considered when planning staging on smaller lots near the town center.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit houses on wooded or wetland-edge lots, where a natural finish blends with the landscape. Shade and damp air near the swamp or ponds slow drying, so an airspace behind the shingles and corrosion-resistant fasteners are worth specifying. Decide up front whether they will be stained, painted or left to weather, since each choice sets a different maintenance cycle. New shingles patched into old ones will look different until the new wood weathers.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With most Millis homes built between the 1940s and the 1970s, a full replacement often reveals mid-century sheathing, sometimes softened at window corners and along the bottom of walls. On the smaller group of 19th-century houses in the center, plank sheathing and uninsulated walls are more likely. All sheathing should be inspected once the old siding is off, and repairs should be listed separately in the written estimate. Re-flashing every window and door is a key part of the job.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Late Victorian houses in the historic center rely on trim for their character: brackets, window hoods, porch posts and decorative bands. Those pieces should be repaired or replaced with matching profiles rather than flat boards. On postwar houses, the trim is usually simpler, and the main issue is rot at the bottoms of door casings, corner boards and garage door jambs. Cellular PVC at those spots holds up better than untreated wood.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With the Charles River, Bogastow Brook, ponds and the Great Black Swamp in or near town, some lots sit on low, wet ground where roof runoff can worsen damp basements. Downspouts should carry water well away from foundations. On wooded lots, guards and larger downspouts reduce clogging. Seamless aluminum has fewer joints to leak, and gutters should be sized for the roof area they drain.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Most Millis roofs sit on houses from the 1940s through the 1970s, and an older roof may have more than one layer of shingles. A tear-off is the chance to check the deck, replace soft boards and add ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys. On the older houses in the historic center, dormers and chimneys need careful flashing. Attic ventilation should be checked during any re-roof.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A targeted repair can make sense when the problem is limited: a few cracked panels, a split board or damage at one corner. Matching older or discontinued profiles and colors is the main obstacle, and the free on-site assessment can establish whether a clean match is available. If the damage was caused by water, the source should be fixed before new material goes on.

story: Medway's oldest road was laid out in 1670 as Old Mendon Road; today it is Village Street, which winds along the Charles River. Water power from the Charles and Chicken Brook led to cotton and paper mills, along with straw and boot factories and home-based industry. Activity centered on Medway Village, where Holliston Street meets Village Street. The Medway Village Historic District, listed in 2008, covers 60 acres in the southeast of town, between a former railroad line, Oakland Street and the Charles. It includes more than 240 historic structures, most built between 1831 and 1897, and the village had a train station from 1861 to 1966.

At the west end of town, the Rabbit Hill Historic District covers about 40 acres around Highland, Main, Franklin and Milford streets. It preserves much of a 19th-century village that grew up around the Second Congregational Church, now the West Medway Community Church. Most of its houses are Federal or Greek Revival, and industry developed along the Charles just outside its boundaries. The Great Black Swamp in the middle of town was undevelopable, which kept Medway and East Medway apart until East Medway became Millis in 1885.

Census estimates count about 4,800 homes, with a median build year of 1976. About 19 percent predate 1940 and about 54 percent predate 1980, so close to half the housing is from 1980 or later. About 86 percent are owner-occupied, and about 7 percent are in two-to-four-unit buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Close to half of Medway's homes were built in 1980 or later, and on these houses vinyl is often the material being replaced or chosen again. On newer homes, the main concerns are housewrap integrity, flashing at openings and good corner and trim details. About 54 percent of homes predate 1980, and for those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted siding or trim is disturbed. Panel profile and trim width matter most on the older houses in Medway Village and Rabbit Hill.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Federal and Greek Revival houses of Rabbit Hill and the 19th-century houses of Medway Village were built with painted wood clapboard, and that remains the material that best suits them. New boards should match the original exposure, and wide corner boards and frieze bands should keep their proportions. Primed boards over a drainage layer, painted soon after installation, last longest. Selective board replacement can preserve much of an original wall.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a good fit for Medway's newer homes, when owners want a painted lap look and longer repaint intervals. The boards need clearance from grade and roofs, which matters on low lots near the Charles River or Chicken Brook. Cutting requires dust control. On older houses, fiber cement can match the look of clapboard if the lap width and trim details are chosen to suit the house.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles are a less obvious fit for the Federal and Greek Revival clapboard of Rabbit Hill, but they can work well on a rear ell, a garage, or a newer house on a wooded lot. Walls that stay damp near the Charles or Chicken Brook last longer with a ventilated gap behind the shingles and stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails. Whether to stain, paint or let the cedar go gray should be settled before installation, because each choice commits the owner to a different upkeep routine.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Medway's housing spans the 19th-century villages and a large share of homes built in 1980 or later, and a full replacement uncovers different issues depending on age. Older houses may have plank sheathing and little insulation; newer houses may have sheathing damage around windows where flashing failed. All exposed sheathing should be inspected, and any repairs should be itemized in the written estimate. Every window and door should be re-flashed while the walls are open.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Federal and Greek Revival houses, like those in Rabbit Hill, depend on trim for their character: pilasters, frieze boards, door surrounds and cornices. Those pieces should be repaired or replaced with matching profiles. On newer houses, the main trim issue is usually rot at the bottoms of door casings, corner boards and garage jambs. Cellular PVC at those locations resists rot and holds paint well.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Village Street follows the Charles River, and Chicken Brook also runs through town, so some lots sit on lower ground where roof water should be kept well away from foundations. Downspouts should discharge to extensions or drainage, and gutters should be sized for the roof area. On wooded lots, guards and larger downspouts reduce clogging. Seamless aluminum has fewer seams to leak.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Medway's roofs cover everything from 19th-century houses in Medway Village and Rabbit Hill to homes built since 1980. Whatever the age, every valley, dormer, chimney and wall joint is a flashing detail that should be renewed rather than reused. A tear-off is the time to inspect and repair the deck, add ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, and check attic ventilation.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small damage, like a cracked panel by the driveway or a soft board beside a back door, rarely justifies new siding on the whole house. The catch on homes from the 1980s and 1990s is that vinyl colors and profiles from that era are often discontinued, so a donor piece taken from a hidden wall is sometimes the closest match. The free on-site assessment can settle whether a patch will blend in. Any leak that caused the damage should be traced and stopped before patching.

story: Holliston split off from the western part of Sherborn and was incorporated in 1724, taking its name from Thomas Hollis, a London benefactor of Harvard College. The oldest houses follow Washington Street, which carries Routes 16 and 126 through town. The Thomas Hollis Historic District runs about a mile along that street between Winter and Highland Streets and holds Federal and Greek Revival houses, the 1822 First Congregational Church and the 1855 Italianate town hall. Most of the center predates the Civil War, with brick commercial blocks added after the railroad arrived around 1900. Farther east, the East Holliston Historic District lines Washington Street and Curve Street near Jarr Brook, where Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival houses went up and serious building stopped around 1870.

Those districts are the exception rather than the rule. Census estimates put the median Holliston home at about 1966, with roughly 72 percent built before 1980 and only about 18 percent before 1940. The town's population nearly doubled between 1960 and 1970, from 6,222 to 12,069, and that decade shows in the housing stock. Of about 5,900 homes, around 87 percent are owner-occupied and only about 6 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings, so most exterior projects here involve a single-family house from the postwar decades whose original materials have now been on the wall for fifty years or more.

The rest of the map is shaped by water and old industry. Lake Winthrop covers about 140 acres, with beaches at Stoddard Park and Pleasure Point, and the Charles River passes near the southern edge of town. Holliston was once the largest shoe producer in the country, and the former Goodwill Shoe Company buildings on Water Street now hold artists' studios. Smaller areas such as Braggville, Gooch Corners, Metcalf, Brentwood and Lakeside grew up around post offices or stops on the Boston and Albany Railroad's Milford line.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A house from Holliston's 1960s growth spurt is the most common candidate for vinyl. Before new panels go on, the original sheathing should be checked for soft spots, and the old siding removed rather than covered where possible, so the walls can be inspected and insulated. Window and door trim on houses of that era is often shallow, so plan on new J-channel or built-out casings so the vinyl ends cleanly. On homes built before 1978, EPA lead-safe rules apply whenever painted surfaces are cut or removed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard belongs on the older houses along Washington Street, where the Thomas Hollis and East Holliston districts preserve Federal and Greek Revival buildings. Matching the exposure of the existing boards keeps a repaired or reclad wall from looking patched. Corner boards, frieze boards and window casings on these houses are part of the style, so they should be kept or reproduced rather than wrapped. Primed, back-sealed boards installed over a drainage plane will hold paint longer than boards nailed straight to old sheathing.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners of Holliston's postwar single-family houses who want the look of painted clapboard without wood's repainting schedule. It is heavy, so walls should be checked for straightness first; a sixty-year-old frame that has settled will show waves under a rigid board. Factory-finished planks cut down on site painting. Clearance at the bottom course matters, because the board should not sit in contact with soil, mulch or a deck surface, a detail that is easy to get wrong where a foundation sits close to grade.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles make sense on houses near Lake Winthrop or anywhere a natural, weathered finish fits the setting. Shingles need to dry from both sides, so a rainscreen mat or furring behind them extends their life, especially on walls that stay shaded. Owners should decide early between letting the cedar weather gray or applying a stain, since a finish chosen after installation has to be kept up from then on. Stainless or hot-dipped fasteners prevent rust streaks running down the face of the wall.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With roughly seven in ten Holliston homes built before 1980, many are reaching the point where patching no longer pays. A full replacement is the time to open the walls, replace damaged sheathing, add a water-resistive barrier and consider continuous exterior insulation, which older houses often lack. Window and door flashing should be redone at the same time rather than reused. For houses inside the Thomas Hollis or East Holliston districts, it is worth asking the town about any review before choosing a material that changes the original appearance.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim carries the character of Holliston's older houses: wide corner boards and cornices on Greek Revival buildings, simpler casings on Federal ones. Rotted sills, rake boards and porch elements should be replaced with matching profiles rather than flat stock. On postwar houses, fascia and soffits are usually where moisture shows first, often behind failing gutters. Cellular PVC or primed wood can both work; the choice depends on whether the trim will be painted to match existing wood elsewhere on the house.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Houses near Lake Winthrop and the Charles River lowlands need gutters that carry water well away from foundations, so downspouts should discharge onto splash blocks or extensions rather than at the base of the wall. Seamless aluminum in a size matched to the roof area reduces leaks at joints. On older homes along Washington Street, half-round gutters may look more appropriate than K-style. Where tall trees hang over the roof, guards can cut down on cleaning, though no guard removes it entirely.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: A 1960s Holliston roof may already carry more than one layer of shingles, and a new roof should start with a tear-off to the deck so rotted boards can be found and replaced. Ice and water membrane at the eaves and in valleys, plus balanced intake and ridge ventilation, help prevent ice dams, particularly on low-pitched roofs. On the older houses near the center, steeper pitches and multiple chimneys call for careful step and counter flashing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small problems such as a cracked vinyl panel, a split clapboard or a loose corner can usually be fixed without replacing a whole wall. Finding a color or profile match is the main challenge on older installations, so salvaging pieces from a less visible side is sometimes the best option. Any damage near windows or the bottom course should be checked for water behind the siding before it is closed up.

story: Mendon is one of the oldest towns in the region, settled around 1660 and incorporated in 1667, and its original grant of roughly 64 square miles later gave land to neighbors such as Uxbridge and Hopedale. The first village did not last: Mendon was largely burned in the winter of 1676 during King Philip's War and was resettled in 1680. Benjamin Albee's water-powered grist mill on the Mill River, built in 1664, was the first in the area. The Middle Post Road, now Route 16, ran through town, and a 1772 milestone marked 37 miles to Boston.

Two National Register districts hold the older houses. The Mendon Center Historic District covers about 400 acres around the triangle of Main, Hastings and Maple Streets, with homes ranging from the 18th century to the mid-20th, and the 1820 Second Unitarian Church designed by Elias Carter. North of it, the North Avenue Rural Historic District follows North Street between Esty and Powers Roads and out along Hopedale Street and Trask Road, a 345-acre farm landscape whose buildings are mostly 19th-century Federal and Greek Revival, including the Seth Davenport farmhouse from about 1780.

Outside those areas, Mendon is a much newer town than its history suggests. Census estimates put the median home at about 1985. Only about 9 percent of houses were built before 1940, and roughly 36 percent date from before 1980, so most of the housing stock went up in the last four decades. Nearly all of the town's roughly 2,200 homes are owner-occupied, about 87 percent, with only about 4 percent in two- to four-unit buildings. Nipmuc Pond, once home to the Lake Nipmuc Park resort, and the commercial strip along Route 16 round out the picture of a rural town that became a bedroom community.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Half of Mendon's houses were built after the mid-1980s, and their original builder-grade siding is often what needs attention now. Thin panels tend to fade and crack on sun-facing walls after a few decades. A replacement should include a check of the house wrap and window flashing, which were not always detailed carefully when houses went up quickly. Thicker panels with an insulated backer can straighten slightly uneven walls and add a modest amount of insulation.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the original skin of the Federal and Greek Revival houses in the Mendon Center and North Avenue districts. On these buildings, the goal is usually to repair or replace boards in kind so the house keeps its proportions. Narrow exposures and hand-planed edges on early boards are hard to match with stock material, so custom milling may be needed. On newer homes, clapboard is a choice for owners who want a traditional look that fits alongside the town center.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement works well on Mendon's newer houses where owners want low upkeep with a painted look. Because the town's housing is younger than most, framing is usually flat and plumb, which suits rigid planks. Butt joints should be flashed and staggered, and the manufacturer's clearances above roofs and decks followed closely to keep the warranty valid. Pre-finished colors avoid repainting for years, though cut ends still need sealing during installation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Mendon's rural edges, particularly the farm settings along North Street and Hopedale Street, where a weathered finish matches older farm buildings. Barns and sheds often need shingles as much as the main house does. A ventilated gap behind the shingles keeps them dry, and copper or stainless flashing at windows avoids staining. Owners should expect shingles on sun-exposed walls to weather differently from shaded sides, which is normal.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a 1980s or 1990s Mendon house is a chance to fix problems that were built in originally, such as missing kick-out flashing at roof-wall intersections or house wrap that was torn and never taped. Opening the walls lets damaged sheathing be found and replaced. Adding exterior insulation under new siding can reduce heating costs, but it changes window and door depths, so trim extensions should be planned before materials are ordered.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On the older houses around Main, Hastings and Maple Streets, trim details such as cornices, door surrounds and corner pilasters define the Federal and Greek Revival styles, and replacements should copy the existing profiles. On newer homes, finger-jointed pine trim from the original build often rots at the bottom ends of casings and corner boards first. Replacing those sections with cellular PVC or properly primed wood, and sealing end grain, prevents the same failure from repeating.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Rural lots in Mendon often leave room to direct downspouts well away from foundations rather than into the nearest planting bed. Seamless gutters sized for the roof area reduce overflow during heavy rain. On farmhouses and outbuildings in the North Avenue area, simpler half-round profiles may fit better than modern K-style. Any house with trees over the roofline may need guards where leaves collect, and gutters on barns should be checked for sagging hangers.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Most Mendon roofs are on houses built since the 1970s, many still carrying their original asphalt shingles toward the end of their service life. A new roof should include a full tear-off, deck inspection, ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys, and balanced ventilation. Older houses in the town center may have board sheathing with gaps that need to be covered or replaced before shingles go on. Chimney and wall flashing should be renewed, not reused.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Spot repairs can handle a damaged panel, a few rotten boards or a loose corner. On newer houses, matching the exact vinyl color can be difficult after years of fading, so pieces are sometimes taken from a less visible wall and replaced there with new stock. Any repair near a roof line or window should include a check for water behind the siding before the wall is closed again.

story: Leominster was carved from Lancaster, incorporated as a town in 1740 and chartered as a city in 1915. Water power from Monoosnoc Brook and the Nashua River, plus the railroad, brought paper mills, piano makers and comb shops by the 1850s. Celluloid made it the Comb City, and later firms such as Viscoloid and Foster Grant earned it the name Pioneer Plastics City; Tupperware started here in 1938 and the plastic pink flamingo in 1956. Mill buildings still mark the map, including the Wachusett Shirt Company and Whitney and Company buildings on Water Street and the Jewett Piano Company building on Adams Street.

That industry filled the city with workers. Population grew from about 2,000 in 1840 to nearly 20,000 by 1920, and housing followed. French Hill, running from 1st Street to 12th Street, was built up with planned triple-decker apartment houses and named for the French immigrants who settled it, while Italian families formed a close community at Lincoln Terrace. The result shows in the census: about 20 percent of Leominster's roughly 19,300 homes sit in two- to four-unit buildings, and only about 62 percent are owner-occupied. About 23 percent were built before 1940, and the median year built is about 1967.

The city sits mostly on a plateau above the Nashua River, with hillier ground to the north and west. South Monoosnoc Hill, at 1,020 feet, is the highest point and was once quarried for granite used in house foundations. Beyond the hills lie the No Town Reservoir and the roughly 4,300-acre Leominster State Forest. The traditional common survives in the Monument Square Historic District along Main Street, Water Street and Grove Avenue, while newer suburban building has spread along Route 2 and I-190.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is common on Leominster's multi-family houses, where owners want to stop painting three stories of wall. On a triple-decker, the work involves tall staging and stacked porches, so the porch ceilings, columns and railings should be planned as part of the job rather than left as wood islands. The sheathing on older buildings is often boards, which should be checked for rot before new panels are hung. Most of these buildings predate 1978, so EPA lead-safe rules apply when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard suits the 19th-century houses around Monument Square and the older streets near the Nashua River, where it was the original finish. Replacing failing sections in kind keeps the look consistent, and matching the exposure of the existing boards matters more than the material brand. New boards should be primed on all sides and installed over a drainage layer. On multi-unit buildings, clapboard costs more to keep painted, which is worth weighing against the building's long-term budget.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a good fit for owners of two- and three-family houses who want a painted look without frequent repainting. It also resists fire better than vinyl, which some owners of closely spaced buildings consider. The planks are heavy and need a solid nailing base, so older board sheathing may need repair first. Planning for tall staging, safe material handling on narrow lots and coordination with tenants should happen before the job starts on French Hill and similar neighborhoods.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are less common on Leominster's dense neighborhoods but can suit houses at the city's hillier northern and western edges, toward Leominster State Forest. Shingles last longest when they can dry out, so a ventilated backing and good roof overhangs help. On older homes, shingles sometimes appear on gable ends or upper stories above clapboard, and repairs should match that pattern. Hot-dipped or stainless nails prevent staining on exposed faces.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: About two-thirds of Leominster's housing was built before 1980, and many older multi-family buildings have been resided more than once. A full replacement should strip earlier layers to expose the sheathing, replace rotted boards and add a modern water-resistive barrier. On triple-deckers, this is the moment to rebuild porch connections and flashing where water often enters. Owners of rental buildings should plan the schedule around tenants, since work on all sides of the building affects access.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Older Leominster houses often carry decorative trim such as bracketed cornices, bay windows and turned porch posts, and these should be repaired or replicated rather than covered with flat coil stock. On multi-family buildings, porch floors, railings and ceilings take the most weather and are frequent repair items. Cellular PVC trim reduces painting on hard-to-reach upper stories. Any trim work on painted surfaces of pre-1978 buildings falls under EPA lead-safe rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On tall, closely spaced buildings, gutters and downspouts should be routed so water does not spill onto a neighbor's lot or onto stacked porches below. Downspouts on three-story houses carry a lot of water and should discharge onto extensions or into drainage that moves it away from the foundation. Houses on the hills toward Leominster State Forest may need guards where trees overhang. Seamless gutters reduce leaks on long runs across multi-family facades.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Leominster's roofs range from shallow-pitched tops on triple-deckers to steeper roofs on older single-family houses. Low-slope sections may need membrane roofing rather than shingles, so the slope should be measured before choosing materials. Ice and water barrier along eaves helps where snow sits on the roof, and ventilation should be balanced. On multi-family buildings, roof access and debris removal require planning on narrow lots.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Spot repairs can address storm damage, a loose panel or a few rotted boards without residing an entire building. On older multi-family houses, damaged areas near porches and window heads should be opened far enough to check for hidden water damage in the sheathing. Matching materials on older buildings sometimes means moving salvaged pieces from a less visible side and filling that spot with new stock.

story: Princeton sits high in the hills north of Worcester. The town center is about 1,175 feet above sea level, and Mount Wachusett, whose 2,006-foot summit straddles the line with Westminster, is entered from the Princeton side. Incorporated in 1759 from land that had belonged to Rutland, the town was named for the Rev. Thomas Prince. Redemption Rock, where tradition places the ransom of Mary Rowlandson, is here, along with the Wachusett Meadow Wildlife Sanctuary and the Wachusett Mountain ski area.

Much of the older building stock is gathered in National Register historic districts. Princeton Center, at the junction of Hubbardston and Mountain Roads, holds the common, the town hall, the library and the First Congregational Church. Just west, the West Village Historic District, also called Pratt's Corner, has Georgian houses from the colonial period and Greek Revival buildings from the early 1800s; in the late 19th century it became a resort area with boarding houses and hotels. Russell Corner, at Merriam and Gregory Hill Roads, keeps fifteen contributing buildings, most from before 1830, including the Abijah Wood house of about 1748, and some older buildings there were turned into small summer homes. East Princeton grew around mills on Keyes Brook, including the Stuart Chair Factory from 1841.

Census figures reflect that mix. About 29 percent of Princeton's roughly 1,400 homes were built before 1940, a high share for a rural town, yet the median year built is about 1975. About 94 percent are owner-occupied and only about 5 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so nearly all work here is on single-family houses, many on large lots at elevation.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is most often considered for Princeton's houses from the 1970s onward. At this elevation, wind exposure on open hillsides matters, so panels rated for higher wind loads and proper nailing into framing are worth specifying. Darker colors can warp on walls in full sun, so manufacturer color guidance should be followed. On older houses in the historic villages, vinyl can hide original trim details, and owners should weigh that before choosing it.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival houses in West Village, Russell Corner and East Princeton were built with wood clapboard, and that is still the natural choice there. Matching board width and exposure, and keeping original corner boards and cornices, preserves the look. New clapboards should be back-primed and installed over a ventilated drainage gap so the boards dry between storms. On pre-1978 buildings, EPA lead-safe rules apply to removing old painted siding.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives Princeton owners a painted-clapboard appearance with less repainting, which can matter on houses with long, hard-to-reach walls. It handles wind well when nailed correctly. The planks are heavy, so access for material delivery on long driveways and steep lots should be considered. Joints need flashing, and the bottom course must stay clear of soil and snow piles, which can sit against walls for weeks at this elevation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit Princeton's summer-resort past, when older buildings in places like Russell Corner were adapted as summer residences. They also suit houses tucked into wooded hillsides. A ventilated backing helps shingles dry after rain and snowmelt. Shingles on north-facing or shaded walls can grow moss or mildew, so trimming back nearby branches and leaving a gap above grade help. Stainless fasteners avoid streaking.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement on a Princeton house is a chance to address air leakage and insulation, which matter in a town where winters at elevation run long. Removing old siding exposes sheathing and lets missing house wrap and window flashing be corrected. For houses in one of the National Register districts, owners may want to ask the town about any local review before changing materials, and keeping original trim profiles helps the house remain consistent with its neighbors.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim work on Princeton's older houses often involves wide cornices, door surrounds and window casings that define their Georgian, Federal or Greek Revival style. Rotted sections should be replaced with matching profiles. Later porches, such as the late-19th-century wraparound on the Abijah Wood house, are part of a house's history too and deserve the same care. On newer houses, fascia and rake boards exposed to wind-driven rain are frequent repair points.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Snow load is a real concern on Princeton roofs, so gutters should be attached with heavy-duty hangers spaced closely, and placed so sliding snow does not tear them off. Where large trees overhang, guards reduce clogging but should not trap snow. Downspouts should carry water away from foundations on sloped lots. On historic buildings, some owners prefer half-round gutters or none at all, relying on drip edges and ground drainage instead.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: At more than 1,100 feet, Princeton gets more snow than the valley towns, and roofs should be built for it. Ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys, solid decking and good attic ventilation reduce ice dams. Metal roofing is worth considering on outbuildings and steeper roofs where snow shedding helps. On older houses in the historic villages, chimney flashing and rotted roof boards are frequent findings when old shingles come off.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Spot repairs can fix storm damage, a few rotted boards or a loose corner without replacing whole walls. On older houses, matching hand-planed clapboard may require custom milling, and the replacement boards should be primed on every face before going up. Repairs near the ground are a good moment to check the lowest courses and sill for rot, since snow can sit against the bottom of the walls for long stretches here.

story: Paxton was formed from parts of Leicester and Rutland and incorporated in 1765, after Europeans first settled the area in 1749. Its meeting house frame went up in 1766 on land given by Seth Howe, and the town bell was cast by Paul Revere. The center sits about 1,158 feet above sea level. Asnebumskit Hill, where an early FM broadcasting antenna began operating in 1939, rises nearby, and Asnebumskit Pond supplies the town's water.

Paxton's oldest working landscape is now Moore State Park. Turkey Hill Brook drops about 90 feet over a 400-foot run there, and at least five mills operated on the site in the 18th and 19th centuries, starting with a grist mill and sawmill as early as 1747. The site later became a private estate, then a 737-acre state park listed on the National Register in 2004, with a restored sawmill, Eames Pond and old mill chutes still visible. Thompson Pond is another local landmark.

Most of Paxton's homes, though, came much later. The population more than doubled from 1,066 in 1950 to 2,399 in 1960 and rose again to 3,731 by 1970. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1967, with roughly 67 percent of homes built before 1980 and only about 10 percent before 1940. About 92 percent of the town's roughly 1,750 homes are owner-occupied and about 7 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so this is overwhelmingly a town of single-family houses from the 1950s and 1960s building boom, set on high ground where snow and wind are part of planning any exterior job.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: For a house from Paxton's 1950s and 1960s growth years, vinyl is often the practical choice when the existing siding has failed. Whatever is on the wall now should be removed or at least inspected so trapped moisture and soft sheathing are found before they are covered. On a hilltop town above 1,100 feet, it is worth asking for panels with a higher wind rating and fastening them into framing at the spacing the manufacturer specifies. If the house predates 1978, EPA lead-safe rules apply once painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Older homes near the center, where the meeting house was raised in 1766, are the obvious place for wood clapboard, and it can also bring back a traditional look on a postwar house that was later covered. Back-priming every board, leaving a small drainage gap behind it and flashing each butt joint help paint last on walls that take wind-driven rain. Exposure should match whatever survives on the house so new and old sections read as one wall.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives Paxton's mid-century houses a painted-board look that holds up to wind and does not burn. Sixty-year-old framing sometimes bows, and rigid planks telegraph every wave, so walls should be checked and shimmed where needed. Clearance above grade, decks and roof lines needs extra attention here, because plowed and drifted snow can rest against the lower courses for much of the winter. Pre-finished boards save repainting, though every field cut still needs sealing.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles suit houses set among trees, and Paxton's landscape includes places like Moore State Park, with its azaleas, mountain laurel and old mill sites along Turkey Hill Brook. On a house, cedar lasts longest when it can dry from behind, so a ventilated mat or furring strips under the shingles is a good investment. Walls that rarely see sun may grow mildew. Deciding between a natural gray weathering and a stain should happen before the first course goes on.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Roughly two-thirds of Paxton's homes are older than 1980, and when siding on one of them is failing in several places, replacing it all may make more sense than chasing repairs. Stripping to the sheathing exposes rot around windows and sills, lets a water-resistive barrier go on, and allows the window and door flashing to be rebuilt. Rigid foam under the new cladding can help a mid-century house in a cold, high town, but it deepens every window opening, so trim should be planned in advance.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Most of Paxton's postwar houses have plain trim, and the pieces that fail first are usually fascia, rake boards and sills that face the prevailing weather. Replacing them with cellular PVC, or with primed wood whose end grain is sealed, slows the cycle of rot. Where an older house near the center still has original cornices or door surrounds, those details are worth repairing or copying. Painted trim on homes built before 1978 is covered by EPA lead-safe rules when sanded or removed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Snow that slides off a roof in Paxton can take a gutter with it, so hangers should be heavy-duty and closely spaced, and the gutter set low enough below the shingle line that a sheet of snow passes over it. Downspouts on sloped lots should be extended so runoff does not collect against the foundation. Leaf guards help under large trees. Seamless aluminum is the usual choice for long runs on mid-century houses because it has fewer joints to leak.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With the town center around 1,158 feet, Paxton roofs carry snow for long periods, and ice dams are the main threat. Ice and water membrane should run up from the eaves and through every valley, and attic intake and ridge vents should be balanced. Roofs from the 1950s and 1960s may have two layers of shingles; tearing both off lets the decking be checked. Low-pitched roofs drain slowly, so wider membrane coverage on them is a sensible precaution.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A few damaged boards, a cracked panel or a loose corner can usually be repaired without residing the house. Faded vinyl or discontinued wood profiles are hard to match, so pieces are sometimes moved from a less visible side. While a section is open, it is worth checking the lowest courses for rot from snow that sits against the walls.

story: Leicester was incorporated in the 1710s on the condition that 50 families settle within seven years, and its first house lots were 30 to 50 acres each. The town later gave up land to form Spencer, part of Paxton and part of Auburn. Leicester became an early industrial center: by the 1780s its mills made about a third of American hand cards, used to straighten fibers before spinning, and by the 1890s about a third of all hand and machine cards in North America. Pliny Earle built the first carding machine for Samuel Slater's mill in Pawtucket.

The town has four villages: Leicester Center, Cherry Valley on the east toward Worcester, Rochdale in the southeast corner, and Greenville, now considered part of Rochdale. Routes 9 and 56 cut the town into quarters. In the center, the Washburn Square-Leicester Common Historic District covers about 21 acres with the 1834 Unitarian church, the 1901 Gothic Revival First Congregational Church, the 1939 town hall, and stately homes along the south side of Washburn Square that became part of the Becker College campus. Dr. Samuel Green's house in Greenville is linked to the first medical school in Massachusetts.

The town center sits about 1,010 feet above sea level, and most of Worcester's Kettle Brook reservoir system lies in the northeast of town, where the villages of Mannville and Lakeside were removed to build it. Population grew strongly in the 1950s and 1960s, and census estimates put the median home at about 1965. About 26 percent of Leicester's roughly 4,300 homes were built before 1940 and about 67 percent before 1980. About 89 percent are owner-occupied and about 6 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Roughly two-thirds of Leicester's homes were built before 1980, with strong growth in the 1950s and 1960s, and vinyl is a common way to end the painting cycle on houses from those years. The old cladding should come off, or at least be inspected, so rotten sheathing is not sealed in. Leicester Center sits around 1,010 feet, and panels with a higher wind rating, nailed into framing, are a reasonable upgrade on exposed lots. For pre-1978 houses, EPA lead-safe rules govern how painted siding is removed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Around Washburn Square and the common, wood clapboard is part of what makes the historic district read as a whole. Repairs there should use boards of the same width and exposure, and new boards should be primed on every face before installation. Elsewhere, clapboard can restore the look of an older house that was covered with something else decades ago. A drainage gap behind the boards helps paint hold up and lets the wall dry after storms.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a fit for Leicester's mid-century houses when owners want the appearance of painted boards but less maintenance. Rigid planks show any bowing, so older walls should be checked and corrected before installation. Butt joints need flashing, and the bottom course has to stay clear of soil and snow. Factory-applied colors reduce repainting, though every cut edge must be sealed on site. The weight of the planks also makes careful staging and handling important.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: In the northeast corner of town, where Worcester's Kettle Brook reservoirs replaced the old villages of Mannville and Lakeside, and on other tree-shaded lots, cedar shingles can suit the setting. They last longest with a ventilated backing that lets them dry after rain and snowmelt. Shaded walls may grow mildew, so keeping branches trimmed back helps. Owners should choose between natural weathering and stain before installation, since a stain must be renewed periodically.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: When siding on one of Leicester's postwar houses is failing on several walls, a complete replacement lets the sheathing be inspected, rotten sections replaced and a water-resistive barrier installed. Window and door flashing should be rebuilt rather than reused. For homes within the Washburn Square-Leicester Common district, owners may want to ask the town about any review before changing materials. Adding exterior insulation is possible but deepens window and door openings, so trim must be planned around it.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Washburn Square-Leicester Common district includes Georgian, Federal and Gothic Revival buildings, and their cornices, corner boards and door surrounds should be repaired or replicated rather than covered with flat coil stock. On the town's postwar houses, fascia boards and window sills are usually the first trim to rot. Cellular PVC or primed wood with sealed end grain can both work. Painted trim on homes built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe rules when disturbed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: About 1.3 square miles of Leicester is water, much of it in the Kettle Brook reservoir system, and roof runoff should be handled with the same care: downspouts extended far enough that water does not soak the soil beside the foundation. On postwar houses with long eaves, seamless aluminum sized to the roof area cuts down on leaking seams. Sliding snow is the other hazard at this elevation, so closely spaced, heavy-duty hangers keep a loaded gutter from tearing away from the fascia.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Leicester grew by more than a third during the 1960s, and a house from that decade may already be on its second or third roof. Replacement should begin with a tear-off to the deck so soft boards can be found. Because the center sits near 1,010 feet and snow lingers, ice and water membrane belongs at the eaves and in valleys, with intake and ridge vents balanced to keep the roof deck cold. On older houses near the common, chimney flashing is a frequent weak point.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Spot repairs can handle wind damage, a few rotted boards or loose panels without residing a house. Matching older wood profiles or faded vinyl may require taking pieces from a less visible side and putting new stock there instead. Repairs near the ground should include a check of the sill and lowest courses for damage from snow that sits against the walls through the winter.
