story: Sterling was known as Chocksett and as Lancaster's second parish before it was incorporated in 1781. Settlers arrived around 1720, and the town common was laid out in 1724. The central village is now the Sterling Center Historic District, bounded roughly by Meetinghouse Hill and Main, Maple, Kendall Hill, Boulding, Worcester and Princeton streets. It holds houses from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in Federal, Greek Revival and late Victorian styles, along with several churches and the 1835 town hall.

Outlying houses tell an older rural story. The Sawyer Homestead on Maple Street, linked to the girl in Mary Had a Little Lamb, was a 1756 one-and-a-half-story house with clapboard siding on a stone foundation until arson destroyed it in 2007; the family began a replica in 2008. On Squareshire Road, the 1794 Stephen Hastings House is believed to be the town's earliest brick house. Pratts Junction was a rail junction, and a branch line served a cider mill in the center until the late 1970s. The town sits at about 500 feet of elevation, near Wachusett Mountain, with Lake Waushacum and the Wachusett Reservoir along its edges.

Census numbers show a split stock. Of about 3,300 homes, the median dates to 1980, so roughly half are older and half newer. About one in eight predates 1940. Close to nine in ten are owner-occupied, and around six percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. Most work here is on single-family houses, from old village homes to subdivisions of the last few decades.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: About half of Sterling's houses were built after 1980, and many are on their original vinyl or wood siding. When it is replaced, the sheathing and window flashing should be checked first. On open, higher lots in a town that sits around 500 feet up, near Wachusett Mountain, wind exposure makes panel fastening and starter details worth extra care. Ask for a written scope listing wrap, flashing and trim.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard suits the Federal and Greek Revival houses in Sterling Center, and it was the siding on the 1756 Sawyer house. Matching exposure, corner boards and window trim keeps repairs consistent with the village's look. Owners near the Common may want to check with the town before making visible changes. For pre-1978 houses, lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can give one of Sterling's post-1980 houses the look of painted clapboard with less maintenance than wood. Its weight and rigidity hold up better than thin vinyl on lots open to wind. Proper clearances at roofs and grade and sealed cut edges are part of a correct installation. Pre-finished boards reduce painting on large walls and keep the color more even over time.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Sterling's rural setting, on a farmhouse, a barn or a newer house set among fields and trees. They need to dry, so a rain-screen gap and good clearance above soil help on shaded walls near Lake Waushacum or on wooded lots. Stainless fasteners prevent streaking, and pre-stained shingles color more evenly. On older outbuildings, check the sheathing before new shingles go on.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: On an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century house in the Center, a full re-side can uncover original boards, irregular framing and old repairs, so the estimate should explain how hidden damage will be priced. On houses from the 1980s and later, a full replacement is a chance to add house wrap and proper window flashing. Either way, plan the scope before work starts.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Federal and Greek Revival houses in Sterling Center rely on cornices, corner pilasters and door surrounds for their character. When these rot, replacement pieces should match original profiles, which are best measured before anything is removed. On newer houses, trim at grade, around garage doors and at deck ledgers fails first, and PVC or composite with proper flashing can stop it from coming back.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Wooded lots put leaves into gutters each fall, so guards and larger downspouts help. Gutters should be hung so sliding snow and ice clear them rather than tear them loose, and sized for the roof area they drain. Direct downspouts away from foundations, particularly on slopes and on lots near Lake Waushacum and the Wachusett Reservoir, where water should not be sent toward the shore.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On a winter roof, ice-and-water barrier at eaves and valleys and balanced attic ventilation are important to limit ice dams. Older village houses with ells and additions need careful flashing where roof sections meet, and brick houses like the one on Squareshire Road need sound chimney flashing. On exposed hillside lots, shingles should be fastened to the manufacturer's high-wind pattern.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A cracked panel, a loose board or a small rotted section can often be repaired without replacing the whole wall. On a village house with original wood siding, a careful repair can keep old material in place rather than starting over with new boards. An on-site look can show whether the damage is isolated or tied to water getting behind the siding.

story: Lynn was settled in 1629, and tanning and shoemaking began here in 1635. By the early 1900s the city led the world in shoe production, and immigrant communities grew alongside the factories. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put the median year built at 1946. About 46 percent of homes predate 1940 and close to four in five predate 1980. Roughly a third of housing units sit in buildings with two to four units, and only about 48 percent are owner-occupied. That means a lot of exterior work here happens on shared buildings, where an owner has to plan around tenants, parking and narrow side yards.

The shore has its own building history. After 1840 the land between downtown and the ocean became a fashionable summer resort. Today it makes up the Diamond Historic District, a 69.5-acre National Register district bounded roughly by Broad and Lewis Streets, Nahant Street, Eastern Avenue and Lynn Shore Drive, which opened in 1910. Its 590 contributing resources include modest Federal houses with central chimneys, Greek Revival buildings, and Italianate, Queen Anne, Second Empire and Shingle Style homes. Colonial Revival houses built between 1890 and 1940 are the most common. Many of these houses look out over Nahant Bay, King's Beach and Lynn Beach.

Inland, neighborhoods such as Wyoma Square, the Highlands, Pine Hill, Tower Hill and the Brickyard cover the rest of the city. Lynn Woods Reservation takes up more than a quarter of the city's land in the northwest. Downtown was rebuilt more than once. A fire in 1889 destroyed 296 buildings, including 142 homes. Because so many houses here are older than 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply whenever painted trim or siding is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical choice for many of the two- to four-unit buildings that make up about a third of Lynn's housing. It keeps repainting off the owner's calendar on tall walls that are hard to reach. On these older frames, ask whether the old clapboard will be stripped or covered, and how the corners, window casings and porch ceilings will be finished. Near Nahant Bay and Lynn Shore Drive, the wind load rating of the panels and the nailing pattern deserve a direct question, because shore-facing walls take the most weather.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: In the Diamond Historic District, most of the 590 contributing buildings are Federal, Greek Revival, Italianate and Colonial Revival houses that were built with narrow wood clapboard. Replacing worn boards with matching profiles and exposure keeps the street face consistent. Primed, back-sealed boards and stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails are worth asking for near the beach, where salt air speeds up corrosion. Before you commit to a material, check whether the property sits inside any local review area.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can replicate the look of painted clapboard on the Colonial Revival houses common in the Diamond District and the older neighborhoods inland. It also resists rot and insects better than wood. Fiber cement is heavy and has to be cut with dust control, which matters on tight Lynn lots where neighbors and tenants are a few feet away. Ask for factory-primed or pre-finished boards, and ask how the butt joints and trim edges will be flashed.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: The Shingle Style houses in the Diamond Historic District were designed around wood shingle walls. Replacing them with cedar in a matching coursing and exposure keeps their character. On walls that face Nahant Bay, shingles weather faster and benefit from a breathable underlayment or rainscreen so they can dry from behind. Plan on stainless steel fasteners close to the water. White cedar left to weather is common, but stained or primed shingles hold color longer.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1946, many Lynn houses already carry two or even three layers of cladding. A full replacement is the time to strip back to the sheathing, check it for rot around windows and sills, and add a weather-resistive barrier the original builders never used. On a multi-unit building, settle access, debris removal and the tenant schedule before work starts. Lead-safe work practices apply on any pre-1978 house where painted surfaces will be disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Lynn's older housing stock carries a great deal of decorative trim: brackets on Italianate houses, Queen Anne spindlework, and the cornices and pilasters of Colonial Revival homes in the Diamond District. When pieces rot, a matching profile in wood or PVC can usually be milled or sourced. Painted trim on pre-1978 houses falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules once it is scraped or cut, so containment and cleanup should be part of the written plan.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Houses near King's Beach and Lynn Beach take wind-driven rain off Nahant Bay, so gutter size and downspout placement matter more than the gutters' look. Seamless aluminum with hidden hangers spaced close together suits the multi-story frames found across the city. Downspouts should discharge away from foundations, especially on tight lots where the neighbor's driveway is a few feet away. Near the edge of Lynn Woods, plan for leaves and consider guards.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Lynn's shoreline neighborhoods sit fully exposed to storms coming across Nahant Bay, so on a reroof there the shingle wind rating and starter-strip details deserve attention. Inland, many multi-family buildings have steep or complex roofs with dormers, and those need careful flashing at every wall intersection. Ask whether the old layers will be fully torn off. Ask too how the decking and attic ventilation will be checked, since many of these roofs are decades past their original install.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Spot repairs work well when the damage is limited, such as a cracked vinyl panel, a split clapboard or a section hit by wind. The new material should match the existing profile and color as closely as possible. Any rot behind the damage should be opened up and assessed before patching. On pre-1978 painted siding, lead-safe practices apply even to small repairs.

story: Salem has an unusually old housing stock. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put the median year built at 1938. About half of all homes predate 1940 and roughly three quarters predate 1980. About 38 percent of units are in buildings with two to four units, and roughly half of all homes are owner-occupied. Some of the oldest houses still stand: the Pickman House (c. 1664), the Gedney House (c. 1665) and the House of the Seven Gables (1668).

The Chestnut Street District holds a large share of the city's Federal-era architecture, including works by the builder and woodcarver Samuel McIntire, Hamilton Hall (1805) and the Peirce-Nichols House. Roughly bounded by Bridge, Lynn, Beckford and River Streets, it has been on the National Register since 1973. It also sits inside the larger, locally designated McIntire Historic District. Other historic districts include Federal Street, Charter Street and Salem Common. Owners in these areas should talk with the city about review before changing materials or details on the exterior.

Two other facts shape exterior work here. On June 25, 1914, a fire that began on Boston Street destroyed 1,376 buildings across 253 acres, though it spared Chestnut Street. Salem is also mostly water. About 55 percent of the city's area is water, and neighborhoods such as Salem Neck, South Salem along the harbor and North Salem across the North River sit close to Salem Harbor, Collins Cove and the Forest River. Salt air and wind off the harbor wear on paint, fasteners and flashing faster than they would inland.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is common on Salem's two- to four-unit buildings, which make up about 38 percent of the housing, because it cuts down on repainting tall walls. On a house with original trim, the details decide whether the job looks right: window casings, corner boards and cornices should stay or be properly wrapped, not buried. Inside the McIntire Historic District and other local districts, check with the city before choosing vinyl, since material changes there may be reviewed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Narrow wood clapboard fits the Federal and Colonial houses around Chestnut Street, Federal Street and Salem Common. Matching the existing exposure and profile matters when only some walls are redone. Near Collins Cove or the harbor, primed and back-sealed boards with stainless fasteners hold paint longer and avoid rust streaking. Plan painting for a dry stretch. Salt air shortens the life of a paint job on walls that face the water.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can stand in for painted clapboard on Salem's many frame houses outside the historic districts, and factory finishes hold up well in coastal air. Cutting it produces silica dust, so on Salem's close-set lots the dust control plan and neighbor protection should be agreed on up front. If the house is in a local historic district, confirm whether a substitute material is acceptable before ordering anything.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a long-standing coastal material, and on Salem Neck, South Salem and other spots near the water they weather to gray without much fuss. A rainscreen or breathable wrap behind the shingles helps the wood dry after wind-driven storms off the harbor. Stainless steel nails prevent rust stains. If the house is in one of the city's historic districts, ask about review first.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1938, many Salem houses have likely been re-sided at least once, and older layers can hide what is happening underneath. A full replacement is the time to find out what is under there and to repair rotted sheathing around windows and sills. Add a proper weather barrier at the same time. EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply to pre-1978 painted surfaces, which covers nearly every house in the older neighborhoods.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Chestnut Street District is known for carved Federal-era detail by Samuel McIntire. Trim across the older neighborhoods often includes cornices, pilasters and door surrounds worth repairing rather than replacing. Where replacement is needed, matching the original profile keeps the facade intact. In a local historic district, trim changes may need review, so check before cutting anything off. Lead-safe practices apply to old painted trim.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Rain off Salem Harbor often blows in sideways, so gutters on houses near the water need solid hangers and downspouts that move water well away from old foundations. If a historic house still has wood or built-in gutters, ask whether they can be relined instead of replaced. On multi-family buildings with tall eaves, oversized downspouts reduce overflow during heavy storms.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: A city where more than half the area is water gets steady wind, and roofs on Salem Neck and along the harbor take the worst of it. High-wind shingle ratings, sealed starter courses and careful flashing at chimneys and dormers are worth discussing. Older roofs over first-period and Federal houses can hide sagging rafters or patched decking, which only a full tear-off will reveal.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small repairs, such as a split board, a loose shingle or a storm-damaged section, can often be handled without touching the rest of the wall. The patch should match the existing material and profile. Any soft wood behind it should be cut out and replaced. Lead-safe practices apply on pre-1978 paint. On a house near the harbor, check the nearby flashing and fasteners too, since corrosion often spreads past the visibly damaged spot.

story: Danvers began as Salem Village, the farming settlement where the 1692 witch trials started. Some of that era survives. The Rebecca Nurse Homestead still stands, and the Salem Village Historic District runs along Centre, Hobart, Ingersoll, Forest and Collins Streets. It holds Colonial, Federal and Greek Revival buildings. Town Meeting made it a local historic district in 1974, with a Historic District Commission to oversee it, and it joined the National Register in 1975. Owners there should contact the commission before planning visible exterior changes.

Most of the town is younger. Its villages, including Burley's Corner, Danvers Center, Danversport, Downtown, Ferncroft, Hathorne, Putnamville and Tapleyville, date mainly to the late 1800s. Then came a burst of growth: the population went from 15,720 in 1950 to 26,151 in 1970. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 reflect that. The median home was built in 1963, about a quarter of homes predate 1940, and roughly seven in ten predate 1980. Only about 11 percent of units are in two- to four-unit buildings, and close to 70 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Most exterior work here is on owner-occupied houses, many of them from the postwar decades.

Geography varies across town. The Porter, Crane and Waters Rivers meet to form the tidal Danvers River, and Danversport sits near sea level. Elsewhere, hills such as Hathorne, Putnam and Folly rise to about 130 to 180 feet. The Ipswich River runs along the western edge, and the Putnamville Reservoir lies to the north.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Much of Danvers was built in the 1950s and 1960s, and many of those single-family homes are ready for new siding. Vinyl is a common choice on houses of that age. Before it goes on, the walls should be checked for soft sheathing, and an insulated or standard panel should be chosen based on the budget. Near the tidal Danvers River in Danversport, ask about panel wind ratings and the nailing schedule.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard belongs on the Colonial, Federal and Greek Revival buildings in the Salem Village Historic District, and on older houses in villages such as Tapleyville and Putnamville. When boards are replaced, matching the reveal and profile keeps the walls even. Inside the local historic district, talk to the Historic District Commission before changing anything visible from the street. Back-priming each board before it goes up helps paint last.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners of postwar Danvers houses who want the look of painted clapboard with less upkeep. It resists rot and pests, but it is heavy and needs careful layout around windows and doors. Ask about factory finishes, which hold color longer than paint applied on site, and about the flashing at every window head and joint. Dust control during cutting should be agreed on in advance.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles work on older village houses and on newer homes where the owner wants a natural finish. In low, damp spots near the Porter or Waters River, shingles dry better over a rainscreen or a breathable underlayment. Weathered, stained and primed finishes all age differently, so pick one based on how much upkeep you want, not only on how it looks on day one.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1963, many Danvers homes are on their original or second siding. A full replacement makes it possible to inspect the sheathing, fix rot around windows and add a modern weather barrier. On pre-1978 houses, original painted wood may sit under later vinyl or aluminum, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply once that paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On postwar houses, replacing rotted fascia, rake boards and window casings with PVC or primed wood with matching profiles is usually straightforward. The older homes in Danvers Center and the Salem Village Historic District are a different matter. Their trim deserves careful matching, and the historic district may review changes. Lead-safe practices apply to old painted trim. A written estimate should list each trim piece being replaced.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On Danvers' hillier streets, roof runoff picks up speed, so downspouts should carry water away from foundations and off sloped driveways. Near Danversport, where the ground sits close to sea level, drainage needs to be planned so water does not pond around the house. Where mature trees overhang the roof, gutter guards are worth considering. Seamless aluminum with hidden hangers is a common, durable option for single-family eaves.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many Danvers homes date from the 1950s through the 1970s, so plenty of roofs are on their second or third replacement. A full tear-off allows the decking to be inspected and ice and water shield to go in along the eaves and valleys. Homes on the higher hills and near the open water of the Danvers River see more wind, so ask about high-wind shingle ratings.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A dented panel, a cracked board or a short run of storm damage can often be fixed without redoing the wall. The patch should match the existing color and profile, and any wet or soft sheathing behind it should be replaced. Lead-safe rules apply on pre-1978 painted surfaces. A free on-site assessment can show whether a repair or a larger replacement makes more sense.

story: Beverly was settled in 1626 and became a city in 1894. Its houses span almost that whole stretch. The John Balch House (c. 1679), the John Hale House (c. 1694) and the Exercise Conant House (1695) still stand. On Front Street between Cabot and Bartlett Streets, the Fish Flake Hill Historic District preserves mid-18th-century Colonial and Federal houses. Sixteen of them are tied to ship captains active in the Revolutionary War. The name comes from the fish-drying racks, or flakes, that stood there into the late 1800s. The district joined the National Register in 1971.

The city divides roughly in two. Much of the western half is relatively urban. East of Woodbury Point the land is more rural, and Beverly Farms and Prides Crossing look out on the ocean. Wealthy families once built summer estates along that shore, though only a few of the original mansions remain. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put the median home at 1956. About 35 percent of homes were built before 1940 and about 72 percent before 1980. Close to one in five units is in a two- to four-unit building, and about 60 percent of homes are owner-occupied.

Water defines much of the city: about a third of its area is water, including Beverly Harbor, the Bass River, the Danvers River and Wenham Lake, plus five beaches. Nor'easters bring heavy rain and snow, and average snowfall is about 51 inches. Houses near the Cove, Lynch Park and the Beverly Farms shoreline take that weather straight off the water.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a sensible fit for many of the mid-century houses that brought Beverly's median build year to 1956, and for the city's two- to four-unit buildings. Ask about panel thickness and wind ratings on homes near the harbor or the Beverly Farms shoreline, where nor'easter winds hit hardest. Window and door trim should be wrapped neatly, with J-channel and flashing installed so water drains out, not in.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Colonial and Federal houses on Fish Flake Hill and Front Street were built with wood clapboard, and matching the original exposure keeps their walls consistent when boards are replaced. Primed, back-sealed boards and stainless nails make sense near Beverly Harbor, where salt air speeds up paint failure and rust. For houses in or near the historic district, ask about any city review before you change materials.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement offers a clapboard look with less maintenance, which suits Beverly's many houses from the 1940s to the 1970s. It holds paint well near the coast and does not rot. Because it is heavy and dusty to cut, staging and dust control need planning on the denser lots in the city's more urban western half. Pre-finished boards save a repaint after installation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit the shoreline in Beverly Farms and Prides Crossing, a stretch of coast once known for summer estates. Shingles on ocean-facing walls dry better over a rainscreen and should be hung with stainless nails. Expect the windward side to weather faster than the rest of the house. That uneven wear is normal and can be evened out with stain if you want a uniform color.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: About 72 percent of Beverly's homes were built before 1980, so many have aging cladding. A full replacement is the right time to check the sheathing around windows and sills, add a weather barrier and fix flashing at decks and roof lines. On pre-1978 houses, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply once old painted surfaces are disturbed. On multi-family buildings, plan access and tenant schedules before work begins.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: From the 18th-century houses on Fish Flake Hill to the surviving estates of Beverly Farms, the city's trim ranges from plain Colonial casings to elaborate cornices. Rotted pieces near the water should be replaced with rot-resistant wood or PVC milled to match. Old paint layers on pre-1978 trim fall under lead-safe rules when they are scraped or cut. Back-priming wood trim before installation also helps it last.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With about 51 inches of snow a year and heavy nor'easter rain, Beverly roofs shed a lot of water. Gutters should be sized for that volume, and downspouts should send it away from foundations, especially on low ground near the Bass River or the Danvers River. On wooded lots in the more rural eastern half, guards help keep leaves out.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Snowfall averaging about 51 inches makes ice and water shield along the eaves and valleys an important part of any Beverly reroof. Houses near the Cove, Lynch Park and the Beverly Farms shore face storm winds off Massachusetts Bay, so high-wind shingle ratings and sealed starter courses deserve a question. A full tear-off shows whether the decking on an older house needs repair.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: When storm damage or a single failed section is the issue, a targeted repair can save the rest of the wall. Matching the existing profile and color, and replacing any soft sheathing behind the patch, keeps the repair from becoming a weak spot. Lead-safe rules apply on pre-1978 paint. Near the water, check nearby fasteners and flashing for corrosion while the wall is open.

story: Lancaster is the oldest town in Worcester County. It was settled in 1643 as a trading post called Nashaway and incorporated in 1653. Its center sits on a north-south ridge inside a bend of the Nashua River and runs for about eight-tenths of a mile along Main Street (Route 70). The Center Village District, on the National Register since 1977, has no surviving 17th-century buildings, but it keeps a few 18th-century houses and many from the 19th century. Nearly all are wood frame and one and a half to two and a half stories tall. Charles Bulfinch's First Church of Christ, finished in 1816, faces the common, along with the 1868 Thayer Library and a 1908 town hall by Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow Jr.

North Village, along North Main Street (Route 117), is a smaller and plainer cluster. John Bennett built a house there in 1717 that still stands, and most of the district's 22 buildings went up before 1860 in modest Federal and Greek Revival forms, with clapboarded walls and sash windows. South Lancaster grew around Atlantic Union College, a Seventh-day Adventist school founded in 1882 that closed in 2018. The Nathaniel Thayer Estate on South Main Street and the college's Founder's Hall are both on the National Register.

Outside those villages the housing is much newer. Census estimates count about 3,000 homes with a median construction year of 1971. Roughly one in five predates 1940, and a little over half predate 1980. About 85 percent are owner-occupied, and only around 7 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. For most owners, the job is a single-family house from the later twentieth century. For a smaller group, it is a clapboard house whose trim and proportions are part of a recognized historic streetscape.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Half of Lancaster's homes were built after about 1971, and many of them are on their first or second round of siding. Vinyl is a reasonable fit for those houses, as long as the old layer comes off and the sheathing is inspected before new panels go on. Ask for an estimate that names the house wrap, the window flashing and the trim pieces. In Center Village and North Village, where wood clapboard defines the street, vinyl will change a house's appearance far more than it would on a newer road, so weigh that before choosing it.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The National Register nomination for North Village describes its houses as wood frame, one and a half or two and a half stories, clapboarded, with sash windows. Replacing boards on a house like that is mostly about matching the exposure and profile already there and keeping the corner boards and casings in proportion. Pre-primed boards with all sides sealed hold paint longer. About one in five Lancaster homes predates 1940. Any house built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules once painted surfaces are disturbed, so containment and cleanup belong in the plan.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives a painted lap look with less upkeep than wood, which suits owners of the town's mid- and late-century single-family homes. The boards are heavy and are cut with dust control, so the crew needs room to stage material near the house. Clearances above grade and above roof lines, plus flashing behind butt joints, are what make it perform. Ask that those details be written into the estimate. On an older house near the common, compare the reveal of the new board with the original clapboard before deciding.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: The Register descriptions of Lancaster's two historic villages mention clapboard rather than shingles. On those streets, cedar shingles are usually better saved for a rear wall, an ell, a barn or an addition. On a later house they can work well if the wall is built to dry: a rain-screen gap or drainage wrap behind them, stainless or hot-dipped nails, and a decision up front about stain, paint or natural weathering. Shingles on a wall shaded by trees stay damp longest and need that drainage most.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement is the moment to see what is under the siding. On a Lancaster house from the 1960s or 1970s, that may be original sheathing, little or no window flashing, and decades of patches. Strip the walls, check and repair the framing, then wrap and flash before the new material goes on. Houses built before 1978 call for lead-safe work practices. If the property is in or near the Center Village or North Village districts, ask the town whether anything governs its exterior before you choose a material.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On the Federal and Greek Revival houses in North Village and around the common, much of the character is in the trim: corner boards, window casings, cornices and, on the 1830 Joseph Andrews House, a full two-story temple front. Rot usually begins where water sits, at sills, cornice returns and the bottoms of corner boards. Repair in kind where the original profile deserves keeping. Where it does not, cellular PVC or primed composite stock takes paint and resists rot. Old painted trim on a pre-1978 house requires lead-safe handling.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Before swapping gutters on one of the older clapboard houses in Center Village or North Village, check whether the house originally had wood or built-in gutters at the cornice. Hanging aluminum on a cornice that was not designed for it changes the look of the front and can trap water behind the fascia. On later houses the basics apply: downspouts sized to the roof area, discharge carried away from the foundation, and guards where trees hang over the roof.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Most of Lancaster's historic houses are one and a half to two and a half stories, and the newer homes are mostly single-family, so roof work is usually manageable from ladders and roof brackets. The scope still deserves care. Find out whether there are old layers or board decking under the current shingles, specify ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, and balance intake and exhaust ventilation so the deck stays cold in winter. On a house near the common, keep the roof color and trim edges consistent with the street.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: For a split board, a loose panel or a soft spot under a window, a repair is often enough. The useful part of the job is finding out why it happened, whether a missing flashing, a gutter overflow or a sprinkler, and fixing that cause along with the boards. On older clapboard homes, matched boards and lead-safe handling of the old paint are part of doing the repair properly.

story: Upton was formed in 1735 from outlying parts of Mendon, Sutton, Hopkinton and Uxbridge. A half dozen streams turned small mills, but there was never enough water for large factories, so the town made its living from shoes and hats. Between 1730 and 1850 Upton was dotted with small shoe shops called ten-footers, and by 1837 it produced about a fifth of the boots made in Worcester County. In West Upton, William Knowlton built a hat company that became known as the largest women's hat factory in the world. Its 1872 Second Empire building at 134 Main Street was converted to senior housing in 1985.

The Upton Center Historic District takes in the town common and parts of Church, Main, Milford, North Main, Warren and School streets. The 1884 town hall and three mid-nineteenth-century churches stand there, and most buildings around the common date to the mid-1800s. Up North Main Street are the 1844 Polly Dean Bradish House and the 1740 Dr. Josiah Dean House, the only 18th-century house left in the center. The road ends at Pratt Pond. The 1938 hurricane destroyed the Congregational church's steeple, which was replaced in 1956 with one donated from Oxford.

Most homes in town are far younger. Upton grew from about 5,600 residents in 2000 to about 7,500 in 2010. Census estimates show roughly 3,100 homes with a median construction year of 1981. Fewer than half predate 1980, around 18 percent predate 1940, and close to 87 percent are owner-occupied. Upton State Forest covers nearly 2,800 acres, mostly within the town, including the last remaining Civilian Conservation Corps camp in Massachusetts.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: About half of Upton's houses were built in or after 1980, and many of them still have their first siding and builder-grade trim. Vinyl is a common replacement for homes of that age. Thicker panels lie flatter on long walls, and a matching soffit and fascia system cuts maintenance. Before panels go up, the wall should be opened at a few windows to see whether the original flashing did its job, because that is where water damage tends to hide on houses of this period. Get the house wrap and trim details in writing.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Around the common and along North Main Street, where most buildings date to the mid-1800s, wood clapboard is the material that fits. Patching an old wall means sourcing boards with the same exposure and keeping the original corner and window trim if it is sound. Back-priming each board before installation helps the paint last. Pre-1978 houses fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when paint is disturbed. Owners inside the Upton Center Historic District should ask the town whether anything applies before changing materials.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits the newer homes built during Upton's growth around the turn of the century, for owners who want painted lap siding without the upkeep of wood. The boards are heavy and must be cut with dust control, so staging space matters. On wooded lots, sort out delivery access and tree clearance before the material arrives. Clearances above grade and above roof lines, along with flashing behind butt joints, should appear in the written estimate rather than being left to the installer's judgment.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: On a lot near the state forest or any stand of trees, walls shaded by trees dry slowly. Cedar copes with that much better when it goes over a rain-screen mat or furring strips, so water drains and the back of each shingle can dry. Specify stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails, two per shingle, and decide on stain, paint or natural weathering before installation. Shingles can give a newer house a softer texture than lap siding. On an older house in the center, check what the house originally had before switching.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With the median home built around 1981, a large share of Upton houses are past forty years on their first exterior. A full replacement lets you deal with sheathing, house wrap and window flashing at once rather than piecemeal. Ask the estimate to explain what happens if rotted sheathing turns up, including how it will be priced and approved, so there are no surprises halfway through. For the town's older houses, built before 1978, lead-safe practices apply when painted materials come off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The mid-nineteenth-century buildings around Upton's common carry much of their detail in cornices, window heads and corner boards. On those houses, repair or replicate profiles instead of wrapping them in aluminum, which hides rot rather than stopping it. On newer homes, rot tends to show first at the bottoms of door casings, garage door jambs and rake boards. PVC or composite trim in those spots is a practical upgrade that takes paint and does not absorb water.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Where trees overhang a roof, and Upton has nearly 2,800 acres of state forest, leaves and needles fill gutters quickly. Guards matched to the kind of debris on your lot, downspouts sized to the roof, and extensions that carry water away from the foundation matter more than gutter size alone. Seamless aluminum keeps joints to a minimum, and hangers should be screwed into solid fascia. If the fascia behind an old gutter is soft, replace it before the new gutter goes up.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: The 1938 hurricane took down the steeple on Upton's Congregational church, and the replacement did not go up until 1956. Wind deserves attention on any roof in town. Follow the shingle manufacturer's high-wind nailing pattern, use a sealed starter course, and install drip edge plus ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys. On wooded lots, have limbs over the roof assessed before reroofing, since a new roof under a dead branch is a short-lived investment.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small damage, such as a cracked panel, a loose board or a soft corner, can often be fixed without redoing a whole wall. Matching the color of older vinyl may be difficult, so ask about borrowing a piece from a less visible wall. Find and stop the source of the water before the repair is closed up. On the older clapboard houses near the common, replacement boards should match the existing exposure, and lead-safe practices apply if the house predates 1978.

story: Ashland was assembled in 1846 from parts of Hopkinton, Holliston and Framingham, and the village was earlier called Unionville. The Boston and Worcester Railroad, built through in the 1830s, and mills on the Sudbury River set its early course. Stone's Public House went up beside the tracks in 1832. In 1878 Boston built reservoirs on the river, halting work on the Dwight Printing Company's granite mills. In the twentieth century Ashland became known as Clock Town: Henry Warren's synchronous timer led to Telechron, which with General Electric employed about 2,000 people at its 1950s peak.

The oldest civic buildings stand along Main Street in the center. The 1855 Ashland Town House is a two-and-a-half-story frame building in the Greek Revival style with Italianate brackets, clapboard siding and a granite foundation, facing the 1835 Congregational meeting house. The Ashland Historical Society is based in the 1748 Ocean House on Myrtle Street.

Most houses arrived later. A post-war boom began in the 1950s, and by the 1980s Ashland was mainly a residential suburb, with older development along Route 135 and shopping centers and condominiums along Route 126. Census estimates show about 8,100 homes with a median construction year of 1984, and only about one in eight predates 1940. Roughly three-quarters are owner-occupied and about 13 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. Ashland State Park, with its 157-acre reservoir, part of Hopkinton State Park and a 550-acre town forest are all within the town.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With the median Ashland home built around 1984, many houses still wear siding from the town's suburban growth years. Replacing it with vinyl is mostly about details: removing the old layer, checking the sheathing at window corners and deck ledgers, and choosing a panel that lies flat on long walls. For condominiums along the Route 126 corridor, find out whether the association controls color and profile before you collect estimates, since that can narrow the choice before any contractor visits.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the original material on Ashland's older buildings. The 1855 Town House on Main Street is clapboarded over a granite foundation. On one of the older houses near the center or along Route 135, matching board width and keeping the trim proportions intact matter more than any material upgrade. Primed, sealed boards installed over a drainage layer give paint a better chance. Pre-1978 paint brings EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules into play, so ask how dust and chips will be contained and cleaned up.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is an option for owners of later-built homes who want painted lap siding without wood's maintenance. The boards are heavy and are cut with dust control, so staging needs more thought on tight lots or on two- to four-unit buildings, which make up about 13 percent of Ashland's housing. Shared walls and driveways may mean coordinating with neighbors. In a quote, look for written ground and roof clearances, flashing at butt joints and the paint or factory-finish system being used.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can give a later suburban house more texture, but they need a wall that can dry. Lots near the Sudbury River, the reservoirs or wooded parkland may stay shaded and damp. On those, install shingles over a drainage mat, use stainless fasteners, and keep the bottom course clear of soil, mulch and roof surfaces. Decide on stain, paint or natural weathering before ordering, because the choice affects the grade of shingle worth buying.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Houses from Ashland's 1950s boom are now around seventy years old and may already have been resided once, possibly over the original. A full tear-off reveals the sheathing and framing that those layers hid. Houses built before 1978 need lead-safe practices when old painted siding or trim is disturbed. Ask for an estimate that separates tear-off, sheathing repair and new siding so you can compare bids line by line rather than on a single total.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Ashland's older buildings carry their character in trim. The Town House shows Italianate paired brackets, dentil moulding, broad corner pilasters and projecting window lintels. On a house with similar detail, repair the original pieces where possible and copy the rest. On newer homes, rot tends to start at door and garage casings and at the bottoms of corner boards. PVC in those places holds paint and does not soak up water, and it can be milled to match existing profiles.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: A July 1989 windstorm caused widespread tree damage in Ashland and damaged several homes. Trees near a house affect its gutters every year, not only in storms: leaves and twigs clog outlets, and overflow ends up against siding and foundations. Seamless gutters with properly sized downspouts, guards suited to the debris, and hangers screwed into solid fascia are the basics. Have overhanging limbs looked at before new gutters go up.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Ashland averages roughly 40 to 50 inches of snow a year, and nor'easters are frequent. That makes the eave details matter: ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys, enough attic insulation and ventilation to keep the deck cold, and drip edge that sends meltwater into the gutter rather than behind it. On condominiums and two- to four-unit buildings, a roof replacement usually needs co-owners to agree on timing, color and access before work starts.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs suit isolated problems such as a cracked vinyl panel, a dented section or a soft spot under a window. A good repair includes finding where the water came from. If the house was built before 1978 and the damage involves painted wood, lead-safe practices apply. A written estimate should say what will be replaced, how it will be matched and whether trim or flashing around the area is included.

story: Millbury began as the North Parish of Sutton, settled in 1716, and became its own town in 1813. Water power built it. John Singletary ran a mill on Singletary Brook from 1735, and the S & D Spinning Mill, built around 1753, is described as one of the oldest continuously operated mills in the United States. Asa Waters and his brother Elijah built mills on the Blackstone River making guns, scythes and sawmill equipment, with an armory dating to 1808. The Asa Waters Mansion on Elm Street, designed by Asher Benjamin and built between 1826 and 1832, is a three-story wood-frame house with a balustraded hip roof and two-story fluted columns.

Bramanville grew up around the Lapham Woolen Mill on Singletary Brook, built from 1879 on the site of the Burbank paper mills, which ran from 1775 to 1836. The mill owners also held workers' housing, a store and an 1883 fire station, all sold to the Mayo Woolen Company after Mowry Lapham died in 1893. Downtown, the 1828 Greek Revival First Presbyterian Society Meeting House by Elias Carter still stands at 20 Main Street.

Census estimates count about 5,800 homes in Millbury with a median construction year of 1965. Roughly a quarter predate 1940 and nearly two-thirds predate 1980. About three in four are owner-occupied, and around 17 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. The town's population rose from about 8,300 in 1950 to about 12,000 in 1970, a jump that lines up with that median year. Today Millbury sits where Route 146 meets the Mass Pike, on the southern edge of Worcester.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Nearly two-thirds of Millbury's homes predate 1980, so many have been resided at least once and some may carry vinyl or aluminum over the original wood. Before new vinyl goes on, stripping back to the sheathing lets the wall be checked; layering over old siding hides problems and can leave window and door trim looking sunken. On two- to four-unit buildings, about 17 percent of the town's housing, vinyl reduces how often large walls need repainting, which matters when several households share the upkeep.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard is the right match on Millbury's nineteenth-century houses near downtown and the old mill sites. A quarter of the town's homes predate 1940, so many walls still have original boards under paint or later layers. Matching exposure and profile keeps a patch from showing. For any home built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed, which is especially relevant on a house carrying more than a century of paint.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: On a two- or three-unit building, fiber cement gives a durable painted finish over a lot of wall area. The trade-off is weight and dust. Boards need staging space and dust-controlled cutting, which can be tight where buildings sit close together. Ask how ladders and staging will be arranged on a narrow lot, and get written clearances above grade and roofs plus flashing at butt joints. On a postwar single-family house, the same details apply with fewer logistics.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit a Millbury house that already has them, or a newer home where the owner wants natural texture. On lots near water or under heavy shade, shingles need a drainage gap behind them so they can dry from both sides. Use stainless nails, keep the bottom course clear of soil and mulch, and choose the finish before installation. If an older house is being restored, check under later siding for evidence of what the original wall looked like.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Houses from Millbury's growth between 1950 and 1970 are now more than fifty years old, and a full replacement is often the point to deal with what has been patched over the years. Remove the old layers, inspect sheathing and sills, add a continuous weather barrier, and flash every window and door before the new siding goes on. All of them were built before 1978, so lead-safe handling of old painted trim and siding belongs in the plan from the start.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Millbury's best-known buildings show what trim can carry: the 1828 meeting house on Main Street has a four-column portico under a pediment, and the Asa Waters Mansion has fluted two-story columns and corner pilasters. On a private home with similar detail, repair or copy the original profiles instead of covering them. On postwar houses, rot usually starts at sills, door casings and the bottoms of corner boards, and PVC or composite stock in those spots resists water. Pre-1978 painted trim needs lead-safe handling.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Millbury's history is a history of water: Singletary Brook, the Blackstone River and the 1944 Worcester Flood Diversion Channel all run through town. Around a single house the task is smaller but similar, getting roof water away from the foundation. Size downspouts to the roof area, add extensions or tie into drainage, and keep discharge off driveways and walks where it can freeze. Guards help where trees overhang the roof.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On a two- to four-unit building, a roof replacement affects every household, so timing, access and parking should be agreed among owners and tenants beforehand. On any older house, check for multiple layers of shingles and for board or skip sheathing underneath, since both change the scope. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys and balanced attic ventilation are worth specifying in writing so they are not left out to lower a bid.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A damaged section, whether a cracked panel, a split clapboard or a soft board near a downspout, can often be repaired without residing the house. The repair should include finding the source of the water. On pre-1978 homes, lead-safe practices apply when painted wood is cut or removed. Where an older siding color has faded, a repair patch may stand out, so discuss whether to take matching material from a less visible wall.

story: Northbridge was settled in 1704 as part of Mendon, later belonged to Uxbridge, and became a separate town in 1772. Its villages, including Whitinsville, Rockdale, Linwood, Riverdale, Northbridge Center and Plummer's Corner, grew along the Blackstone and Mumford rivers. The Whitin family shaped nearly all of them. Whitin Machine Works, which ran from 1831 to 1964, became the largest maker of textile machinery in the world, and the family built housing, schools and community buildings for its workers. Most of the town's 19th-century architecture survives.

That housing is still visible. The Whitinsville Historic District, on the National Register since 1983, covers the mill village that grew around Paul Whitin's 1826 brick mill, along with worker housing and the 1938 post office. In Rockdale, the Rockdale Common Housing District on McBride, Plantation and Taft streets holds tenements the Whitins built between about 1880 and 1920. They include six-unit rowhouses and triple-decker blocks from about 1917 with Colonial Revival porches and polygonal bays. The Linwood Historic District, around an 1866 cotton mill, contains a Second Empire owner's house plus tenements, dormitories and duplexes.

Census estimates count about 7,200 homes in Northbridge with a median construction year of 1973. About a quarter predate 1940 and a little over half predate 1980. Roughly 17 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, and about 70 percent are owner-occupied. The town grew again between 2000 and 2010, so mill-village blocks and three-story tenements share the town with much newer single-family houses.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: On a two- or three-family house, vinyl cuts down on repainting large walls, which matters when several households share the cost. On the Whitin-built tenements and duplexes in Whitinsville, Rockdale and Linwood, though, the trim gives the buildings their look: porch details, window bays and corner boards. Covering those with aluminum coil or oversized vinyl trim erases them. If vinyl is the choice, ask for a plan that keeps or replicates the trim rather than capping it, and for full tear-off instead of layering.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: About a quarter of Northbridge's homes predate 1940, and much of the town's 19th-century building stock survives. On those houses, new clapboard should match the old exposure and be primed on all sides before installation. On buildings with porches and bays like the Colonial Revival details on Rockdale's 1917 triple-deckers, the siding has to tie neatly into complicated trim, which takes more time than a plain wall. Homes built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits the town's later single-family homes, roughly half of which were built after 1973. It can also work on a multi-family building where the owner wants a painted finish that lasts longer between coats than wood. Staging is the main consideration: tenement blocks reach three stories, and the boards are heavy. Expect pump jacks or a lift, dust-controlled cutting, and written clearance and flashing details in the estimate.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit a single-family house on the edges of town, where the valley gives way to horse farms. On lots near the Mumford or Blackstone rivers or the West Hill Dam reservoir, shaded walls dry slowly. Shingles there should go over a drainage layer with stainless fasteners, and the bottom course should sit well above grade. For buildings inside the historic districts, check what the original wall was before switching to shingles.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: On a three-story multi-family building, a full replacement is a large job that runs up three floors and around porches. Plan staging, tenant access and a schedule that limits how long any wall stays open. On a 1960s or 1970s single-family house, the same steps apply on a smaller scale: strip, inspect sheathing, wrap, flash, then side. Northbridge has plenty of both, and many of each were built before 1978, so lead-safe practices are part of the work.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Rockdale tenements have Colonial Revival porches and polygonal bays, and the Linwood owner's house is Second Empire. Trim on buildings like these includes brackets, porch columns, railings and cornices, and it usually rots from the top surfaces down. Repair in kind where the detail is intact and replicate where it is not. Flash or slope horizontal surfaces so the new work sheds water better than the old did. Old paint on this trim calls for lead-safe handling.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Tall multi-family buildings collect a lot of roof water into a few downspouts. Size gutters and downspouts for the full roof area, carry discharge away from foundations, porches and walkways, and think about where water goes when neighboring houses sit close together. On single-family homes near the rivers or wooded edges of town, leaf guards help keep outlets clear. Hangers should go into solid fascia, so rotted boards behind old gutters need replacing first.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Northbridge's mix of three-story tenements and single-family homes means roof work varies widely. On tall buildings, staging and fall protection shape the schedule, and porch roofs are often low-slope surfaces that need a membrane rather than shingles. On newer single-family houses, the priorities are ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, balanced ventilation, and drip edge that carries water into the gutter.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small problems, like a cracked panel, a loose board or rot at a porch connection, can often be repaired without residing. Find the cause first, which is frequently an overflowing gutter or a missing piece of flashing. On pre-1978 buildings, lead-safe practices apply to painted wood. On a multi-family building, let tenants know when and where the work will happen so access and parking are sorted out ahead of time.

story: Harvard was settled in 1658 along the road linking Lancaster and Groton and incorporated in 1732, when its common was laid out. It stayed mostly agricultural until the mid-twentieth century, and apple orchards are still part of the landscape. The town is largely wooded, with rolling hills, fields and wetlands. Bare Hill Pond sits near the middle, and a ridgeline runs along the east side, where the Oak Ridge Observatory was built in 1931 at about 609 feet on Pinnacle Road.

The Harvard Center Historic District, on the National Register since 1997, radiates from the triangular common along Still River Road, Massachusetts Avenue, Oak Hill Road and Old Littleton Road. It covers about 125 acres and 59 historically significant houses from the 18th to the 20th centuries, though most buildings postdate 1831. Landmarks include the 1872 Gothic Revival town hall and the Romanesque Bromfield School and library. On Shaker Road, South Shaker Road and Maple Lane, the Harvard Shaker Village Historic District keeps buildings from a Shaker community known for plain architecture. Most are now private homes. Fruitlands sits on Prospect Hill, and the village of Still River lies on the west side of town.

Census estimates show about 2,300 homes, nearly 90 percent owner-occupied, with a median construction year of 1975. About 16 percent predate 1940, close to 60 percent predate 1980, and only about 3 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. The town's Historical Commission oversees changes in the Harvard Common and Shaker Village historic districts under state law, and a 2025 public hearing dealt with new windows, a deck and a barn renovation.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: In Harvard's local historic districts, around the common and in Shaker Village, the Historical Commission oversees exterior changes, so a move to vinyl there should start with a conversation with the commission. Elsewhere, most homes are later-twentieth-century single-family houses, often surrounded by trees, where vinyl's low upkeep has appeal. Choose a heavier panel, leave room for trees close to walls, and have the sheathing checked during tear-off before anything new goes on.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the natural choice for the older houses around the common, where most buildings date from after 1831 and some reach back to the 1700s. Matching exposure, corner boards and window casings keeps a repair consistent with the neighbors. Inside the Harvard Common district, check with the Historical Commission before changing materials or details. Homes built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when old paint is disturbed, which affects how scraping and board removal are handled.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can give a newer Harvard home a painted lap look without the upkeep of wood. Tree cover is the main site issue: keep the bottom course clear of soil and leaf litter, and follow the manufacturer's clearances above roofs and decks. Get butt-joint flashing and the finish system in writing. On a house inside one of the local historic districts, the commission's review comes before the material choice, not after.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: The Shakers who settled in Harvard were known for plain architecture, and their surviving buildings are now mostly private homes. Owners in or near the Shaker Village district who are thinking about shingles, or any change of material, should start with the Historical Commission. On newer houses in wooded parts of town, cedar shingles suit the setting, but shaded walls dry slowly. Install them over a drainage mat with stainless fasteners and decide on the finish ahead of time.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Close to 60 percent of Harvard's homes predate 1980. For a house from the 1960s or 1970s, a full replacement is a chance to add a proper weather barrier and window flashing, which earlier work may lack. Strip to the sheathing, repair what is soft, and confirm whether the house is inside a local historic district before choosing materials. For houses built before 1978, lead-safe practices apply when old paint is disturbed during removal.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Harvard Center district mixes Greek Revival, Gothic Revival and Romanesque buildings, and the houses around the common carry trim from several eras. Restoring cornices, window casings and porch details in kind keeps a house consistent with its street. On newer homes, rot-prone spots such as door casings, sills and the bottoms of corner boards are good candidates for PVC, which takes paint and resists moisture. In the local districts, trim changes visible from the street fall under the commission's oversight.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Harvard is largely wooded, and on most lots leaves and twigs are the main gutter problem. Guards matched to the debris, larger downspouts and regular cleaning keep water moving. Near Bare Hill Pond and the town's wetlands, direct discharge so it does not pool against foundations or carry soil toward the water. On older houses near the common, keep the gutter profile in line with the house's period.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Houses on the eastern ridge, where the observatory sits at about 609 feet, and on open hillsides near the orchards can take more wind than those in sheltered spots. Use the shingle manufacturer's high-wind nailing pattern, seal the starter course, and put ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys. On wooded lots, trim limbs back from the roof before new shingles go on. In the local historic districts, ask the commission about roofing material and color first.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: For a few damaged boards or a cracked panel, a repair usually makes more sense than new siding. Fix the cause, such as a leaking gutter or missing flashing, at the same time. On painted houses built before 1978, plan for lead-safe handling. In the Harvard Common and Shaker Village districts, like-for-like repairs are the simplest path, but asking the Historical Commission first avoids surprises.

story: Milton sits in the hilly ground between the Neponset River and the Blue Hills, with Brush Hill on the west side and Milton Hill on the east. It is an old town, organized in 1640 and incorporated in 1662, and its first industry grew up along the Neponset at Lower Mills, where a grist mill of 1634 was later converted into the Walter Baker chocolate factory. In the China Trade era, Boston families built country estates on Milton Hill, Brush Hill and Upper Canton Avenue. Many of those estates were divided into house lots after World War II, and home building slowed sharply after the 1960s.

That history shows up in the Census numbers. The median home dates to about 1945, close to half of all houses were built before 1940, and roughly four in five predate 1980. About 85 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and only around 12 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings, so most of the roughly 9,300 housing units are lived in by the people who own them.

Eight National Register historic districts cover parts of town, among them Milton Hill, Brush Hill, Milton Centre, Scott's Woods and the Railway Village near East Milton Square, which grew after the 1826 Granite Railway and lists Colonial and Greek Revival buildings. On Milton Hill the district is described as high-style homes from the 18th to early 20th centuries. For exterior work, that means a lot of original wood, old paint layers, and trim profiles worth matching rather than covering. The hills and the Blue Hills edge also mean exposed sites: the Blue Hill Observatory records an average wind speed above 15 mph at the summit.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl makes the most sense on Milton's later housing, the lots carved from estates after World War II, where the original siding is often plain and the trim simple. On older houses in the Milton Hill or Railway Village areas, vinyl can bury corner boards, window casings and cornice detail, so the trim should be measured and detailed before any panel goes up. With roughly four in five homes built before 1980, existing painted surfaces may contain lead, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) work rules apply whenever that paint is disturbed during tear-off.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard is the original skin on a large share of Milton's older houses, and close to half the town was built before 1940. In the Railway Village, where the National Register lists Colonial and Greek Revival buildings, replacing failed boards with matching exposure and profile keeps the wall reading as it was built. Before ordering, a few boards should be pulled to check the sheathing and to confirm the existing reveal, since older clapboard was often laid at narrower exposures than stock product.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can stand in for painted clapboard on postwar Milton houses where the owner wants a wood look with less repainting. It is heavy and needs careful handling and the right fasteners, which matters on the hilly lots common between the Neponset and the Blue Hills, where staging on slopes takes extra setup. On the older historic streets, the board width and exposure should be chosen to match neighboring wood siding so the change is not obvious from the street.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingle siding has a real history here: architect William Ralph Emerson, known for the Shingle style, has a place in Milton's story. On estate-era houses and later homes along Brush Hill and Canton Avenue, cedar shingles are a period-appropriate choice. Weaving at the corners, coursing that lines up with window heads, and a ventilated or drained backing all help shingles last. Exposed hillside walls facing the prevailing wind deserve a close look at flashing above windows and doors.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full tear-off on one of Milton's pre-1940 houses usually exposes board sheathing, old building paper and sometimes earlier siding layers. That is the time to repair rot, add a modern water-resistive barrier and re-flash every window. Because so many houses in town date from before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when old painted siding comes off. Homes inside one of the eight National Register districts may have documented features worth keeping, so photos of the existing trim before demolition are a good idea.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is where Milton's older houses carry most of their character: cornices, corner boards, window casings and porch details on Greek Revival and later buildings on Milton Hill and around East Milton Square. Rotted sections can often be replaced piece by piece with matching profiles instead of wrapping everything in coil stock. PVC or primed wood are both options; the choice should depend on how visible the piece is and whether the rest of the house stays painted wood.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Wooded lots near the Blue Hills Reservation and the old estate grounds drop a lot of leaves, and the many kettle ponds left by glaciers make it worth thinking about where downspouts discharge. Larger downspouts and guards suit houses under mature trees. On older homes with built-in or box gutters, the wood gutter and the fascia behind it should be inspected for rot before choosing between relining and switching to hung aluminum gutters.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Milton's hills and the Blue Hills edge leave some houses exposed to steady wind; the Blue Hill Observatory records an annual average above 15 mph at its summit. On exposed sites, shingles rated for higher wind and full-length starter strips at eaves and rakes are worth specifying. Older roofs on pre-1940 houses may have board decking with gaps that need new sheathing, and chimneys on these homes often need re-flashing when the roof is replaced.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Localized damage, such as a few split clapboards, a loose shingle course or a soft spot under a window, can often be repaired without replacing a whole wall. The aim is to match the existing material and exposure, find the source of any water, and fix the flashing along with the boards. On pre-1978 houses, lead-safe practices apply when painted siding is cut or removed.

story: Melrose was farmland known as North Malden until the Boston and Maine Railroad arrived in the 1840s and put three stops in what are now Wyoming Hill, Melrose/Cedar Park and Melrose Highlands. Boston workers looking for a country setting started commuting, the town incorporated in 1850, and through the late 1800s farmland was split into smaller lots for houses and shops. Melrose became a city in 1900.

Today the city reads as a commuter suburb built mostly before World War II. According to the Census, the median house dates to about 1938, a little over half were built before 1940, and roughly 84 percent are older than 1980. About two-thirds of homes are owner-occupied and around 14 percent of housing sits in two- to four-unit buildings, so a fair number of jobs involve a shared building or a landlord. There are close to 12,800 housing units in all.

Neighborhood names follow the rail stops and the land: Wyoming, Cedar Park, Melrose Highlands, Mount Hood, the East Side, Horace Mann, and Oak Grove/Pine Banks. Ell Pond sits near the center, Swains and Towners Ponds are on the east side, and the eastern edge of the Middlesex Fells, Sewall Woods and Pine Banks Park bring trees close to many yards. Downtown along Main Street is a National Register district listed for its late Victorian and revival-style civic buildings. Before changing the look of an older house, it is reasonable to ask the city whether any local review applies.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is common on the many pre-1940 houses in Melrose that were resided decades ago, and it can be a practical choice for a two-family where several owners or a landlord want low upkeep. The trade-off is detail: older houses from the railroad-suburb years often have window casings, frieze boards and porch trim that vinyl accessories cannot reproduce well. Those pieces should be planned first. Because most homes predate 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Much of Melrose was built on lots split from farmland in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and painted wood clapboard was the usual cladding for that era. Replacing worn sections with new clapboard keeps the original look and lets the house be painted to match its neighbors. Pre-primed, back-primed boards and a proper rainscreen gap help paint last longer, particularly on shaded walls near the Fells or Sewall Woods that stay damp after rain.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable fit for a Melrose owner who wants the lines of painted clapboard without as much repainting. Where houses stand close together on lots carved out in the late 1800s, cutting dust and staging space between buildings need planning, and wet-cutting or a dust-collecting saw should be used near a neighbor's windows. Trim details at corners and windows should be worked out before ordering so the boards meet the existing casings cleanly.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit older homes where the original siding was shingle or where a gable or upper story was shingled above clapboard on the lower walls. On wooded streets near Pine Banks Park or the Fells, shingles shaded by trees dry slowly, so a breathable backing and good clearance from soil and roof surfaces help them last. Stained or naturally weathered shingles also avoid the peel-and-scrape cycle of painted clapboard.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A complete re-side on a house from Melrose's growth years may start with removing one or more later layers over the original wood, and any older material should be identified before it is disturbed. Once the wall is open, the sheathing, window flashing and any rot at sills should be addressed before new material goes on. With roughly four in five homes built before 1980, lead-safe practices apply when painted wood is removed. For two- and three-unit buildings, schedule and access should be agreed with every owner or tenant in advance.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Porches, window casings, cornices and rake boards take the most weather on Melrose's older houses, and they are often the first wood to rot. Where only parts of a porch or cornice have failed, matching profiles can be milled or bought and set in without stripping the whole house. Cellular PVC works well for low, splash-prone pieces such as porch skirts and bottom trim, with painted wood kept where profiles need to match the original.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Mature trees around the Fells, Sewall Woods and Pine Banks drop a heavy leaf load, so oversized downspouts and leaf guards are worth considering on wooded streets. Close lot spacing means downspouts should discharge away from both the home's foundation and the neighbor's. On older houses, check whether the fascia and rafter tails are sound before hanging new gutters, since new gutters on soft wood will not hold.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On Melrose houses from the late 1800s and early 1900s that have dormers or porch roofs tying into walls, a replacement involves a lot of step and counter flashing. A tear-off is the time to check the decking, since older roofs often sit on spaced boards. Valleys and the joints where porch roofs meet the house should get ice-and-water membrane, and chimneys should be re-flashed rather than sealed over.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small repairs are common on older homes: a cracked board, a section damaged by a gutter overflow, or rot under a window sill. The repair should match the existing siding and exposure, and the cause of the damage should be fixed at the same time. In a two-family, a repair on one unit's wall should be coordinated with the other owner or tenant. On pre-1978 houses, lead-safe practices apply when painted siding is disturbed.
