story: Reading is an old town that grew up mostly in the 20th century. It was incorporated in 1644, and Parker Tavern, built in 1694, still stands as its oldest surviving building. The Andover-Medford Turnpike, now Route 28, came through in 1806 and the Boston and Maine Railroad in 1845. Through the 1800s the town made furniture, clocks, organ pipes, shoes and caskets, and by the early 1900s it had become a small residential community with commuter service to Boston. After World War II growth picked up quickly: population rose about 37 percent between 1950 and 1960.

Census figures match that story. The median home in Reading dates to about 1960, only around a quarter were built before 1940, and roughly three in four predate 1980. About 82 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and only about 7 percent of housing is in two- to four-unit buildings, so most of the town's nearly 10,000 housing units are single-family homes owned by the people living in them.

The older core still has depth. The Common Historic District, centered at Main and Salem Streets, includes an 1817 Federal-style house and a row of 19th-century houses on Harnden and Salem Streets. The Woburn Street Historic District, between Summer and Temple Streets, has sixteen houses, mostly Colonial Revival and Queen Anne, along with Federal, Greek Revival, Italianate, Shingle-style and Craftsman examples. Reading has close to 90 individual National Register listings in all. Outside that core, work is more likely to involve postwar houses that are now due for their second or third round of siding and roofing.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With a median build year around 1960, a big share of Reading's houses are postwar homes with simple walls and modest trim, which is where vinyl works well. Many have already been re-sided once, so a new job may start with removing an older layer and checking the sheathing underneath. A heavier panel and properly flashed window openings make a bigger difference than the color choice. On houses built before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when old painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The older streets near the Common and along Woburn Street were built with painted wood siding, and the Woburn Street district alone includes Federal, Greek Revival, Italianate and Queen Anne houses. On homes like those, new clapboard should match the existing exposure and corner treatment so a repaired wall blends with the rest. Back-priming the boards and leaving a drainage gap behind them helps the paint hold up between repaints.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a good match for Reading's many postwar houses when the owner wants a painted-board look with longer intervals between repaints. The material is heavy and brittle until fastened, so it should be stored flat and cut with dust control. Window and door trim details need to be decided at the start, because fiber cement usually sits thicker than the old siding and can leave existing casings looking recessed.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are part of Reading's architecture too: the Woburn Street Historic District includes a Shingle-style house at 206 Woburn Street. On homes with shingled gables or full shingle walls, replacement shingles should match the existing exposure and corner style. Shingles last longest when they can dry from both sides, so a ventilated underlayment is worth considering, especially on shaded walls near conservation land.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a 1950s or 1960s Reading house usually means stripping one or two layers, checking the sheathing, and adding a modern water-resistive barrier. Window flashing is often the weak point on houses of this age, so every opening should be re-flashed while the wall is open. Insulation can be added at the same time if the owner plans for it. Lead-safe (RRP) rules apply on pre-1978 houses when painted siding comes off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On postwar houses, trim tends to be simple: fascia, rake boards, corner boards and window casings. Those are often the first pieces to rot, especially at the bottom of corner boards and window sills. Older homes near the Common and on Woburn Street have more elaborate cornices and porch details that may need custom profiles. In either case, replacing only the failed pieces and sealing the joints properly can keep a sound house from needing a full re-side.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Reading has a lot of conservation land and vernal pools, and drainage matters on lots near wet areas. Downspouts should carry water well away from the foundation, and extensions or underground lines may be worth it where the yard slopes back toward the house. Lots with mature trees benefit from guards and larger downspouts, and fascia boards should be checked for soundness before new gutters are hung.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On Reading's postwar houses with simple gable or hip roofs, the main items on a replacement are decking condition, ventilation, and flashing at chimneys and walls. Ridge and soffit venting is often inadequate on houses of this era and is worth correcting during a tear-off. Older homes in the historic core may have steeper roofs and more dormers, which add flashing work and time.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs usually involve a few damaged boards, a section behind a leaking gutter, or rot around a window. The replacement material should match the existing siding, and the water source should be found and fixed at the same time. On a postwar house that has already been re-sided, matching an older vinyl color or profile can take some searching. Lead-safe practices apply when painted siding on a pre-1978 house is disturbed.

story: Stoughton was set off from Dorchester in 1726 and spent most of its first two centuries as a farming town that turned into a shoemaking center. A local history of its old houses, updated from a 1967 survey by Bertha Reynolds for the Massachusetts Historical Commission, describes the town until about 1900 as villages of single homes separated by woods and farms: North Stoughton with a church and store, South Stoughton with a railroad station, West Stoughton with several factories, and the Center with stores and churches. The same history notes that many early houses have been lost and that the survivors have been altered for modern use.

Most of today's housing came much later. The Census puts the median home at about 1969, with only around 17 percent built before 1940 and roughly 71 percent before 1980. About three-quarters of homes are owner-occupied and around 10 percent of housing is in two- to four-unit buildings, across roughly 11,700 units. In practice that means a large stock of homes from the 1950s through the 1970s, many now on their second set of siding and roofing, plus a smaller group of older houses around the Square, West Street and Bay Road.

The landscape matters for exterior work. Ames Long Pond, the Bird Street Sanctuary and other conservation land keep woods close to many neighborhoods, and the town's highest hill rises to about 350 feet. Heavy snow is a real factor: in the 2022 blizzard, Stoughton recorded 30.9 inches, the highest total in Massachusetts.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl suits the 1950s to 1970s houses that make up much of Stoughton, where wall lines are simple and trim is modest. On a re-side, the condition of the sheathing and the window flashing matters more than the panel itself, so a few test openings before ordering are worthwhile. Houses near woods and ponds stay shaded and damp, which favors a siding that does not need paint. On homes built before 1978, lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The older houses around Stoughton Square, West Street and Bay Road are the ones most likely to have original wood clapboard under later layers. Where the owner wants to keep or return to wood, the new boards should match the original exposure and be primed on all sides before installation. Because local history notes that surviving early houses have been altered over time, the existing trim and wall layers should be opened and checked before planning the new siding.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement works well on Stoughton's postwar houses for owners who want a painted-board look with less upkeep than wood. It holds paint longer than wood, but the cut edges and butt joints need to be sealed and flashed according to the manufacturer's instructions. On houses with long, uninterrupted walls, planning the joint layout ahead of time keeps seams from lining up in a visible column.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a less common choice on Stoughton's newer housing but suit the older houses left from its farming and village years and owners who want natural wood. Homes near Ames Long Pond or the Bird Street Sanctuary sit among trees, where shingles dry slowly, so a breathable underlayment and a gap at the bottom course help prevent rot. Stain or natural weathering avoids the peeling that paint can bring on shaded walls.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year around 1969, many Stoughton houses are on their original or second siding and are reaching the point where a full replacement is worth considering. Opening the walls is a chance to replace damaged sheathing, add a water-resistive barrier, and re-flash windows that were installed decades ago. Houses built before 1978 call for lead-safe (RRP) handling if old painted siding comes off. Insulation upgrades can be scheduled into the same project.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Fascia, soffits and rake boards on 1960s and 1970s houses are often original wood and are frequently the first parts to rot, especially where gutters overflow. Replacing them with primed wood or PVC and adding vented soffit material can address both rot and attic ventilation. On older homes around the Square, cornices and window casings may need profiles matched rather than wrapped.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Heavy snow is a real concern in Stoughton, which recorded 30.9 inches in the 2022 blizzard, the highest total in the state that storm. Gutters should be hung with hidden hangers spaced closely enough to carry snow and ice loads. Wooded lots near ponds and conservation land drop leaves and needles, so guards and larger downspouts help, and downspouts should discharge well away from foundations.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Snow load and ice dams are the main issues for roofing here, given storms like the 2022 blizzard that left Stoughton with more than 30 inches. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and in valleys, along with balanced soffit and ridge ventilation, reduces the risk of ice damming. Many 1950s-1970s roofs have had more than one layer installed, so a full tear-off and deck inspection is the usual starting point.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs often cover a few cracked panels, storm damage after a high-wind event, or rot behind a leaking gutter. The goal is to match the existing material, fix the source of any water, and leave the wall sealed. Faded siding may not match new stock exactly, so pulling replacement pieces from a less visible wall is one option. When painted siding on a pre-1978 house is disturbed, lead-safe practices apply.

story: Wakefield was settled in 1638 as part of Lynn Village, incorporated as South Reading in 1812, and renamed in 1868 after Cyrus Wakefield, whose Rattan Works grew into a company that once employed a thousand people. The railroad arrived in 1844, and the town's suburban growth followed. On Yale Avenue, near the center, a National Register district preserves eight houses, seven of them from the 1860s and 1870s, mostly Italianate, built largely for Boston businessmen. Southwest of the town center, the Wakefield Park district along Park Avenue was laid out in 1888 as a garden suburb, with houses mixing Queen Anne, Shingle and Colonial Revival details.

According to the Census, the median house in Wakefield dates to about 1956, about a third were built before 1940, and roughly 71 percent predate 1980. About 71 percent of homes are owner-occupied and around 21 percent of housing is in two- to four-unit buildings, so shared walls, multiple owners and tenants are part of many exterior projects. There are about 11,750 housing units in town.

Neighborhoods follow the water. Lake Quannapowitt, about 247 acres, anchors downtown and the West Side, Lakeside and East Side, while Crystal Lake serves as a drinking-water reservoir. Greenwood covers most of the south end, Woodville the center-east, and Montrose the northeast near Heron Pond. Storm exposure is real: a 2020 microburst snapped trees and downed lines, with the heaviest damage in Greenwood. Wakefield has close to 95 National Register properties, including the Church-Lafayette Streets and Common districts.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a common choice for Wakefield's postwar houses and for the two- to four-unit buildings that make up about a fifth of local housing, where landlords and co-owners often want low maintenance. Long walls on a multi-family building need careful attention to panel expansion and joint layout. On older houses with ornate trim, such as those near Yale Avenue or Park Avenue, detail should be planned before panels go up. Lead-safe (RRP) rules apply on pre-1978 houses when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Painted clapboard is the original siding on many of Wakefield's older houses, including the 1860s and 1870s Italianate homes in the Yale Avenue district. Matching the exposure and corner treatment of the original boards keeps a repair or partial replacement from standing out. Boards should be primed on all sides, and a drainage gap behind them helps the paint last on walls facing Lake Quannapowitt or other open, windy exposures.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners in Wakefield who want the look of painted clapboard with less frequent repainting, whether on a postwar single-family or an older two-family. It is heavy, so staging on tight lots between multi-family buildings needs planning, and cutting dust should be controlled near neighbors. Trim at windows and corners should be designed in advance because fiber cement is often thicker than the old siding.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles are part of Wakefield's building history: the Wakefield Park district on Park Avenue includes houses combining Shingle and Colonial Revival styles. On homes like these, replacing shingles with matching exposure and coursing keeps the original look. On wooded lots in Greenwood or Montrose, shingles shaded by trees stay damp longer, so a ventilated backing and clearance at the bottom course help them last.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a 1950s house or an older multi-family usually involves stripping existing layers, repairing sheathing, adding a water-resistive barrier and re-flashing windows. With about 71 percent of Wakefield's homes built before 1980, lead-safe (RRP) practices are often required when old paint is removed. For two- and three-unit buildings, the schedule should be agreed with all owners and tenants, and access to each side of the building planned in advance.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Older houses near the Common, on Yale Avenue and in the Wakefield Park area were built in Italianate, Queen Anne and related styles, which usually means more cornice, porch and window trim than a postwar house carries. Where those pieces have rotted, matching profiles can be milled and installed in sections. Postwar houses have simpler fascia, rake and corner boards, which can be replaced in primed wood or PVC. Sealing joints well and fixing gutter overflow helps prevent repeat rot.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Mature trees across Greenwood, Woodville and Montrose drop a lot of debris, and the 2020 microburst showed how much damage falling limbs can do. Gutter guards, larger downspouts and sturdy hidden hangers help. On lots close to Lake Quannapowitt, ponds or other wet ground, downspouts should carry water well clear of foundations. On older houses, check the condition of the fascia before hanging new gutters.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Wakefield has seen heavy snow, including 27.5 inches during the 2013 Nemo storm, and strong wind, including the 2020 microburst in Greenwood. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, adequate ventilation, and shingles with higher wind ratings make sense on exposed houses. Older homes with steep roofs, dormers and porches need more flashing work, and decking on pre-1940 houses should be checked during tear-off.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs commonly involve storm-damaged panels, a few rotted boards, or a section behind a leaking gutter. The goal is to match the existing siding and fix the water source at the same time. After a storm, it helps to photograph the damage before anything is removed, and to check the trim and flashing nearby as well as the siding itself. When painted siding on a pre-1978 house is cut or removed, lead-safe practices apply.

story: Bellingham was settled in 1713 and incorporated in 1719, mostly on land that had been part of the old Dedham Grant, with the Charles River running through it. Early descriptions call much of the ground swampy, and during the industrial era several ponds were built on that wet land to power mills. The best-documented mill settlement was Caryville, in the northeast corner along the Franklin line. Its mill opened in 1813, and William H. Cary later rebuilt and enlarged it and put up three tenement houses for workers. The village's big 1918 mill building stood until it was demolished in 2016.

The Bellingham most residents know took shape in the 1960s. Population roughly doubled between 1960 and 1970, from under 7,000 to nearly 14,000, and Interstate 495 was built across the north end of town in 1965. Caryville faded as a separate village as the suburbs grew around it. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1973 for the town's roughly 6,700 homes. About 62 percent were built before 1980 and only about 12 percent before 1940. Close to four in five are owner-occupied, and about 7.5 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings.

For exterior work, the typical Bellingham project is a house about half a century old that is on its second or third round of siding, roofing and gutters. The north end along I-495 and Route 126 has grown commercially, while the south is mostly suburban. Because so much of the town was once wet ground, moisture is worth watching at foundations, sill plates and the bottom courses of siding. The smaller group of pre-1940 houses are the exception and call for a closer look at original materials before anything is removed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Most Bellingham houses date from the 1960s through the 1980s, so new vinyl usually replaces an earlier generation of siding rather than original wood. The old layer should come off so the sheathing can be inspected; covering over it hides any soft spots. Pay particular attention to the lowest courses and the corners closest to the ground on lots that were once swamp or sit near the old mill ponds, since trapped moisture tends to show up there first. Starter strips and J-channel should leave the bottom edge able to drain.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: About 12 percent of Bellingham homes were built before 1940, and those older houses are where clapboard makes the most sense, though it also gives postwar houses a more traditional face than vinyl. If original clapboard survives under later siding, some of it can occasionally be repaired instead of replaced, depending on how much rot there is at sills and window heads. Wood clapboard needs priming on all sides before installation. Houses built before 1978 may have lead paint, so EPA lead-safe practices apply whenever old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank is a reasonable choice for Bellingham owners replacing tired siding on houses from the town's 1960s and 1970s growth years. It is much heavier than vinyl and has to be nailed into framing or solid sheathing, so the condition of the wall behind it matters more. The manufacturer's clearances above grade, decks and roof lines should be kept, which is worth checking on houses that sit low on damp ground. Factory-painted boards cut down on repainting, but cut ends still need to be sealed.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are not the obvious match for a 1970s Bellingham house, but they suit older homes and work well as an accent on gables or entries. Shingles need to dry from behind, so a ventilated rainscreen or a drainable housewrap is a good idea, especially on shaded walls or near the Charles River and the town's ponds, where the air stays humid. Owners should decide up front whether to let the cedar weather naturally or keep it stained, since stain has to be renewed every several years.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement makes sense when a Bellingham house from the 1960s or 1970s has original or first-generation siding that is cracked, faded or loose on several walls. Doing every wall at once lets the house be stripped to sheathing, wrapped again and have its windows and doors flashed in the right order, which is hard to do one side at a time. With roughly 62 percent of local homes built before 1980, it is also the moment to handle any lead-painted trim or siding under EPA lead-safe rules.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On Bellingham's postwar houses, trim is usually where rot shows up first: fascia behind overflowing gutters, window sills, garage door jambs and corner boards close to the ground. Replacing those pieces with cellular PVC or primed composite stock reduces future painting. On the town's older houses, matching the original wood profiles keeps the house consistent. Trim repairs should be done before or during a siding job, not afterward, so flashing and drip edges can be tied in correctly behind the new siding.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Bellingham's mean elevation is listed at under 300 feet, and much of the land was described as swampy before mills and roads changed it. That makes it important for gutters and downspouts to carry roof water well away from the foundation instead of dropping it beside the house. Downspout extensions, splash blocks or underground leaders should be planned around the lot's actual grading. Where trees overhang the roof, guards can reduce cleaning, but the guard type should match what actually falls into the gutters.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: A large share of Bellingham roofs sit on houses from the 1960s and 1970s building wave, and many of those are on at least their second asphalt roof. A full tear-off, rather than a layover, lets the decking be inspected and replaced where it has softened. Ventilation is often the weak point on houses of that age: soffit intake and ridge exhaust should be balanced to keep the attic dry. Ice and water barrier along the eaves and in valleys helps limit winter leaks from ice dams.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Not every problem calls for new siding. A few cracked vinyl panels, a loose corner, a section torn off in a storm or a run of rotted boards above a deck can usually be fixed on their own. The main difficulty on older vinyl is matching color and profile, since many lines from past decades are discontinued. If an exact match is not available, panels can sometimes be borrowed from a less visible wall and replaced there with a close match.

story: Europeans settled Lunenburg in 1718, and the town was incorporated in 1728. The oldest part of town still shows that history. The Lunenburg Historic District, added to the National Register in 1988, covers about 102 acres along Main Street between two triangular intersections and includes 77 historically significant buildings. Most are wood-frame houses built in the vernacular styles of their day, with Federal and Greek Revival especially well represented. The Cushing House, from about 1724, and the Stillman Stone House, from about 1730, are among the oldest.

Outside the center, the town was shaped by water and by growth after World War II. Population rose about 78 percent in the 1940s and another 62 percent in the 1950s. Hickory Hills Lake, a privately owned 319-acre reservoir first flooded in 1926, became a lake community after a corporation bought it in 1935 and built roads around it. Lake Shirley, shared with the town of Shirley, has a shoreline described as heavily developed with year-round homes and a few seasonal cottages. On Whalom Lake, the Whalom Park amusement park closed in 2000, and its site became a 240-unit apartment complex.

Census estimates put the median year built at about 1972 for Lunenburg's roughly 4,900 homes. About 60 percent were built before 1980 and about 12.5 percent before 1940, and around 81 percent are owner-occupied. The town sits at about 500 feet. For exterior work, lake houses need careful moisture detailing and good drainage, postwar homes are often due for a full round of roofing and siding, and the Main Street houses call for a lighter hand with original wood.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Much of Lunenburg's housing went up in the decades after World War II, and vinyl is a practical option on houses from that era. On lake properties around Lake Shirley and Hickory Hills Lake, walls facing open water take more wind-driven rain, so the housewrap and window flashing behind the panels matter more than the brand on the box. Darker colors on sunny south and west walls should be rated for heat. Old siding is best removed rather than covered so the sheathing can be checked.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The 77 historic buildings in the Lunenburg Historic District along Main Street are mostly wood-frame, and wood clapboard is the natural match there. When boards fail, replacing only the damaged runs with the same profile and exposure keeps the house consistent with its neighbors. Owners in the district may want to ask the town whether any local review applies before changing materials. Many of these houses predate 1978, so EPA lead-safe rules apply when old paint is scraped, sanded or removed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives a painted-clapboard look on Lunenburg's postwar houses and lake homes with less upkeep than wood. It is heavy, so the wall behind it should be sound, and it should be cut with dust control because of silica. Near Lake Shirley, Whalom Lake and Hickory Hills Lake, where moisture runs high, the bottom edge needs the manufacturer's clearance above decks, patios and roof lines. Cut ends should be sealed before the boards go up, and joints should be flashed.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit some of Lunenburg's lake houses and older homes, and left untreated they weather to a soft gray. On sites close to the water, shingles dry more slowly, so a ventilated rainscreen behind them helps. Stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails avoid rust streaks. One advantage of shingles is that individual pieces can be replaced as they wear, without disturbing a whole wall, which makes long-term upkeep easier on houses that see a lot of weather off the lakes.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement makes the most sense on Lunenburg houses from the 1950s through the 1970s, when the town grew fastest, if the siding is worn out on every wall. Stripping to sheathing lets damaged boards be replaced, gaps in insulation be seen and windows be flashed again in the right order. In the Main Street historic district, removing all of a house's original wood is harder to justify, and selective repair is usually the better first step before deciding on a full tear-off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Federal and Greek Revival houses on Main Street depend on their wide corner boards, cornices and window casings for their character, so trim replacement there should copy the original profiles closely. On postwar homes the work is more about rot at fascia, rake boards and window sills, and cellular PVC or composite trim can cut down on repainting. In either case, joints should be detailed so water drains away, and new trim should be installed with flashing above windows and doors.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lots near Lake Shirley, Whalom Lake and Hickory Hills Lake often slope toward the water, so downspouts should discharge where roof runoff will not cut a channel down the bank; the Hickory Hills lake management group reported shoreline erosion in 2012. Where trees overhang the roof, guards reduce cleaning but should suit the debris. On the older Main Street houses, gutter style and size should fit the cornice rather than hide it. Hangers need to be fastened into solid wood to carry winter ice.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Ice dams are a common winter problem on roofs with poor attic ventilation, and many of Lunenburg's houses from the 1950s and 1960s were not built with much. A replacement is the time to add balanced soffit and ridge venting and to run ice and water barrier along the eaves and in valleys. During tear-off, the decking should be checked; older plank decks sometimes need new sheathing over them. On lake houses, flashing at walls and chimneys deserves extra care because of the added moisture.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small repairs, such as replacing a few cracked vinyl panels, a rotted clapboard or a section damaged by a falling branch, can usually be done without disturbing the rest of the wall. On older wood houses, matching the original exposure and profile keeps the repair from standing out, and the new wood should be primed on all sides. On vinyl, finding a matching color can take some searching, especially for siding installed decades ago.

story: Spencer split from Leicester and was incorporated in 1753, and it became a stop on the Boston Post Road stage route; colonial-era milestone markers still trace the old road. The first mill was built in 1740 on the Seven Mile River. In the 1800s the town turned industrial. Elliot Prouty began drawing wire in 1812, and at one point Spencer had 11 factories and 26 buildings for wire drawing. Josiah Green and the Prouty family built shoe and boot factories, and the population grew to almost 8,750 by 1890.

That boom shaped the town center. As bootmaking moved from home workshops into centralized factories in the later 19th century, the center expanded to house the workers. The Spencer Town Center Historic District was first listed on the National Register in 1986 along Main Street between High and North Streets. It was later enlarged to take in residential streets including Grove, High, Mechanic, Pleasant and Wall Streets, plus Luther Hill Park; the 2003 boundary increase alone counts 129 contributing buildings. The district's listed styles are mid-19th-century revival and late Victorian.

Census estimates show how much of that older housing remains. About 29 percent of Spencer's roughly 5,700 homes were built before 1940 and about 68 percent before 1980, with a median year built of about 1968. About a quarter of homes are in two- to four-unit buildings, and only about 63 percent are owner-occupied. The town's listed elevation is about 925 feet. For exterior work, that adds up to many century-old wood-frame houses, a large share of multi-family buildings where owners and tenants both need to be considered, and roofs and gutters that should be planned for snow and ice.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Two- to four-unit buildings make up about a quarter of Spencer's housing, and vinyl is often chosen on them because it ends the repainting cycle for owners who manage rentals. On larger multi-unit buildings, staging, access and notice to tenants need to be planned ahead. Original wood siding underneath may hide rot at sills and window heads, so removing it rather than covering it lets that damage be found and fixed. Old paint on pre-1978 buildings brings EPA lead-safe rules into play when it is disturbed.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Spencer's center grew in the late 19th century around its boot and wire factories, and streets such as Grove, High and Pleasant still carry much of that era's housing within the town center historic district. On houses from that period, any original wood siding is worth assessing before it is torn off. New clapboard, in wood or fiber cement, can keep the look of those streets if the original exposure and corner details are matched. With about 29 percent of local homes built before 1940, lead-safe practices are a routine part of the job.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits Spencer's older multi-family buildings when owners want the look of painted clapboard with longer paint cycles. It is heavier than vinyl, so the framing and sheathing on a century-old building should be checked first, and walls that are out of plumb may need furring to keep courses straight. The boards do not burn, which some owners of multi-unit buildings value. Cutting fiber cement releases silica dust that should be controlled, particularly when tenants are home next to the work.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Late Victorian architecture is among the styles listed for the Spencer Town Center Historic District, and shingles, plain or cut in patterns, are a common feature on houses of that type. Where gables or upper stories carry decorative shingles, new cedar can often be cut to match the original shapes. Shingles should go up with corrosion-resistant nails over a surface that lets them dry from behind. On full walls, cedar can be left to weather or stained, depending on what fits the house.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on an older Spencer house can mean removing more than one layer: original clapboard, then perhaps asbestos-cement shingles, aluminum or vinyl added later. Each layer should be identified before removal, since asbestos-cement shingles require specific handling. With about 68 percent of homes built before 1980, stripping to sheathing also exposes painted surfaces that must be handled under EPA lead-safe rules. On rental buildings, scheduling around tenants and protecting porches and entries during the work matter as much as the siding itself.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Houses from Spencer's late-19th-century growth may have bracketed eaves, porch railings and decorative window heads that cannot be replaced with stock lumber. Where those pieces are rotted, they can be copied in wood or cellular PVC to match the originals. Porches on multi-family buildings take heavy daily use, so post bases, railings and stair stringers deserve close inspection. Water usually gets in where trim meets a horizontal surface, so new pieces should be flashed and caulked with that in mind.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Given the town's elevation of about 925 feet, gutters in Spencer should be planned for snow and ice loads. Hangers should be closely spaced and fastened into rafter tails or solid fascia, not into trim alone. Multi-family buildings often have large roof areas, and oversized gutters and downspouts handle their runoff better. Where houses sit close together in the older center, downspouts should be directed so water does not flow toward a neighboring foundation or across a shared driveway.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With roughly 29 percent of homes built before 1940, Spencer has a lot of roofs on old framing. Removing every old layer down to the deck lets rot, sagging and undersized rafters be found and addressed before new shingles go on. Ice and water barrier along the eaves and valleys is worth specifying at this elevation, and attic ventilation should be checked, since many older houses were not built with any. On multi-family buildings, coordinating access and debris removal with tenants is part of the plan.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Spencer often involve older materials, so a good match may mean finding a specific clapboard profile, shingle shape or discontinued vinyl color. Small areas of damage, such as a cracked panel, a rotted board near a porch roof or a section hit by a falling limb, can usually be fixed without residing the whole wall. On rental buildings, a prompt repair keeps water out of units below.

story: Lincoln was incorporated in 1754 from the southeast part of Concord and pieces of Weston and Lexington. Most of its land is still zoned for residential and agricultural use, a sizable share is public conservation land, and Mass Audubon's Drumlin Farm is also in town. The civic center is the Lincoln Center Historic District, listed on the National Register in 1985, which runs along Bedford, Lincoln, Old Lexington, Sandy Pond, Trapelo and Weston Roads and includes Greek Revival, late-Victorian and Georgian Revival buildings. The Codman House estate is another early landmark.

Lincoln is also known for modern houses. In 1938 Walter Gropius built his family home at 68 Baker Bridge Road, clad in vertical white-painted redwood boards under a flat roof. With nearby houses by Gropius, Marcel Breuer and Walter Bogner, it forms the Woods End Road Historic District. In 1953 a cooperative of families started Brown's Wood, off Laurel Drive and Moccasin Hill Road, where every house had to be contemporary in style. Lincoln adopted a local historic district by-law in 1981, and a 2018 initiative added 28 modern houses to it, eleven of them in a new Brown's Wood district.

Census estimates put the median year built near 1972 for about 2,900 homes. Roughly 64 percent were built before 1980 and about 14 percent before 1940. About 57 percent are owner-occupied and about 14 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings; part of Hanscom Air Force Base lies within the town. For exterior work, Lincoln asks for more care than most places: flat roofs, vertical boards and slim details on its modern houses, older wood buildings around the center, and a Historic District Commission that oversees houses inside the district.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a poor fit for many Lincoln houses. On the modernist homes of Brown's Wood or the Woods End Road area, it would change the character of designs built around wood boards, and properties inside the local historic district fall under the Historic District Commission. It can still be a practical choice on simpler or newer houses outside the district. Owners should confirm a property's status with the town before choosing materials, and should expect panel profile and trim choices to matter more than usual here.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard suits the older houses around Lincoln Center, where the district includes Greek Revival and late-Victorian buildings. Replacement boards should match the original exposure and profile, and repairing sound boards is often better than replacing whole walls. About 14 percent of local homes were built before 1940, and EPA lead-safe practices apply whenever pre-1978 paint is disturbed. For houses inside the historic district, it makes sense to talk with the Historic District Commission early, before materials are ordered.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement comes in planks and flat panels, so it can work both on Lincoln's traditional postwar houses and on some contemporary designs. On a mid-century house originally clad in vertical wood, though, a horizontal plank would alter the design, and a vertical or panel product is a closer match. Wherever it is used, the specified clearances above roofs and grade, and sealed cut ends, are what keep it performing. The weight of the boards also means the wall behind should be checked before installation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar runs through Lincoln's architecture. The Loud House at 1 Woods End Road, designed in 1938, has a gray wood-shingle facade, and the modern houses around it used redwood and fir boards. Replacing shingles or boards in kind keeps a house consistent with its original design. A ventilated installation helps cedar dry, which matters on shaded sites near woods or conservation land. Corrosion-resistant fasteners prevent dark streaks, and natural cedar can be left to weather or sealed to hold its color.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement on a Lincoln house deserves more planning than usual. The modern houses of the 1930s through the 1950s used vertical redwood, tongue-and-groove boards and flat roofs, and swapping them for a generic product can erase what makes them significant. On traditional houses and later homes outside the historic districts, a full tear-off lets sheathing, insulation and window flashing be upgraded together. With about 64 percent of local homes built before 1980, lead-safe practices will often apply.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim on Lincoln's modern houses is minimal by design: thin fascias, flush window casings and exposed beam ends. Replacing rotted pieces means copying those slim profiles, not adding bulky colonial-style casings. Around Lincoln Center, the older buildings have larger cornices and casings, and matching them is the goal there. Rot usually starts where water sits, at sills, beam ends and roof edges, so new trim should be flashed and sealed to shed water at exactly those points.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Flat-roofed modern houses such as those on Woods End Road drain differently from pitched roofs, often through scuppers or internal drains, and those outlets need to stay clear. On pitched roofs, gutters near woods or conservation land fill quickly with leaves and needles, so guards and accessible downspouts help. Wherever the water goes, it should be carried away from foundations and walkways, and on sloped lots it should be directed so it does not run back toward the house.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Lincoln has an unusual mix of roofs. The Gropius House and the Breuer House on Woods End Road were built with flat roofs, and roofs like these need membrane systems, careful drainage and solid edge flashing rather than shingles. Elsewhere, older and postwar houses carry pitched roofs suited to asphalt or wood shingles. Matching the roofing system to the design is the first decision on any replacement, and on historic-district properties it is worth confirming what review applies.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs on Lincoln houses may involve vertical boards, cedar shingles or clapboard, depending on the house and its era. Small damaged sections can usually be replaced with matching stock and finished to blend with the rest of the wall. On older and modern houses alike, keeping as much original material as possible is often the better approach than replacing an entire elevation.

story: Dover lies on the south bank of the Charles River, about 15 miles southwest of Boston. It was set off from Dedham as a district in 1784 and incorporated as a town in 1836. The Benjamin Caryl House on Dedham Street, built around 1777 for the first minister of what was then Springfield Parish, is owned by the Dover Historical Society, and the society's Sawin Museum stands in Dover Center at Centre and Dedham Streets. On the river, the Elm Bank estate, with a Neo-Georgian manor designed in 1907 by Carrere and Hastings, is listed on the National Register.

The town's biggest change came after World War II, when the population grew from about 1,700 in 1950 to about 4,500 by 1970, and it has grown slowly since. Almost all residential zoning requires lots of one acre or more. The housing numbers follow from that. Census estimates put the median year built around 1970 for Dover's roughly 2,000 homes, with about 61 percent built before 1980 and about 10 percent before 1940. Nearly 98 percent are owner-occupied, and two- to four-unit buildings are almost absent at about half a percent.

For exterior work, Dover is a town of single-family houses on large lots, most of them now more than 45 years old and likely on at least their second roof. Big lots usually leave room for a dumpster and staging, though long driveways should be protected from heavy trucks. Winter has always been a factor here: in the early 1960s about three-quarters of the town budget reportedly went to snow removal.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is an option for Dover owners whose main goal is low maintenance on a large single-family house. On a bigger facade, a thicker panel, wider trim accessories and a profile that suits the house help it look less flat. Since the median home in town dates to about 1970, the existing siding is often decades old, and it should come off so the sheathing can be inspected and the windows flashed again before anything new is installed. Long walls need careful planning of panel overlaps.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Painted clapboard fits Dover's older houses, from the Caryl House era onward, and it is a common choice for owners who want a traditional finish on a later home. Cedar and fiber cement clapboard both work; wood needs repainting on a regular cycle, while factory-finished boards stretch that interval. On historic houses, repairing original boards is worth considering before replacement. For homes built before 1978, EPA lead-safe rules apply when existing paint is scraped, sanded or removed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits Dover owners who want a painted-wood look on a large house without cedar's paint schedule. Because nearly every home in town is an owner-occupied single-family house, a project can be scheduled around one household. The boards are heavy and produce silica dust when cut, so handling and dust control need planning. On long walls, laying out butt joints so they fall in sensible places, and flashing behind each one, makes a visible difference in the finished job.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a traditional finish for a single-family house on a large lot. Left natural they weather to gray, and stained they hold a color longer. Walls shaded by trees dry slowly, so a rainscreen gap behind the shingles and periodic cleaning of mildew help them last. Near the Charles River and the Noanet Woodlands, humidity and shade are worth factoring into the choice between natural and stained finishes and into how the wall is ventilated.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With about 61 percent of homes built before 1980 and almost no multi-family buildings, a full replacement in Dover usually means one large single-family house at a time. Stripping to sheathing allows insulation, housewrap and window flashing to be upgraded together, which is hard to do in sections. A big lot usually leaves room for a dumpster and staging off the street, but driveways and septic areas should be identified first so heavy equipment stays off them.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Larger houses tend to carry more trim: cornices, porch columns, window casings, garage door surrounds and decorative entries. In Dover, replacing rotted pieces with matching profiles in wood or cellular PVC keeps a house's proportions intact. On the oldest houses, such as the 18th-century homes the town's historical society has preserved, original trim is part of the character and should be repaired before it is replaced. New trim should be primed on all sides or made of a material that does not need it.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On large Dover lots with trees close to the house, gutters can fill quickly with leaves and needles, and guards matched to the debris type cut down on cleaning. Downspouts should carry water well away from foundations; on a lot of an acre or more there is usually room to run it to a drywell or a well-graded spot. Hangers should be strong enough to hold snow and ice, and gutters on long eaves may need more than one downspout.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Dover's population nearly tripled between 1950 and 1970, so many roofs sit on houses from that period. On a replacement, ice and water barrier at eaves and valleys, plus balanced attic ventilation, help prevent ice dams. Where a house has dormers, additions or chimneys, flashing at those walls deserves extra attention. A full tear-off lets the decking be checked; on larger roofs, protecting landscaping and driveways from falling debris is part of planning the job.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: For a few damaged boards or shingles, a targeted repair is usually enough. On larger houses, matching paint color and siding profile across a big wall is the main challenge, so the repair may need to be painted out to the nearest corner or trim break. Small repairs also give a chance to check whether the damage came from a leak behind the wall.

story: Medfield was settled in 1649 and incorporated in 1651, and half of it was destroyed in King Philip's War. Several of its oldest houses survive. The Peak House at 347 Main Street, rebuilt after the attack, has the highest-pitched roof on record in Massachusetts for a colonial house. The Dwight-Derby House on Frairy Street dates to 1697, and parts of the Lowell Mason house, moved to Green Street in 2011, have been dated by tree rings to 1651. Other National Register listings include the Inness-Fitts House and Studio on Main Street and Vine Lake Cemetery.

Most of Medfield's homes are far newer. The town grew sharply in the decades after World War II, reaching about 9,800 people by 1970. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1970 for roughly 4,800 homes, with about 64 percent built before 1980 and about 13 percent before 1940. Around 86 percent are owner-occupied, and only about 5 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. The former Medfield State Hospital, opened in 1896 and closed in 2003, is being reused; in 2022 the town sold about 45 acres, including the core campus, to a developer that proposed several kinds of housing.

The Charles River borders almost a third of the town, and the 491-acre Rocky Woods reservation in the northeast, along with Noon Hill, adds wooded, hilly land with miles of trails. For exterior work, Medfield presents two very different jobs: a large stock of single-family houses from the 1950s through the 1970s that now need roofs, siding and gutters, and a small group of very old buildings where original material should be protected.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical choice on many of Medfield's postwar single-family homes, especially those from the 1960s and 1970s that still carry their first or second siding. Before installation, the old siding should come off so the sheathing can be inspected and the windows flashed again. Choosing a panel profile, color and trim width that suit the house helps it sit comfortably on streets where houses from several eras stand side by side. Vented soffit panels can be added at the same time.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the right match for Medfield's oldest houses, including First Period homes such as the Dwight-Derby House, and it is a natural choice for owners who want a traditional finish on a newer house. On older buildings, replacing only the failed boards at matching exposure keeps original fabric in place. Pre-1978 paint means EPA lead-safe practices apply, and on 17th- and 18th-century buildings a preservation-minded approach is worth discussing before any original siding comes off.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank is a common upgrade for owners replacing aging wood or vinyl on Medfield homes from the 1960s and 1970s. It gives the look of painted clapboard with a longer repainting interval. It must be installed with the specified clearances above roofs, decks and grade, and cut ends should be sealed. On lots near the Charles River or close to wetlands, the clearance at grade is especially important, since splash-back and standing water shorten the life of any siding.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles work on many house types, and in Medfield they suit both older homes and newer houses where owners want a natural texture. Near Rocky Woods, Noon Hill and other wooded land, shaded walls dry slowly, so a ventilated installation and good roof-water control help shingles last. Natural cedar weathers gray; stained shingles hold their color longer but need recoating every several years. Stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails prevent rust streaks down the face of the wall.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: On Medfield houses built between the 1950s and the 1970s, full replacement makes sense when the siding is failing on most walls. Removing it all lets the sheathing, housewrap and window flashing be updated together, which is hard to do one section at a time. With about 64 percent of homes built before 1980, lead-safe practices will often apply. For the town's older houses, especially First Period or 19th-century homes, a full tear-off of original wood siding is rarely the best first step.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Exterior trim in Medfield ranges from simple fascia and casings on postwar houses to the more detailed cornices, doorways and corner boards of older homes. Rot tends to start at window sills, rake boards and the bottoms of door casings, where water sits longest. Replacing failed pieces with matching profiles in wood or cellular PVC keeps the house consistent, and new pieces should be flashed so the same spots do not fail again within a few years.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With the Charles River along nearly a third of the town and ponds such as Hinkley Pond and Kingsbury Pond, some Medfield lots may sit low or stay damp. Gutters and downspouts should move water away from foundations and toward ground that drains. On lots near Rocky Woods or other wooded land, guards can reduce cleaning. Hangers should be strong enough to carry snow and ice, and downspout outlets should not discharge onto walkways that freeze.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Medfield's best-known roof belongs to the Peak House, the steepest on record in Massachusetts for a colonial house, but most local roofs sit on homes from the 1960s and 1970s. On those, a full tear-off lets the decking be checked, and balanced soffit and ridge venting help limit ice dams. Ice and water barrier at the eaves, in valleys and around chimneys is a standard part of a sound replacement, as is new drip edge and step flashing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small repairs, such as replacing a few boards, panels or shingles after storm or tree damage, can usually be done without redoing the wall. Matching color and profile is the main challenge on older siding, and on very old houses, keeping original boards wherever they are still sound is usually preferable. A repair is also a good time to check for a leak at a window or roof edge that may have caused the damage.

story: Watertown packs a lot of housing into a small footprint. The town covers only about four square miles, most of it north of the Charles River, and holds roughly 17,200 housing units. Census figures put the median year built at 1947, with about 44 percent of homes dating from before 1940 and close to 78 percent from before 1980. The most telling number for exterior work is this one: about 43 percent of homes sit in buildings with two to four units, and fewer than half are owner-occupied.

The neighborhoods have their own histories. Watertown Square is the traditional hub of the town, and the Abraham Browne House on Main Street dates to around 1700. Bemis, in the southwest corner between Main Street, the Charles and the Waltham line, takes its name from Seth Bemis, who ran mills on both banks of the river near Bridge Street. East Watertown and Coolidge Square run toward Cambridge and Mount Auburn Cemetery, and the West End borders Waltham. Along Arsenal Street, the former Watertown Arsenal, which operated from 1816 to 1995, has been redeveloped as a commercial and arts district.

In practice, many exterior projects here involve a shared building rather than a single house. Owners of the two units may need to agree on color, material and timing, and tenants have to be told when ladders and staging are going up. Side yards between buildings are often narrow, which affects where materials can be stored and how scaffolding is set. Because so much of the housing is older than 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices apply whenever painted siding or trim is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: On a two-family building, vinyl is usually chosen because it covers a large wall area at a moderate cost and does not need repainting between tenants. The details deserve attention: on older Watertown buildings, porches, bay windows and stacked entries create many inside and outside corners, and each one needs proper J-channel and flashing. The siding should be hung loosely enough to move with temperature changes. Before it goes on, any rotted sheathing should be replaced rather than covered, because vinyl will hide a problem but not stop it from spreading.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: With about 44 percent of Watertown homes built before 1940, it is worth finding out what is under the current siding before choosing a new one; older wood siding sometimes survives beneath later layers. Owners who want a traditional painted look can install new clapboards in wood or fiber cement. Matching the original exposure, where it can be measured, keeps the building in proportion. In a town where neighboring buildings are close together, it also helps to think about how the new siding will be painted and maintained from a narrow side yard over the years.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement board is heavy and is usually cut with dust control, which matters on tight Watertown lots where the next building may be ten feet away. Planning a cutting station, a dust plan and a storage spot before work starts makes the job go smoother for neighbors and tenants. The material holds paint well and resists rot, which suits multi-unit buildings where owners want long intervals between exterior work. Manufacturer clearances above roofs, decks and ground level should be followed, since warranty terms depend on them.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can cover a whole house or just a gable end or dormer on a larger building, which is a common way to add texture to a multi-unit facade without changing every wall. Shingles need a drainable wrap or a rain-screen layer behind them so the backs can dry. On buildings near the Charles, where morning damp lingers, that drying space matters even more. Natural cedar weathers to gray; if owners want a uniform color, a stain or factory-finished shingle should be decided before installation.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement on a two- or three-unit Watertown building is a bigger undertaking than on a single house: more wall area, more windows, and usually more than one household to coordinate. Removing old layers often exposes original sheathing, and that is the time to check it, fix rot and add a weather-resistive barrier. Since many buildings predate 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted siding comes off. A free on-site assessment and written estimate should spell out the scope for each elevation, including staging along narrow sides.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: An older building with more than one unit can carry a lot of trim: porch columns and railings, window casings, frieze boards and cornice details on every floor. Where that trim is painted wood, it has often been scraped and recoated many times. Where the wood is sound, repair and repainting can keep the original profiles. Where it has rotted, PVC or primed composite stock can be milled to similar shapes. Because the trim is usually painted, EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply on pre-1978 buildings.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On a dense street, where a building's roof drains makes a real difference to the neighbors. Downspouts should discharge away from foundations and, where possible, away from the narrow walkways between buildings, where ice can form in winter. Multi-unit buildings often have long eaves and porch roofs that need their own gutters. Seamless aluminum gutters sized to the roof area, with enough downspouts, reduce overflow. Where large trees overhang the roof, guards or a regular cleaning schedule are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many Watertown roofs cover two- and three-unit buildings, so a replacement affects several households at once and should be scheduled with tenants in mind. On older buildings it is common to find more than one layer of shingles; tearing off to the deck allows rotted boards to be replaced and ice-and-water membrane to be installed at the eaves and valleys. Close neighbors mean debris control and dumpster placement need planning, often with a permit or street-use arrangement worked out ahead of time.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Many repairs on Watertown buildings involve replacing a few damaged courses, a cracked vinyl panel, or rotted wood around a porch or window. Matching an older siding profile or color can take some searching. The cause should be found before the patch goes on, whether that is a missing flashing, a gutter overflow or a leak behind a porch roof.

story: Wrentham is one of the older towns south of Boston, settled in 1660 and incorporated in 1673, then largely burned during King Philip's War a few years later. Yet most of its houses are much younger. Census figures put the median year built at 1984, and only about 16 percent of the roughly 4,600 homes predate 1940. Fewer than half were built before 1980. About 82 percent are owner-occupied, and buildings with two to four units are uncommon.

The town covers about 23 square miles and sits on the divide between four river basins: the Charles, Taunton, Blackstone and Ten Mile. Lake Pearl and Lake Archer lie toward the middle of town, and Mirror Lake straddles the line with Norfolk. Families from Dorchester and Hyde Park once came to the lakes for summer vacations, and many of those seasonal cottages later became year-round homes. Sheldonville, also called West Wrentham, is the rural western section with its own ZIP code and working orchards. Wrentham Center has small shops around the town common, where the Original Congregational Church at 1 East Street is listed on the National Register.

That mix shapes exterior work. Lakeside homes that began as cottages may have been expanded more than once, so walls, rooflines and foundations from different decades meet on the same house. Houses built from the 1980s onward, now several decades old, are reaching the age when original siding, trim and roofs come due. The town's smaller stock of older houses, near the center and out in Sheldonville, may need more care, and for those built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A large share of Wrentham homes went up from the 1980s on. Where those houses were sided in vinyl from the start, after several decades the siding can be faded, brittle or loose at the corners. Replacing it gives a chance to inspect the wrap and sheathing beneath and correct flashing at windows and decks. For houses near Lake Pearl or Lake Archer, a darker or textured product that resists fading can be a sensible choice on walls that face the water and get strong afternoon sun.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Older houses around Wrentham Center and the town common, and older homes in the farming section of Sheldonville, suit clapboard siding, whether in wood or fiber cement. Matching the exposure and corner board style of the original keeps the house consistent with its neighbors. Owners of an expanded former lake cottage sometimes use new clapboard to tie an original section and later additions together under one look, which can make a house assembled in stages read as one building.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement planks hold paint well and do not rot, which is useful on houses that sit close to the water at Lake Pearl, Lake Archer or Mirror Lake, where shaded walls stay damp. The required clearances above grade, decks and roofs matter here, since lakeside lots often slope and wet soil splashes onto the bottom courses. On a newer home, fiber cement is a common upgrade from original vinyl and changes the look of the house without changing its shape.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit both ends of Wrentham's housing: a cottage-style home near one of the lakes and an older house or barn out in the orchard country of Sheldonville. Shingles last longer when they can dry from behind, so a rain-screen or drainable wrap is worth including, especially on shaded walls near water. Owners should decide early whether they want natural weathering or a stain, since sunlight on open lots and shade on lakeside lots can make the same shingles age differently on different sides of the house.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement on a former lake cottage often reveals how many times the house was added on to. Removing the siding exposes where old and new framing meet, which is the right time to fix sheathing, add a continuous weather barrier and correct window flashing. On a 1980s or 1990s house built in one go, the work is usually more straightforward. Either way, a free on-site assessment and a written estimate should describe what happens if damaged sheathing is found once the old siding is off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim needs differ across town. Builder-grade pine trim on newer homes often fails first at the bottom of door casings and garage door jambs, where water collects. Older houses near Wrentham Center may have decorative cornices or window caps worth keeping. Cellular PVC trim resists rot and is a common replacement in spots that stay wet. On any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted trim is removed or sanded.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lakeside lots and wooded house sites in Wrentham can collect leaves and pine needles quickly, so gutter guards or a regular cleaning schedule should be part of the plan. Where a lot slopes toward Lake Pearl, Lake Archer or Mirror Lake, downspout discharge should be directed to spread water out rather than send it straight downhill. Larger homes with long rooflines benefit from oversized downspouts so heavy rain does not overflow at the corners.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many homes from the town's 1980s and later building years are now on their first or second roof, and some original roofs are near the end of their life. A full tear-off allows inspection of the decking and installation of ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys. On former lake cottages with low-slope additions, those sections may need a different roofing material than the main roof. Attic ventilation should also be checked, since many additions were built without adequate airflow.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Typical repairs in Wrentham include replacing storm-damaged vinyl panels, rotted trim at the base of walls, and siding damaged near decks or along lakeside walls that stay damp. Before patching, the source of the water should be identified so the same area does not fail again. On a house that grew from a lake cottage, the patch may also cross the line between two building eras, which needs care to blend in.

story: Norwood was a parish of Dedham known as South Dedham until 1872, when it became its own town. Its housing reflects that industrial past. Census figures put the median year built at 1960, with about a quarter of the roughly 13,800 homes dating from before 1940 and about 72 percent from before 1980. Nearly one in five homes is in a building with two to four units, and the owner-occupied share is only a little more than half.

The industry came with the printing firms. The Norwood Press, formed from three Boston companies in the 1890s, printed school and college textbooks, and the Plimpton Press was another of the town's book printers. Mills, tanneries and presses drew workers, many of them immigrants. In South Norwood, roughly from Dean Street to Mylod Street, the Norwood Historical Society records that lots were subdivided around 1900 and builders put up triple-decker apartment buildings rather than single-family homes for families from Lithuania, Syria, Poland, Italy and elsewhere. Along Washington Street, many buildings had shops on the ground floor and apartments above. The town hall on the town square and the Morrill Memorial Library, built in 1898 and 1899, date from the same period.

Much of the rest of Norwood filled in during the middle of the 20th century, which explains the 1960 median. The Neponset River runs through town, and Wikipedia gives average snowfall of about 56 inches. For homeowners, that means two kinds of work are common: careful projects on tall, multi-unit buildings from around 1900, and updates to mid-century houses. Both usually involve paint from before 1978, so EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when it is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical option for many mid-century Norwood houses, where the goal is to stop repainting and tighten up the exterior. On a three-story building in South Norwood, the job is different: tall walls need staging rather than ladders, and stacked porches create many corners that need careful flashing. In either case, the old siding should be assessed first. Covering rotted clapboards with vinyl hides the problem instead of fixing it.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: On a building from Norwood's printing and mill era, the current siding may not be the first. New clapboard in wood or fiber cement can bring back a painted, traditional look on a building that has been covered with aluminum, vinyl or asbestos shingles over the decades. If old cladding might contain asbestos, it should be tested before removal. Matching the original exposure and the width of the corner boards helps a tall building keep its proportions.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement planks are a good fit for owners of older two- and three-unit buildings who want a painted look without the upkeep of wood. The boards are heavy and long, so on a three-story building the staging plan needs to account for lifting material to upper floors safely. On mid-century houses elsewhere in town, fiber cement can be installed with factory paint, which cuts down on site painting and makes future touch-ups simpler.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit some of Norwood's older single-family houses and can be used on gable ends or dormers of larger buildings. They need a drainage space or breathable wrap behind them so the backs can dry. For an owner of a multi-unit building, the trade-off is maintenance: stained or natural shingles need periodic attention, and on a three-story wall, that means staging each time. Pre-finished shingles reduce that work.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a South Norwood triple-decker or a building along Washington Street is a large project with several elevations, many windows and tenants to coordinate with. Removing old layers is the moment to check sheathing, fix rot around porches, and install a continuous weather barrier. Pre-1978 painted surfaces call for EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices. A free on-site assessment and written estimate should spell out staging, tenant access and how unexpected damage would be handled.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: A turn-of-the-century apartment building can carry porch columns, rails, brackets and cornices on every level, and painted wood trim of that age has usually been coated many times. Sound trim can be repaired and repainted; rotted sections can be replaced with PVC or composite stock milled to match. Mid-century houses usually have simpler trim, but window sills and door frames often need attention. EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when pre-1978 painted trim is disturbed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Tall multi-unit buildings and stacked porches in Norwood shed a lot of water, and a single undersized downspout can overflow onto porches below. Seamless gutters sized to the roof, plus enough downspouts, reduce that. With snowfall averaging around 56 inches, gutter hangers should be strong enough to carry ice, and downspouts should discharge away from foundations and walkways where ice can build up.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Roofs in Norwood range from older multi-unit buildings, some with low-slope or flat sections, to pitched roofs on mid-century houses. A flat section needs a membrane system, not shingles, and attention to drains and parapet flashing. Pitched roofs benefit from tear-off to the deck, ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, and a check of attic ventilation. On a rental building, scheduling should take tenants into account.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Norwood often involve rotted wood around porches, damaged sections of older siding, or cracked vinyl. On older buildings, the cause, such as a failed gutter or porch flashing, should be fixed along with the damaged siding so the repair holds. On a multi-unit building, a small repair can often be handled from a ladder on one side, without staging the whole wall or disturbing every tenant.
