story: Walpole is made up of three postal areas, each with its own ZIP code: Walpole, East Walpole and South Walpole. The town covers about 21 square miles roughly 18 miles south of downtown Boston. Its housing is mostly from the later 20th century. Census figures put the median year built at 1977, with about 13 percent of the roughly 9,800 homes dating from before 1940 and a little more than half from before 1980. About 84 percent are owner-occupied, and buildings with two to four units are rare.

The older layer of the town follows the Neponset River. Mills for cotton, lumber and paper were built along it to use the falls, and the largest was the Bird Company complex in East Walpole. After the company stopped operating there in 1980, most of its buildings were torn down, and a housing development now covers much of the old mill site. Francis William Bird Park, an 89-acre landscaped park owned by The Trustees of Reservations, is also in East Walpole. The Walpole Town Forest marks the area where the town's first sawmill stood near School Meadow Brook. Blackburn Hall, a red brick building dedicated in 1932, still belongs to the town.

For exterior work, that means most houses are owner-occupied and built around the 1970s give or take a couple of decades, with a smaller set of older homes and newer housing on former industrial land. Wikipedia notes the area averages about 56 inches of snow a year and is exposed to nor'easters, which affects roofing details and gutter choices. Houses built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many Walpole homes date from the decades around the 1977 median, and plenty of them have original or second-generation siding that is now faded or brittle. Replacing it is also a good moment to upgrade the wrap and window flashing, which older installations often lacked. For larger homes on open lots, a thicker panel with a stronger nailing hem holds up better in wind from nor'easters, and color choices should account for heavy sun exposure on south and west walls.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The roughly one in eight Walpole homes built before 1940 suit traditional clapboard. Wood or fiber cement can bring back a painted look on a house that has been covered with vinyl or aluminum. Keeping the original exposure and trim widths matters on these houses, since the proportions of the siding are a large part of their character. On newer homes, clapboard-style fiber cement offers a similar look with less upkeep.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a common upgrade for 1970s and 1980s Walpole houses whose original siding has worn out. It is heavier than vinyl and needs specific fastening, so it should be installed according to the manufacturer's instructions to keep the warranty valid. Factory-painted boards reduce maintenance. Clearance above grade and roofs needs attention, especially on houses whose landscaping has built up soil against the bottom courses over the years.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit a house on a wooded lot, such as those near the Town Forest, as well as older homes in any of the three villages. They need to dry from behind, so a rain-screen mat or a breathable wrap should be part of the installation, especially on shaded walls. Natural shingles weather unevenly between sunny and shaded sides, so owners who want an even color should choose stained or pre-finished shingles from the start.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: On a Walpole house from the 1960s through the 1980s, full replacement usually means removing the original layer, checking sheathing, adding a modern weather barrier and redoing window and door flashing. Houses built before 1978 may have painted surfaces covered by EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules. A free on-site assessment and written estimate should explain how damaged sheathing will be handled if it is found once the old siding comes off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim on mid- to late-century Walpole homes is often finger-jointed pine or similar stock that starts to rot at the bottom of door casings, garage jambs and corner boards. Replacing the worst pieces with cellular PVC solves the problem in the spots that stay wet. On older houses, original moldings may be worth repairing and keeping. EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when pre-1978 painted trim is disturbed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Walpole homes near wooded land, such as lots bordering the Town Forest, can collect leaves and needles that clog gutters quickly. Guards can reduce cleaning, but they should be chosen for the type of debris on the lot. With snowfall averaging about 56 inches, hangers should be spaced closely enough to support ice loads. Downspouts should carry water well away from the foundation, especially on lots that slope toward the house.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Since much of Walpole's housing went up in the 1960s through 1990s, many houses are on a second roof or due for one. Nor'easter winds make the starter course and edge details important, along with nailing to the shingle manufacturer's high-wind pattern where it applies. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys helps with ice dams after heavy snow. A tear-off allows the decking to be inspected and attic ventilation to be checked.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Walpole commonly involve wind-damaged panels after a storm, rotted trim at the base of walls, and damage from gutters that overflowed. Finding a matching color on older siding can take some work, and the source of any water damage should be fixed before the patch goes on. A small, well-matched repair is often all a sound wall needs, and it can postpone a full replacement for years.

story: Dedham was settled in 1635 and incorporated the following year, and it holds one of the most notable houses in the country: the Fairbanks House, which Wikipedia describes as the oldest surviving timber-frame house in the United States, dated to 1637. Mother Brook, dug in 1639 to link the Charles and Neponset rivers, powered the mills of East Dedham. The old center is now the Dedham Village Historic District, listed on the National Register in 2006, covering about 55 acres around High, Court and Washington streets with buildings in the Federal and Italianate styles, along with the Norfolk County Courthouse.

Most of Dedham's roughly 10,800 homes are newer than that. Census figures put the median year built at 1956, with about 30 percent of homes from before 1940 and about 76 percent from before 1980. Around 73 percent are owner-occupied, and about one in ten homes is in a building with two to four units. The town is divided into distinct neighborhoods. Oakdale sits near the geographic center, with homes on Woodleigh Road designed by Henry Bailey Alden. Riverdale is an island formed by the Charles River and Long Ditch. East Dedham lies between Mother Brook and the Boston line, and Precinct One, or Upper Dedham, is in the northwest corner near Westwood and Needham. Greenlodge, the Manor, Ashcroft and Fairbanks round out the list.

For homeowners, the age range matters. A Federal-era house in the historic center, an architect-designed home on Woodleigh Road and a house built during the postwar decades each call for a different approach. With most homes built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With the median Dedham home built in the mid-1950s, vinyl is a common choice for owners of postwar houses who want to stop repainting. For houses in or near the Dedham Village Historic District, owners should check with the town about any applicable review before changing materials. On any house, vinyl should not be installed over rotted wood, and window and door flashing should be redone as part of the work.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the traditional siding on many of Dedham's older houses, from the Federal and Italianate buildings in the village center to the roughly 30 percent of homes built before 1940. Wood or fiber cement clapboard can match the original look. Matching the original exposure, corner boards and the way siding meets window casings keeps an older house in proportion. Before replacing original siding on a house in the historic district, any local requirements should be confirmed with the town.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement planks resist rot and insects, which is useful near water, including houses in Riverdale or along Mother Brook, where walls may stay damp. The boards need correct clearance from the ground, roofs and decks, and cut edges should be sealed. Factory-finished products reduce painting. On a postwar house, fiber cement can replace worn original siding while keeping a painted-clapboard look that fits the neighborhood.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles work on many Dedham houses, either as full cladding on an older home or as an accent on a gable or dormer of a postwar one. They should be installed over a drainage layer so they can dry from behind, which matters on lots close to the Charles or Mother Brook. Owners should decide between natural weathering and a stain before installation, since mixing old and new shingles on the same wall can look uneven for years.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on an older Dedham house often uncovers several eras of work, including old board sheathing, earlier additions and patched framing. That is the time to repair rot, install a continuous weather barrier and flash every opening. On houses built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply. A free on-site assessment and a written estimate should describe the scope and how damage found during removal will be handled.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Older Dedham houses, particularly in the Dedham Village Historic District, often have detailed cornices, window caps and porch elements that are worth repairing instead of replacing. Where wood has rotted, new pieces can be milled to match the original profile. On postwar houses, trim is usually simpler, and cellular PVC is a durable choice at sills and the bottom of casings. EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when pre-1978 painted trim is disturbed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With Wikipedia citing average snowfall around 62 inches, Dedham gutters need sturdy hangers and good pitch so meltwater drains rather than freezing in place. Houses in Riverdale and along Mother Brook sit close to water, so downspouts should carry water well away from foundations. Older houses with built-in or box gutters need inspection before any changeover, because those systems are part of the cornice and leaks can rot the framing behind them.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Dedham's mix of older and postwar houses means roofs vary widely in pitch and complexity. Older houses may have several roof planes, dormers and chimneys, each requiring careful flashing. Given the area's snowfall, ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys and good attic ventilation help limit ice dams. A tear-off to the deck allows old board sheathing to be checked and repaired before new roofing goes on.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Dedham often involve rotted clapboards near the ground or under roof edges, damaged trim and cracked vinyl. On older houses, matching the original profile may require custom work. The cause should be found and fixed along with the damage. On a house in the village historic district, matching the existing material and profile closely keeps the repair from standing out.

story: For most of its history, Burlington was a farm town known for hops and rye, with a few small shoe shops. It was settled in 1641, and the Francis Wyman House dates to 1666, but early railroads bypassed the town and growth came late. Then Route 128 arrived. Between 1955 and 1965 Burlington was the fastest-growing town in Massachusetts, and a 2013 Boston Globe article reported that the population went from about 3,250 to about 21,980 over twenty years beginning in 1950.

The housing numbers reflect that boom. Only about 6 percent of Burlington's roughly 10,400 homes were built before 1940, while about 62 percent were built before 1980, and the median year built is 1972. About 74 percent are owner-occupied, and buildings with two to four units are rare. The same Globe article described many homes from the boom as ranches and split entries, and noted that developers were buying some of them and replacing them with center-hall colonials, while condominiums and apartments were adding to the mix.

The land also matters. Elevations range from about 150 feet at the Great Meadow to about 290 feet at Greenleaf Mountain. Mill Pond Reservoir in the eastern part of town is the largest body of water, and the Landlocked Forest, Mary Cummings Park and the Mill Pond Conservation Area add large areas of open land. For exterior work, the typical project is a house from the 1950s through the 1970s whose siding, trim and roof are on their second or third round. Houses built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Ranches and split entries from the Route 128 boom are the most common homes for vinyl projects in Burlington. Many have siding that has been replaced once already, so it is worth checking whether the new siding will go over sound sheathing or over earlier layers that should come off. Split entries have tall front walls and a change in wall plane between the levels, and that transition needs proper flashing to keep water out.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The small number of Burlington houses that survive from its farm years, about 6 percent of homes predate 1940, suit traditional clapboard. On boom-era ranches, fiber cement clapboard is often used to give a more traditional painted look. Matching corner boards and window trim to the clapboard width keeps a single-story house from looking busy. On new colonials replacing older homes, clapboard is a common choice that fits the style.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a common upgrade for Burlington ranches and split entries whose original siding has worn out. It is heavier than vinyl and needs the right fasteners and clearances from grade, decks and roofs. On split entries, where the lower level sits close to the ground, maintaining the bottom clearance matters. Factory-finished boards reduce painting over time. Cut edges should be sealed or primed as the manufacturer requires.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can give a 1950s or 1960s Burlington house a different character, especially on a cape or on the upper level of a split entry. Shingles need a drainage layer or breathable wrap behind them. Homes on lots backing onto conservation land such as the Landlocked Forest or the Mill Pond area may get more shade, which slows drying, so stain or pre-finished shingles are worth considering.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: For many boom-era homes in Burlington, full replacement means removing two generations of siding, checking the original sheathing and adding a modern weather barrier. Window flashing on these houses was often minimal when they were built. Houses built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules. A free on-site assessment and a written estimate should spell out what is included if damaged sheathing turns up.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Ranches and split entries tend to have long runs of fascia and soffit and simple window trim. The fascia often rots behind gutters, and soffits may lack ventilation. Replacing both with aluminum-wrapped or PVC materials, and adding soffit vents where needed, is common work. On older farmhouse-era homes, original trim details may be worth repairing. EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when pre-1978 painted trim is disturbed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Long, low rooflines on Burlington ranches carry water a long way to the corners, so gutter sizing and the number of downspouts matter. Homes near wooded conservation areas can collect leaves quickly, so gutter guards are worth considering. Downspouts should discharge well away from the foundation, particularly on split entries, where the lower level is partly below grade. Hangers should be spaced to carry snow and ice along those long eaves.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many Burlington roofs sit on low-pitched ranches and split entries from the boom years, and low slopes are more prone to ice dams and wind-driven leaks. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys, plus correct underlayment for the pitch, helps. A tear-off allows the decking to be checked. Attic ventilation is often limited on these houses and should be reviewed during reroofing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Burlington often involve cracked or loose vinyl panels, rotted fascia behind gutters, and damage at the lower walls of split entries. Matching older siding colors can take some searching, and the water source should be fixed along with the damage. On a split entry, damage near the lower level often comes from snow piled against the wall, so clearance at the bottom course deserves a look.

story: Wayland was the first settlement of Sudbury Plantation in 1638, broke away as East Sudbury in 1780 and took its present name in 1835. The town has two distinct centers. Wayland Center, at the junction of Routes 20 and 27, is a National Register historic district listed in 1974: a cluster of mostly one- and two-story wood-frame buildings, the majority built before 1850 in the Federal or Greek Revival style, plus the 1881 train station that helped turn the town into a Boston commuter suburb. About three miles south along Route 27 is Cochituate, the village whose growth came from shoe factories and which sits beside Lake Cochituate and Dudley Pond.

The Census picture is mostly mid-century. Of roughly 5,200 homes, the median one was built around 1962 and about seven in ten predate 1980, while only about one in five goes back before 1940. Close to 88 percent are owner-occupied and fewer than 5 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings, so most exterior projects involve a single household making its own decisions about a detached house. The older stock is concentrated in places like the Center, where original trim and clapboard profiles are part of what makes the district what it is.

Water shapes a lot of the town. The Sudbury River winds through meadows in Wayland, and in 2010 heavy rain left the Pelham Island area cut off until the water went down. Lake Cochituate began as a reservoir for Boston, developed between 1848 and 1863. For houses on low ground or near the shoreline, the bottom courses of siding, sill trim and downspout discharge deserve more attention than they would on a hilltop lot. Homes built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules whenever painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With a median build year in the early 1960s, many Wayland houses have already been resided at least once. Vinyl can make sense on those postwar homes, especially where the original wood has been painted many times. Before any panels go up, the sheathing should be opened and checked, because sixty-year-old walls sometimes hide soft spots around windows and at the sill. Lots near Dudley Pond or the Sudbury River meadows also deserve a look at grade clearance so the lowest course is not sitting in splash-back.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the original skin on most of the pre-1850 buildings in the Wayland Center Historic District, which is listed on the National Register. Homeowners there, or in any older house along Route 27, usually get the best result by matching the existing exposure and corner-board width rather than switching profiles. Where only one elevation has failed, replacing those boards and blending them into sound ones is often more sensible than stripping the whole house. It is worth contacting the town about any local review before changing the look of a historic facade.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits owners who want the look of painted lap siding without the repainting cycle of wood, and in Wayland that often means a mid-century house that has outgrown aluminum or old vinyl. It is heavy, so the framing and sheathing underneath matter, and on houses close to Lake Cochituate or Dudley Pond the bottom edge should sit well clear of soil and decks. Proper clearances at roof-wall intersections and factory-recommended flashing at butt joints keep the boards from wicking water.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit naturally on the wooded, low-density streets away from Wayland Center, and they pair well with older barns and outbuildings like the two nineteenth-century barns counted in the Center district. Shingles weather to gray on their own or can be stained. Shaded walls under heavy tree cover stay damp longer, so ventilation behind the shingles, using a rainscreen mat or furring, helps them dry between storms. Breathable housewrap and stainless or hot-dipped fasteners are worth specifying.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full tear-off is the moment to fix what has been hidden for decades. In Wayland that typically means houses from the 1950s and 1960s with original sheathing, minimal insulation and no housewrap. Stripping every wall allows rotted boards to be replaced, windows to be reflashed and a continuous weather barrier to be installed before the new cladding goes on. Because about seven in ten homes in town predate 1980, many projects also need lead-safe work practices when old painted siding comes off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim carries much of the character of Wayland's older buildings. The Federal and Greek Revival houses near the Route 20 and Route 27 junction rely on corner boards, cornices and door surrounds that are hard to replicate with stock profiles. On those, it is often better to repair or custom-mill pieces than to wrap them. On mid-century houses, rotted fascia and rake boards are common where gutters have overflowed, and PVC or primed wood replacements are reasonable choices once the water source is fixed.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On wooded lots and low, wet ground, gutters do more than finish the roof edge. Leaf load can fill a five-inch gutter quickly in autumn, so larger gutters, wider downspouts or guards are worth considering on heavily wooded lots. On properties near the Sudbury River meadows or the Pelham Island area, which flooded in 2010, where the downspouts discharge matters as much as the gutter itself. Extensions or underground leaders that carry water away from the foundation are worth planning.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Much of Wayland's housing dates from the postwar decades, which means many roofs are on their second or third layer or have reached the end of an architectural shingle's life. A tear-off down to the deck shows whether sheathing has delaminated. On tree-shaded lots, valleys and north-facing slopes hold moss and debris, so ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys and good attic ventilation help. Older buildings in Wayland Center may warrant a different material choice to keep their historic appearance.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Not every problem calls for new siding. A cracked panel, a split clapboard near a hose bib or a patch opened by woodpeckers can usually be fixed in place, as long as the replacement matches what surrounds it. In the historic Center, matching means the same board profile and exposure. Whatever caused the damage, often an overflowing gutter or a missing kick-out flashing, should be corrected in the same visit. Pre-1978 paint calls for lead-safe handling.

story: English settlement in Sherborn started along the Charles River in the 1650s with a few timber garrison houses, and the town was incorporated in 1674. None of those garrisons survive, but parts of the Morse-Barber House at 46 Forest Street are said to date to that year. According to the town's National Register nomination, most 18th-century houses were simple two-story, central-chimney farmhouses, with some smaller central-chimney cottages, and many still stand in the southern and eastern parts of town. Two districts were listed in 1986: Sherborn Center, where local housewrights built finely detailed Federal houses and side-hall Greek Revival homes, and Edward's Plain-Dowse's Corner on North Main Street, where tanners, whipmakers and cider makers worked out of houses and small shops, several since converted to homes.

Between 1900 and 1930 wealthy Bostonians built country estates near the Charles. The roads stayed essentially unchanged until after World War II, and the town has no industrial land. The Census counts only about 1,600 homes; the median was built around 1968, roughly three-quarters predate 1980, and about one in five predates 1940. Close to 90 percent are owner-occupied.

The land is the other half of the story. The nomination counts 22 hills of 250 feet or more, with Brush Hill the highest, and estimates that about 16 percent of the town is swamp, marsh or bog draining toward the Charles. Farm Pond is a spring-fed kettle pond. Exterior work here often means long driveways, exposed hilltop walls and damp low-lying sills on the same property. Pre-1978 houses fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules whenever painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl tends to suit Sherborn's newer houses, built as the town saw some subdivision after World War II, more than the old houses on Western Avenue or South Main Street. On those mid-century homes, a good installation starts with checking the sheathing and adding a proper weather barrier, then using trim details that keep window and door casings from looking thin. Houses on exposed hilltops near Brush Hill take more wind, so nailing schedules and locking courses should follow the manufacturer's high-wind guidance.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Much of Sherborn's historic stock, from the central-chimney farmhouses of the 1700s to the Federal houses in Sherborn Center, was built with clapboard walls. Replacing failed boards with matching exposure, preserving corner boards and avoiding a too-wide modern reveal keeps an old house consistent. Primed or factory-finished cedar or pine helps the paint last. For a building listed on the National Register or inside one of the two 1986 districts, it is worth speaking with the town before changing materials.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement offers a painted lap look for owners of estates and newer houses who would rather not repaint wood every several years. Because a large share of Sherborn is wetland and bog, houses near low ground should keep the bottom course clear of grade and use kick-out flashing wherever a roof meets a wall. The material is heavy and needs careful staging on long or sloped driveways, which are common on the town's larger rural lots.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit Sherborn's rural setting and the barns and outbuildings that survive on old farm properties. They are a reasonable choice for additions to older homes and for estate outbuildings near the Charles River. Shingles on north walls or under dense woods stay wet longer, so a ventilated gap behind them, corrosion-resistant nails and a breathable stain help them last. White cedar can be left to weather, but trim and corner details need care to look right.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: When the whole envelope is failing on a 1950s to 1970s Sherborn house, a full replacement allows the sheathing to be inspected, insulation to be upgraded where possible and windows to be reflashed. On older houses the decision is harder, because an early wall may have original boards worth saving. Removing everything should follow a careful inspection, and if paint is disturbed on a pre-1978 house, lead-safe practices must be used. Long driveways may also affect dumpster placement and delivery planning.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Sherborn Center's Federal houses were built by named local housewrights, and the Greek Revival homes on North Main and Washington Streets carry wide corner boards, fascias and pedimented gables. That kind of trim is worth repairing with matching profiles rather than wrapping in aluminum. On converted shop buildings in Edward's Plain, window and door casings may be simpler but just as old. For newer homes, rot-resistant PVC trim at the bottom of corners and around entry doors cuts down future maintenance.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Big lots, mature woods and a town that is about one-sixth wetland mean gutter planning should consider both leaves and where the water ends up. Oak and pine debris can clog downspouts in a single season, so guards or larger outlets help on wooded properties. On houses near Farm Pond or the low land along the Charles, downspouts should discharge well away from foundations. Older farmhouses without gutters may need a careful look at fascia condition before any are hung.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Sherborn's hills put many houses on exposed sites where wind lifts shingle edges, while homes in the valleys sit under heavy tree cover that holds snow and debris. Both conditions call for ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys, starter strips rated for wind and good attic ventilation. On early houses with central chimneys, flashing and the chimney cap deserve particular attention. Estate houses from the early 1900s may have complex roof lines where a repair-first approach makes sense.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: On a house that has stood since the 1700s, a repair is often the more respectful choice: replacing a handful of split clapboards, re-securing a loose corner board or rebuilding a rotted section of sill trim. New pieces should match the old in width and thickness. Fixing what caused the failure, such as a leaky roof edge or soil piled against the wall, keeps the repair from coming back. Painted surfaces on pre-1978 houses need lead-safe practices.

story: Shirley was settled by English colonists around 1720 as part of the Groton plantation and later became a town of its own. It has two National Register districts that tell two different stories. Shirley Center is the colonial core: a town common with Brown, Center, Horsepond, Parker and Whitney Roads radiating out, lined with Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival buildings including the town hall and First Parish church. Shirley Village, in the south of town, grew around mills on Catacoonamug Brook and the railroad that arrived in 1845. Its 441 listed properties include the surviving Phoenix Mills building, brick schoolhouses, a Richardsonian Romanesque library and a large number of vernacular wood-frame houses built south of the tracks in the later 1800s.

The rest of the town tells a newer story. Of roughly 2,400 homes, the median was built around 1984, so about half went up in the mid-1980s or later, and only about 44 percent predate 1980. About one in five goes back before 1940. About 77 percent of homes are owner-occupied, about 4 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, and part of Devens lies within Shirley's borders.

Shirley is bounded by the Squannacook and Nashua rivers and includes Mulpus Brook, Catecunemaug Brook, Spruce Swamp and Tophet Swamp. A Shaker community operated here from 1793 to 1908, and its remains are preserved on the grounds of the state prison. For an older house in the Village, the work is usually about saving or matching 19th-century wood. For a house from the 1980s or later, it is more often about first-generation vinyl, builder-grade trim and roofs reaching the end of their life. Homes built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many Shirley houses built since the 1980s already have vinyl, and the first generation of it is now fading, cracking at corners or loosening at the J-channel. A replacement is the time to check the housewrap behind it and to upgrade to a thicker panel with better trim. On the older wood-frame houses in Shirley Village, vinyl can hide problems, so rotted sills and window bottoms should be repaired before anything covers them.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The vernacular frame houses south of the railroad in Shirley Village and the older buildings around Shirley Center were generally built with wood clapboard walls. Where the original boards are failing, replacing them with the same exposure and corner-board width keeps a house consistent with its neighbors in these National Register districts. Back-primed boards and stainless fasteners reduce future peeling. Before changing a house's look, it can help to ask the town about any local review.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives owners of 1980s and 1990s houses a way to move off tired vinyl toward a painted look without returning to wood. Its weight means walls should be checked for flatness first, since builder-grade framing sometimes bows. On lots near Spruce Swamp, Tophet Swamp or the brooks, the bottom course should stay well above grade and every roof-wall intersection should get kick-out flashing so water does not run behind the boards.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a reasonable fit for outbuildings, additions and wooded lots near the Squannacook and Nashua rivers. The plain, functional style associated with Shirley's Shaker past is a useful reminder that simple detailing usually looks best. Shaded walls dry slowly, so a ventilated gap behind the shingles, corrosion-resistant nails and a breathable finish help. On older houses, shingles should be considered only where they suit the existing style of the building.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Full replacement makes the most sense in Shirley on houses where the cladding, sheathing and trim are all aging at the same time. That often describes homes from the 1980s with their first siding, or late-1800s Village houses where repeated patching no longer holds. Stripping to the sheathing exposes rot around windows and at sills, allows a continuous weather barrier and lets openings be reflashed. Lead-safe practices apply when older painted layers come off pre-1978 houses.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: The Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival buildings around the Shirley Center common rely on cornices, corner boards and door surrounds that are not easy to buy off the shelf. Repairing them with matching profiles keeps the district's character. In Shirley Village, porches and window trim on 19th-century frame houses often show rot first. On newer houses, swapping finger-jointed builder trim for PVC or primed solid stock at high-splash spots is a practical upgrade.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Between the river corridors, the brooks and two large swamps, a lot of Shirley property is near wet ground, so moving roof water away from the foundation matters. Gutters sized for the roof area, downspouts placed at the right corners and extensions that discharge downhill are the basics. Wooded lots need guards or larger downspouts to keep leaves from backing up, and the fascia behind an old gutter should be checked for soft spots before a new system is hung.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: A large share of Shirley housing dates from the 1980s onward, so many of those roofs are on their first or second replacement. A tear-off to the deck shows whether old plywood or OSB has delaminated. Wooded lots near the rivers hold moisture and moss on north slopes, which makes good ventilation and ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys worthwhile. Village houses from the 1800s may have complex rooflines and chimneys that need careful flashing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: When only part of a wall is failing, a targeted fix is usually enough. Typical examples are a cracked vinyl panel on a 1990s house, a loose corner post, or a few rotted boards near the porch of a Village house. The repair should be paired with a look at why it failed, since gutter overflow and missing flashing are frequent culprits. Painted wood on houses built before 1978 should be handled with lead-safe methods.

story: Rutland sits at the geographic center of Massachusetts and is described as the highest town between the Berkshires and the Atlantic, with its town common at about 1,200 feet. Incorporated in 1713, it once included land that later became Barre, Hubbardston, Oakham, Princeton and part of Paxton. Today it has five villages: New Boston, West Rutland, Muschopauge, North Rutland and Turkey Hill. Its best-known old house is the General Rufus Putnam House at 344 Main Street, built between 1760 and 1765. Its 1972 National Register nomination describes a two-story frame house with a hipped roof, two interior chimneys and its original clapboards.

The hilltop air shaped Rutland's later history. In 1898 the state opened a tuberculosis sanatorium here, described as the first state-operated sanatorium in the country. The facility, later known as Rutland Heights State Hospital, closed in 1991 and was demolished in 2004. Rutland State Park covers about 300 acres around Whitehall Pond, a shallow pond used for swimming and boating.

In housing terms, Rutland is the newest town in this group. The Census counts about 3,400 homes with a median build year around 1990, and fewer than one in ten predate 1940. Roughly 56 percent were built after 1979, and about 89 percent are owner-occupied, with only about 4 percent of homes in two- to four-unit buildings. For most homeowners, the questions are about first-generation vinyl, roofs approaching replacement age and gutters that face real winters on high ground. Older farmhouses and village houses still need lead-safe (RRP) care whenever paint is disturbed on a pre-1978 building.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many of Rutland's homes went up in the 1980s and 1990s with vinyl siding, and that first generation is starting to fade, chalk or crack, especially on south and west walls. Replacing it is a chance to check the housewrap and window flashing that builders installed then. At the town's elevation, open lots take more wind, so heavier panels, proper nailing and well-secured starter strips are worth the extra cost.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: When the Rufus Putnam House on Main Street was nominated to the National Register in 1972, its clapboards were described as original to the 1760s house. That is a good reminder that well-maintained wood can last a very long time. For older homes in the center or the villages, matching the existing board width and exposure keeps repairs from standing out. On newer houses, factory-primed cedar or pine clapboard is an option for owners who want real wood and are prepared to paint it.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits many of Rutland's 1980s to 2000s houses as an upgrade from builder-grade vinyl. It handles sun and cold well when installed with proper gaps and flashing. It is heavy and needs flat, sound walls, so sheathing should be inspected first. Snow that piles against lower walls on high ground means the bottom course should keep the manufacturer's clearance above grade, decks and roofs.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: With the woods and trails around Rutland State Park and Whitehall Pond, cedar shingles fit well on many rural lots. They can be left to weather or stained. On a high, open site, shingles take wind-driven rain and need full coverage and corrosion-resistant fasteners. In shaded woods, walls stay damp, so a ventilated gap or rainscreen mat behind the shingles helps them dry and lengthens their life.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Because most Rutland homes are from the 1980s onward, a full replacement often coincides with the first major repair cycle of the house. Removing the old siding allows the sheathing to be checked, a continuous weather barrier added and windows reflashed. On a high, exposed lot, that is also a good time to air-seal and add exterior insulation board if the budget allows. On older farmhouses, lead-safe practices apply when painted layers are removed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Builder-grade finger-jointed trim on 1980s and 1990s Rutland houses often rots first at the bottoms of corner boards, door casings and garage jambs. Replacing those sections with PVC or primed solid stock and sealing the end grain prevents a repeat. On older houses near the common, trim is often simpler but older, and repairing it with matching profiles is usually better than covering it. Fascia rot should be fixed before new gutters go up.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On Rutland's high ground, snow and ice loads on gutters can be significant, so gutters should be hung securely with hidden hangers spaced closely and pitched correctly. Guards help on wooded lots but should be chosen with snow load in mind. Where houses sit on slopes, downspouts need to carry water away from foundations and driveways, since meltwater that refreezes on walkways is a winter hazard.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With the town common at around 1,200 feet, many Rutland houses sit on high, open ground where snow and wind are part of every winter. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and in valleys, wind-rated starter strips and good attic ventilation help prevent ice dams. Since most homes in town were built after 1980, many roofs are on their original shingles or their first replacement, so a tear-off down to the deck is the time to check sheathing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Damage on Rutland houses is often localized: a vinyl panel cracked in cold weather, a corner knocked loose by snow sliding off the roof, or a section of trim softened where meltwater runs down the wall. Those can usually be repaired without residing, provided matching material is still available. Correcting the snow shed or the drip edge that caused the problem matters as much as the patch itself. Lead-safe methods apply on pre-1978 painted surfaces.

story: Uxbridge was set off from Mendon in 1727, and Farnum House, dating to about 1710, hosted the first town meeting. The Blackstone River runs through town, and so did the Blackstone Canal, which carried horse-drawn barges to Providence until the railroad ended canal traffic in 1848. Daniel Day built a woolen mill in 1809, power looms arrived in 1820, and textile work went on for roughly 140 years. The mill villages were small settlements of their own, with mills, shops, worker housing and farms: Ironstone, Hecla and Wheelockville, and North Uxbridge with Rogerson's Village, where the Crown and Eagle Mills were built on the Mumford River in the 1820s and later converted to senior housing.

That history shows in the Census. Of roughly 5,600 homes, about 31 percent were built before 1940, and close to 18 percent are in buildings with two to four units. The median build year is about 1976, and roughly 80 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Uxbridge also has dozens of National Register listings, and Elmshade, the Taft family homestead once owned by state senator Bezaleel Taft Jr., is cited as typical Georgian architecture.

The town's elevation ranges from about 200 to 577 feet, and the river valley, canal and West Hill Dam area mean many houses sit close to water. In the mill villages, where worker housing was built close to the mills, staging and access can be tighter than on a suburban lot. Roughly half of all homes predate 1980, and any built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: In Uxbridge's mill villages, vinyl is often a practical choice for buildings with two to four units, where one owner may be maintaining a large wall area for several households. Before it goes on, the old wood beneath should be checked, especially around porches and window sills. Covering rot only hides it. On newer houses from the 1970s onward, a replacement is also the time to improve the weather barrier and add flashing tape at openings.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Historic houses in Uxbridge, from Federal-era farmhouses to mill-village homes in Hecla or Rogerson's Village, were usually built with wood clapboard. Matching the existing exposure, corner-board width and trim keeps repairs from standing out, particularly in National Register areas. Pre-primed boards help paint last. Before altering a historic facade, it can help to contact the town or historical commission to ask what, if any, review applies.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement offers mill-village owners and landlords a painted look with less upkeep than wood, which matters on multi-family houses where maintenance falls on one owner. The boards are heavy and need sound framing, so older walls should be opened and checked. Close lots in the villages can make staging and ladder placement tight, which affects scheduling. Houses near the Blackstone or Mumford rivers should keep the bottom course well clear of wet ground.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit the farmhouses and outbuildings that still survive on the town's edges, and they can work as an accent on gables of older houses. They are less common on the mill-village houses, where clapboard dominated. Shingles near the river or under heavy tree cover stay damp, so a ventilated backing and corrosion-resistant nails are worth specifying. A stain or bleaching oil can even out color as the wood weathers.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: About three in ten Uxbridge homes predate 1940, so a full replacement here often uncovers board sheathing, balloon framing or gaps with no insulation. Stripping everything allows those problems to be fixed and a weather barrier to be installed properly. On two- to four-unit buildings, coordinating with owners and tenants on access and timing matters. Lead-safe practices must be followed whenever painted siding comes off a pre-1978 house.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Porches, cornices and window casings are where mill-village houses in North Uxbridge, Hecla and Wheelockville usually show their age first. Rebuilding them with matching profiles keeps the character of these neighborhoods. Georgian and Federal houses such as those in the town's National Register listings have more elaborate trim that is worth repairing rather than covering. On newer homes, PVC at splash zones and around doors reduces maintenance.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: The Blackstone and Mumford river valleys and the closely spaced mill-village lots put a premium on directing roof water properly. On houses that sit close together, downspouts should discharge away from the foundation and not onto the next lot. Older multi-family buildings with large roof areas may need oversized gutters and extra downspouts. Wooded lots on the town's higher ground need guards or regular cleaning to keep leaves out.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Uxbridge's older multi-family houses often have large, simple roofs, while the Federal-era homes may have chimneys and dormers that complicate flashing. A tear-off to the deck shows whether old boards need replacing. Close lots in the mill villages can make debris removal and staging harder, so planning matters. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys and balanced ventilation help with the snow and ice the town gets from November through April.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Many repairs in Uxbridge are on older buildings where one wall or one porch has taken the worst of the weather. Replacing a few rotted clapboards, a damaged section of vinyl or a failed corner board can buy years before a larger project. On buildings with two to four units, scheduling around tenants is part of the job. The cause, whether a gutter, a downspout or splash from a walkway, should be fixed too. Lead-safe practices apply on pre-1978 paint.

story: Littleton grew out of Nashoba Plantation, the Praying Indian village John Eliot established in 1645 between Lake Nagog and Fort Pond. In 1717 the town moved its meetinghouse from the Newtown area to the Town Common, and by the 1800s Littleton was known for apple orchards and cider. The Fitchburg Railroad arrived in 1844, and stores and businesses grew up around the Common and the Depot. The Conant Houghton Co. Mill was built near the Common in 1880, and a vinegar and juice plant moved to the Depot in 1930.

Construction of Warren's Grist Mill at Mill Road and Warren Street began in 1750, and the Houghton Memorial Building, designed by Perkins & Betton, went up in 1894-95 and later housed the Littleton Historical Society. Most of the town's houses, though, are far newer. In the 1950s and 1960s, families moving out from Arlington, Cambridge, Lowell and Somerville settled here, and Digital Equipment Corporation built a large facility on King Street near the Common in the 1970s. The Census counts about 4,000 homes with a median build year around 1977. Only about 16 percent predate 1940, about half predate 1980, and fewer than 3 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. About 84 percent are owner-occupied.

Water is a big part of the town. Around Mill Pond, also called Lake Warren, neighborhoods such as Long Lake and Spectacle Pond include many summer cottages or camps that have since been converted to year-round homes. A converted camp may have been added onto in stages, and its walls were not originally built for winter, so the exterior can need as much attention as the interior. Pre-1978 homes fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many Littleton houses from the 1960s and 1970s now need new cladding, and vinyl is a common choice for those homes. On converted camps around Long Lake and Spectacle Pond, the walls behind any siding may lack sheathing or insulation, so they should be inspected before vinyl goes on. Choosing a thicker panel and installing a proper weather barrier helps the result hold up on lakefront lots that see more wind and moisture.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: For the town's older houses, including those near the Common and the Depot that grew up after the railroad arrived, painted wood clapboard is the traditional choice. Matching the original exposure and trim keeps repairs consistent on 18th- and 19th-century houses. Pre-primed boards and stainless fasteners help paint last. For postwar houses, clapboard is a choice for owners who want real wood, but it needs periodic repainting, which should be factored into the decision.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement works well on Littleton's postwar and 1970s houses for owners who want a painted look with less upkeep than wood. On converted lake cottages, the extra weight means walls and framing need to be checked first, and some may need reinforcement or new sheathing. Near the shoreline at Long Lake, Spectacle Pond or Lake Nagog, the bottom course should be kept well above grade and decks to avoid moisture damage.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a natural fit for the former summer cottages around Mill Pond, Long Lake and Spectacle Pond, and many lakeside houses look right with them. On damp or shaded lake lots, shingles should be installed over a ventilated layer so they dry, with corrosion-resistant fasteners. They can be stained or left to weather. Shingles also suit additions to older farmhouses on the town's outskirts where orchards once stood.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement is often the right call for converted lake camps, where the original walls were built for summer use and may lack proper sheathing, insulation or flashing. Stripping the old siding allows these problems to be fixed before new cladding goes on. On 1960s and 1970s houses, the same process can reveal rot around windows and sills. Lead-safe practices apply when painted siding is removed from pre-1978 homes.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On Littleton's 18th- and 19th-century houses, original cornices, corner boards and door surrounds are worth preserving with matching profiles. On postwar houses, rot often appears first at corner boards, door casings and garage trim, and PVC or primed solid wood are durable replacements. Converted camps may have trim that was never designed for year-round exposure, and upgrading it during other work is often worthwhile.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With ponds, lakes and many wooded lots, gutters in Littleton face leaf load and need to send water away from foundations near the water table. On converted lake cottages, foundations can be shallow, so downspouts should discharge well away from the house. Guards or larger downspouts help on lots with tall oaks and pines. Older fascia boards should be checked for rot before new gutters are hung.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Roofs on Littleton's postwar and 1970s houses are often on their second or third replacement, and the converted camps around the ponds may have low-pitch roofs or additions with tricky tie-ins. A tear-off to the deck reveals whether sheathing needs replacing. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys and adequate attic ventilation help prevent ice dams, which are a particular risk on low-slope sections of converted cottages.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A loose shingle on a lakeside cottage, a cracked panel on a 1970s house or rot where a deck meets the wall can usually be handled as a repair. Finding the source matters: deck ledgers and roof-wall intersections without flashing are common causes on converted camps. Matching weathered shingles or older vinyl colors can take some searching. Lead-safe methods apply whenever painted surfaces on pre-1978 homes are cut or removed.

story: Charlton was first settled in 1735 and became a town in 1775. Farming carried it through the 1800s, and woolen mills appeared along some of its brooks by the early 1900s. The oldest buildings are concentrated in two National Register districts. Northside Village, on Stafford Road where it meets Northside and Cemetery Roads, has thirteen buildings, most of them older than 1850, among them the 1797 Rider Tavern, once a stagecoach stop between Worcester and Hartford, and the 1848 No. 2 Schoolhouse. The Charlton Center district along Main Street, between Mugget Hill Road and Masonic Home Road, mixes Federal and Gothic Revival houses with Late Victorian, Shingle style and Colonial Revival buildings, including the Shingle-style Overlook and the 1905 Town Hall.

Those historic pockets are a small share of the housing. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 count about 5,200 homes with a median construction year of 1985. Only about 8 percent were built before 1940 and roughly 40 percent before 1980, which leaves a majority built in the last four and a half decades. About 85 percent are owner-occupied, and fewer than one home in ten is in a two- to four-unit building. For most owners, then, the exterior question is not restoration but renewal: original siding, trim, gutters and roofing on houses that are now thirty to forty years old.

The town is large, about 44 square miles, and its listed elevation is 896 feet. Buffumville Lake, an Army Corps of Engineers flood-control reservoir of about 200 acres, the Capen Hill Nature Sanctuary, Route 20, Route 31, Route 169 and the Massachusetts Turnpike all fall within its borders. Houses on higher, open ground take more wind and hold snow longer than sheltered valley sites, and that is worth factoring into material and fastening choices.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With a median build year of 1985, a good part of Charlton's housing is old enough that its first round of siding is due for a decision. Vinyl suits these houses because most were built with plain detailing and standard framing. On exposed hilltop lots, a heavier-gauge panel and correct nail spacing matter more than color choice, since wind is what loosens lightweight vinyl first. Ask that the wall be checked for flatness before installation; a wavy sheathing plane shows through thin panels, especially in low morning or evening light.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard makes the most sense on Charlton's older houses, such as those in the Charlton Center and Northside Village districts, where Federal, Greek Revival and Gothic Revival houses were originally sided in wood. When boards are replaced, matching the original exposure and corner treatment keeps the house reading correctly from the street. On houses built after 1980, wood clapboard is a choice of appearance rather than history, and it commits the owner to a repainting schedule. Primed boards with all ends and cuts sealed before installation hold paint longer.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable middle path for the many Charlton houses built in the 1980s and 1990s whose owners want a painted look without wood maintenance. It is heavy, so the condition of the sheathing and how well it holds fasteners should be checked before the old siding goes back on the truck. Clearance between the bottom course and the ground, and between siding and roof surfaces at dormers and porch roofs, needs to follow the manufacturer's requirements, because fiber cement edges absorb water if they sit in snow or splashback.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit some of Charlton's older buildings, including the Shingle-style work found in the town center, but they ask more of the owner than other claddings. On wooded or shaded lots, shingles stay damp longer and can grow moss on north walls, so the stain or finish and the air gap behind them deserve attention. A rainscreen mat or furring behind the shingles helps them dry. Where a house sits in open, sunny ground, untreated shingles weather evenly to gray; on mixed exposures the color change can be patchy for years.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement is the point to look behind the cladding. On a 1980s or 1990s Charlton house, that usually means checking the original housewrap or felt, the window flashing and the sill area where water collects. About 40 percent of local homes were built before 1980, and on those, older layers of siding may be stacked under the current one. Removing everything down to the sheathing costs more but reveals rot and lets new flashing tie in properly. If any painted surface predates 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices apply when it is disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is where Charlton's older houses show their age first: window casings, corner boards, rake boards and the sills under them. In the Main Street and Stafford Road historic areas, trim profiles are part of the architecture, so a replacement should copy the old dimensions rather than default to stock lumber sizes. On newer houses, cellular PVC trim is often used at the lowest and wettest spots, such as sills, skirt boards and garage door jambs, while painted wood stays where profiles are more detailed. Joints should be sealed and flashed, not only caulked.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Many Charlton lots back onto woods, and the town's land area is large relative to its housing. Leaves and pine needles fill gutters quickly on those lots, so a larger gutter and downspout, along with a guard suited to the type of debris, can reduce maintenance. Pitch should be checked so water does not sit in long runs. Downspouts on sloped lots need to discharge well away from the foundation, and the extensions should not drain toward a driveway that freezes. Hidden hangers spaced closely help gutters carry ice and snow sliding from the roof.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Charlton's listed elevation is 896 feet, and houses on open hilltops are exposed to wind and hold snow on the roof for long stretches. Ice and water membrane at the eaves and in valleys is worth extending further up the roof on low-slope sections and over porches. Shingle wind ratings and the nailing pattern should match the exposure of the site. Many houses here date from the 1980s and later, and on those the attic ventilation is worth reviewing during a reroof, since balanced intake and exhaust reduce ice dams.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Charlton cover the usual range: a cracked vinyl panel, a loose course after a windstorm, a rotted clapboard near a downspout or deck ledger. Matching color and profile is the main challenge on older vinyl, which fades over time. On historic houses, patching with matching wood is often preferable to replacing whole walls. A repair visit is also a reasonable time to have the surrounding flashing looked at, since the visible damage is often the end of a leak that started higher up.

story: Blackstone separated from Mendon and was incorporated in 1845, taking its name from the early settler William Blaxton. It is small, about 11 square miles, with the Blackstone River running along its southern edge and Woonsocket and North Smithfield, Rhode Island, just across the line. The town is a collection of named places rather than a single center: Waterford, Millerville, New City, High Rocks, East Blackstone, Farnum's Gate, Five Corners, Central Village, Wheelockville and Privilege among them. It sits inside the Blackstone River Valley National Heritage Corridor.

Industry shaped the housing. The Blackstone Manufacturing Company, founded in 1808, built the village known as New City or High Rocks around Butler, Canal, Church, County, Ives, Main and Mendon Streets. Its worker housing was mostly wood-frame tenements of two to six units, originally clapboarded, in Greek Revival, Italianate and Queen Anne styles; that area became a National Register district in 1995. East Blackstone, around the junction of Elm and Summer Streets near the Rhode Island border, is older still, with the c. 1760 Seth Kelly House, mostly early 19th-century Federal and Greek Revival houses, a brick school from about 1830 and a stone store.

Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 show what that history means today. Of roughly 4,000 homes, the median was built in 1967, about 22 percent predate 1940 and about 62 percent predate 1980. Around 21 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, and about 73 percent are owner-occupied. Exterior work here often means multi-family houses, older wood under newer siding, and painted surfaces that may contain lead.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many of Blackstone's older two- to six-unit houses were re-sided at some point, and vinyl is a practical choice for a multi-family building where the owner wants low upkeep across a large wall area. The tall, flat walls of a mill-era tenement show every wave in the sheathing, so the substrate should be shimmed or furred where needed. On buildings near the property line, as in parts of New City, staging space can be limited, and the plan for ladders, scaffolds and debris should be agreed with neighbors before work starts.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Blackstone Manufacturing Company's housing was originally finished in clapboard, and the East Blackstone houses date largely from the first half of the 19th century. On those buildings, wood clapboard keeps the original proportions intact. When old siding is stripped, the original boards are sometimes still underneath and can guide the replacement exposure. Because about 62 percent of local homes predate 1980, lead paint is a real possibility, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when pre-1978 paint is disturbed during removal or preparation.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: For a two-family or three-family building where clapboard character matters but repainting every few years does not appeal, fiber cement lap siding is worth pricing. It can be ordered in an exposure close to old clapboard. Its weight and the need for proper ground and roof clearances make it important to look at the condition of the sills and lower wall framing first, which on 19th-century houses near the river may have taken on moisture over many decades. Cut edges need to be sealed and painted.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are less common on Blackstone's mill-era housing than lap siding, but they suit gable ends, Queen Anne details and some later houses. Where a building sits close to its neighbor or in shade, shingles dry slowly, so a ventilated backing and a good stain matter. On a multi-unit building, shingles are a larger commitment in labor and upkeep than lap siding, and it makes sense to weigh that against how long the owner plans to hold the property.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1967 and more than a fifth of homes built before 1940, a full replacement in Blackstone can uncover more than one generation of siding, sometimes with the original clapboard still underneath. Any older layer of unknown material should be identified before it is torn off, since some older sidings require special handling. Taking the wall down to sheathing allows rot at sills and around windows to be repaired and new flashing installed. On a multi-family building, the work plan should account for tenants, entry doors and porches.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Greek Revival and Italianate houses in New City and East Blackstone carry trim that defines their style: wide corner boards, frieze boards, bracketed eaves and window hoods. Replacing those pieces with flat stock changes the building's look more than new siding does. Where trim is rotted, copying the profile in wood or cellular PVC keeps the character. Porch trim on multi-family houses, where stairs and decks meet the wall, is a common point of decay and should be flashed when rebuilt.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Blackstone sits low along the river, with a listed elevation of 187 feet, and on older houses with stone or brick footings, keeping roof water away from the foundation matters. Gutters should be sized for the roof area, which on a large multi-unit building can be considerable, and downspouts should lead water away from walkways and shared driveways. On tenement buildings with several entries, a gutter or diverter over each door keeps meltwater from refreezing on the steps.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many of Blackstone's older multi-family buildings have broad gable roofs, sometimes with low-slope porch roofs attached. The porch sections need a membrane or low-slope system rather than shingles. During a reroof on a 19th-century house, the roof deck may be original boards with gaps between them, which may need new sheathing before modern shingles go on. Chimneys, which are common on older buildings, should be flashed and counter-flashed properly. On houses with mansard roofs, such as the remodeled Lyman Paine House in East Blackstone, the steep sides require their own detailing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Blackstone often focus on the lower parts of walls and the areas around porches, where splashback and snow do the most damage. On older houses, a repair may expose original clapboard or an older siding layer beneath the current one, and the plan should account for that before work begins. Matching faded vinyl can be difficult, so it is worth asking whether panels can be borrowed from a less visible wall.
