story: Westford began as West Chelmsford and was incorporated on September 23, 1729. In the late 18th and 19th centuries its economy rested on granite, apples and worsted yarn, and after the Civil War it became a residential suburb for workers in Lowell's factories. From the 1970s, technology firms spread along Route 110, and the town grew into a large commuter suburb of about 31 square miles.

The older housing is organized by village. Westford Center, along Main Street between Graniteville and Leland Roads, contains the 1794 Westford Academy building and First Parish Church, the 1871 Italianate town hall and Colonial, Federal and Greek Revival houses on the side streets; it was listed on the National Register in 1998. Forge Village grew around the Abbot Worsted Company mill, founded in 1854, with housing on the streets near Forge Pond and the junction of East and West Prescott Streets. Graniteville developed around granite quarries and C. G. Sargent's mill after the railroad arrived in 1847, with most of its housing from the second half of the 19th century. Nabnasset, by Nabnasset Lake, has many smaller homes close to the water. Parker Village completes the list of villages residents traditionally name. Both Forge Village and Graniteville became National Register districts in 2002.

Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 count about 9,200 homes with a median build year of 1983. Around 16 percent were built before 1940 and about 45 percent before 1980; roughly 86 percent are owner-occupied and only about 2 to 3 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. The result is a town with village cores of 19th-century wood houses surrounded by decades of single-family development.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Most of Westford's housing is single-family and was built from the 1970s onward, so vinyl usually goes onto houses whose first siding has simply worn out. In subdivisions where neighboring houses went up at the same time, a profile and color that suit the house's proportions make more difference than any upgrade in panel thickness. Around Nabnasset Lake, the wall facing open water catches more wind, which argues for a heavier panel and careful nailing. Sheathing and window flashing should be inspected before new panels go on.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The town's 19th-century wood houses are concentrated in Westford Center, Forge Village and Graniteville, all three on the National Register. Clapboard is what keeps those buildings honest to their period, and copying the existing exposure, corner boards and window casings matters as much as the board itself. Pre-primed boards installed over a drainage layer and painted promptly hold their finish well. On any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices apply when old paint is scraped, sanded or removed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is often weighed by Westford owners of houses from the 1980s and 1990s who want the look of painted lap siding without a repainting cycle. Factory-finished boards keep the color consistent and cut down on painting on site. The material is heavy and has to be cut with dust control, which affects setup on the smaller lots near Nabnasset Lake and in the village centers. Clearances above roofs, decks and grade need to follow the manufacturer's specifications.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit some older Westford houses and a number of later designs with simple massing. Many lots in town are wooded, and shingles under trees dry slowly, so a ventilated backing and a breathable stain help prevent mildew and decay. On a house inside one of the historic villages, it is worth confirming what the original cladding was before switching from clapboard to shingles, since that change alters how the building reads from Main Street or Prescott Street.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1983, a large share of Westford houses still wear their original siding, now around forty years old. A full replacement is the moment to look at the housewrap, the window and door flashing, and the sheathing at the bottom of walls. In Forge Village and Graniteville, where most houses are from the second half of the 19th century, stripping a wall can reveal original clapboard or several later layers. Going down to sheathing lets rot be repaired before new cladding hides it again.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Federal and Greek Revival houses near the Common in Westford Center rely on trim for their character: corner pilasters, frieze boards and cornices. When those parts decay, replacements should copy the original profiles rather than substitute stock boards. On late 20th-century houses, trim tends to fail first at window sills, garage door jambs and where decks meet the wall. Cellular PVC works well at those wet spots, while painted wood stays where a profile needs to be shaped.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Many Westford houses sit on wooded lots, and gutters there can fill with leaves in autumn and with needles year-round. A guard chosen for the trees on the lot, rather than a one-size product, cuts down on cleaning. Larger houses with several roof planes concentrate water at valleys and inside corners, which may call for oversized downspouts at those points. Downspouts should discharge well clear of the foundation, especially on houses with finished basements.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Westford's listed elevation is 407 feet, and snow tends to stay on roofs through much of the winter. Ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys, plus balanced attic ventilation, reduce the risk of ice dams. Houses built in the 1980s and 1990s often have complicated rooflines with dormers, valleys and wall intersections, and each of those needs step flashing and careful detailing during a reroof. On 19th-century houses in the villages, the roof deck may be original boards that need new sheathing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repair calls in Westford typically involve panels loosened by wind, boards damaged near decks or downspouts, or a section struck by a falling branch on a wooded lot. Matching faded vinyl or a discontinued profile is the usual difficulty. On wood-sided houses in the villages, individual clapboards can often be replaced to match. Where rot is the problem, the source is often a missing kick-out flashing or a leaking gutter seam above it, and fixing only the board leaves the cause in place.

story: Carlisle was settled by English colonists in 1651 on land drawn from Acton, Billerica, Chelmsford and Concord. It became a district of Concord in 1780 and a separate town in 1805. Its oldest houses are timber-framed. The George Robbins House at 523 Curve Street, dated by its construction to about 1700, is five bays wide with a late 18th-century leanto, and the Zeb Spaulding House at 1044 Lowell Road, from about 1725, is a two-and-a-half-story clapboarded house with a large central chimney. Both are on the National Register as First Period buildings.

The town has kept a low density. It enforces a minimum two-acre lot size on new development, and conservation land covers about a quarter of its area, including the 909-acre Great Brook Farm State Park with its working dairy and Meadow Pond, and part of the Great Meadows National Wildlife Refuge along the Concord River. The center around the Old Burying Ground, the Gleason Public Library and the Ferns Country Store site on Lowell Street, where a store has stood since 1844, remains small.

Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 count only about 1,800 homes. The median year built is 1976; around 13 percent predate 1940 and nearly 58 percent predate 1980. About 94 percent are owner-occupied, and roughly 2 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings. In practical terms, exterior work in Carlisle involves large single-family houses set back on wooded or open land, plus a group of very old wooden houses that call for careful handling.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is used in Carlisle mostly on houses built from the 1960s through the 1980s, which make up much of the housing stock. On a house set back on a two-acre lot, color and proportion are what a passerby sees, so samples are worth viewing on the actual wall in daylight. Wide, tall walls on large houses expand and contract more in total, so panels must be hung loosely enough to move. Vinyl is a poor fit on the First Period houses, where wood clapboard is part of the historic fabric.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Carlisle's oldest buildings, such as the Zeb Spaulding House on Lowell Road, were clapboarded, and on houses of that age the boards, their exposure and the way they meet the corner boards are part of the record. Replacement should match those details closely. On any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when old paint is disturbed. With nearly 58 percent of homes predating 1980, that covers a large part of the town. Back-primed boards installed over a drainage gap hold paint longer.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: For a Carlisle house built in the 1970s or 1980s that needs new siding, fiber cement offers a painted lap look with less maintenance than wood. Long walls on larger houses mean many butt joints, and those joints need flashing behind them. On a site surrounded by woods, the bottom courses should sit high enough above grade and mulch that they do not stay wet. The material's weight makes fastening into studs, not just sheathing, important.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Carlisle's wooded setting and many of its later houses. Under tree cover, shingles stay damp longer and can grow mildew and moss on shaded walls, so a ventilated backing and a breathable stain are worth the extra cost. Where a house sits in open farmland or meadow, shingles weather evenly. On First Period houses, shingles should replace shingles; switching from clapboard changes the historic character.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1976, many Carlisle houses have reached the age at which a full re-siding is considered. A full replacement is the time to look for rot at sills and in walls exposed to weather, to correct missing or failed window flashing, and to add a drainage layer. On older houses, the sheathing may be boards rather than panels, and gaps may need attention before new siding goes up. Work on pre-1978 houses requires EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On Carlisle's older wooden houses, original trim such as wide corner boards, window casings and cornices should be repaired or copied rather than replaced with generic profiles. On houses built from the 1960s onward, trim tends to fail at the sills of windows and doors, at garage door jambs, and where decks meet the wall. Those low, wet pieces can be swapped for cellular PVC without changing the look much. Where trim meets the roof on large, complex houses, kick-out flashing prevents water from running into the wall.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Carlisle's houses are surrounded by conservation land and wooded lots, and gutters fill quickly with leaves and pine needles. Guards suited to the type of trees and generously sized downspouts help. On large lots, downspouts can be extended well away from the house or connected to drywells, which is useful where houses sit on low ground near wetlands. Hangers should be spaced to carry the weight of ice in winter.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Large houses on open or wooded lots in Carlisle often have broad roofs with dormers and valleys. Trees overhanging roofs drop debris and keep shingles damp, which shortens roof life on shaded slopes; trimming back branches before a reroof is worth considering. A self-adhered membrane along the eaves and through the valleys, together with an attic that breathes evenly from soffit to ridge, keeps meltwater from backing up under the shingles. On First Period houses, expect old board decking and a massive central chimney whose flashing deserves extra time.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Carlisle often involve damage from falling branches, woodpeckers on cedar, and decay at the bottom of walls near mulch beds or grade. Single clapboards or shingles can usually be pieced in to match. On the oldest houses, a patch keeps more original material in place than a wall-by-wall replacement would. Lifting a few courses around the damage also shows whether water has reached the sheathing.

story: Waltham was settled in 1634 as part of Watertown, became a town in 1738 and a city in 1884. Its growth followed the Charles River. By 1813 the Boston Manufacturing Company was running what is described as the first integrated textile mill in the United States, powered by dams on the river, and in 1854 the Waltham Watch Company opened its factory; the surviving watch-company buildings on Crescent Street, on the river's south bank, date from 1879 to 1913. Housing for the people who worked in those mills spread outward from the river and from Central Square, the civic center around the Common.

That history is still legible street by street. On Charles Street, west of Central Square, four 1865 workers' houses, two-and-a-half-story wood-frame buildings, one of them a duplex, form a small National Register district, and there are Boston Manufacturing Company houses on River Street. East Main Street keeps a short row of Greek Revival and Italianate houses, including the 1844 Lyman Reed House, a temple-front Greek Revival. At Piety Corner, around Lexington and Bacon Streets near Totten Pond Road, there are Federal houses, mansard-roofed Second Empire houses, Carpenter Gothic and Queen Anne houses, and an 1875 octagon house at 361 Bacon Street. Larger estates, Gore Place from 1806, the Lyman Estate from 1793 and the 1886 Robert Treat Paine Estate, sit at the edges. Neighborhood names include the South Side, Banks Square, Warrendale, the Highlands, Lakeview, Cedarwood and Kendall Park.

Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put Waltham at about 26,700 homes with a median build year of 1961. About 28 percent were built before 1940 and about 69 percent before 1980. Roughly 23 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, and only about half are owner-occupied, so many exterior jobs here are on rental or owner-occupied multi-family buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: In a city where about a quarter of homes are in two- to four-unit buildings and about half are rented, vinyl is often chosen for its low upkeep on large wall areas. On close-set lots, scaffolding and ladder placement may require access across a neighbor's yard, which should be arranged in advance. Tall, flat walls on older multi-family buildings show waves in the sheathing, so shimming or furring may be needed. Panels must also be kept clear of gas meters and dryer vents, and trimmed correctly around them.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Waltham has a deep stock of 19th-century wooden houses, from the 1865 workers' houses on Charles Street to the Greek Revival and Italianate houses on East Main Street. On those buildings, clapboard keeps the original look, and matching the exposure and corner boards matters. Some older houses used other wood finishes, such as the flushboard siding on the George W. Chamberlain House, which needs its own approach. EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when pre-1978 paint is disturbed, which covers most of the city's older housing.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable option for owners of Waltham's mid-century and older multi-family buildings who want a painted lap look with less upkeep than wood. On dense streets, cutting fiber cement creates silica dust, so cutting should be done with dust control and away from neighbors' windows. The material's weight means fastening into framing matters, and clearances at porches, steps and roof lines need to follow the manufacturer's specifications.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles appear on Waltham's Queen Anne and Shingle-influenced houses, such as the Charles P. Nutting House on East Main Street, which combines Queen Anne and Shingle elements. On those buildings, shingles are part of the design, and patterns in gable ends should be copied when replaced. On densely built streets, walls facing a neighbor a few feet away get little sun and dry slowly, so a ventilated backing and a breathable finish help.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With a median build year of 1961 and about 28 percent of homes from before 1940, a full replacement in Waltham often reveals original wood siding under one or more later layers. Removing those layers lets rot at sills and around windows be repaired and proper flashing installed. On multi-family buildings, the work affects several households, so access to entrances and porches needs planning. EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when pre-1978 paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Waltham's older houses carry trim that defines their style: the bracketed cornices of Italianate houses, the mansard trim on Second Empire houses at Piety Corner, and porch details on many multi-family buildings. Replacing these with flat stock alters the building's character. Where trim is rotted, copying the profile in wood or cellular PVC keeps the look. Porches on multi-family buildings, where stairs meet the wall, are a common source of decay and should be flashed during rebuilding.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: On Waltham's closely spaced lots, where houses may be only a few feet apart, downspouts need to send water away from both the house and the neighbor's foundation. Gutters over entrances on multi-family buildings help keep steps free of ice. Larger roofs on multi-unit buildings collect a lot of water, so gutters and downspouts should be sized to handle it. Street trees and yard trees can fill gutters, and guards may be worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many of Waltham's older houses have porch roofs and flat or low-slope sections on rear additions, which need membranes rather than shingles. Mansard roofs, such as those on the Second Empire houses at Piety Corner, have steep sides with their own detailing. On a reroof of a 19th-century house, the deck may be original board sheathing that needs new plywood. Chimney flashing and wall intersections should be redone rather than reused. On close-set lots, staging and debris removal must be planned.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Waltham often involve the lower parts of walls, areas around porches, and spots where gutters or downspouts have overflowed. On older buildings, a repair may uncover original wood or older siding beneath the current layer. Sun-faded vinyl seldom matches a new carton. On multi-family buildings, repairs near entrances should be scheduled so tenants can still get in and out.

story: Norfolk's land was once part of Dedham and then the northern part of Wrentham. Farms abandoned during King Philip's War were resettled later in the 17th century, and small industrial villages formed around water power: City Mills, with sawmills and gristmills dating to 1680; the mill village at Mann Pond, now Highland Lake, which later had a paper mill; and Stony Brook, where three cotton companies started after 1812. Pondville took shape after 1730. The Norfolk County Railroad arrived in 1849, and in 1870 North Wrentham separated and was incorporated as Norfolk.

The old center survives along Rockwood Road, Route 115, between the commuter rail line and Boardman Street. That stretch became a National Register district in 2017. Most of its houses date from about 1850 to 1900, with the Mann House at 16 Rockwood Road from about 1806 and the Darius Ware House at number 29 from about 1814. The Norfolk Grange Hall, built as a Baptist church in 1863, is a clapboarded wood-frame building on a granite foundation with quoined corners and a two-stage tower. The town lies in the upper valley of the Charles River, and the former Norfolk Airpark is now conservation land called Leland Wild.

The town grew quickly after 1925, when a hospital and a state prison opened near the Walpole line, and Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 put the median build year at 1984. Of roughly 3,600 homes, about 8 percent predate 1940 and about 41 percent predate 1980. Nearly 95 percent are owner-occupied, and only about 3 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so most exterior work here is on single-family houses from the last half century.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Most Norfolk homes were built after 1980, and on those houses vinyl replacement is often a matter of replacing the original panels with heavier, better-insulated ones. Insulated vinyl with a foam backing can stiffen the wall and add a little insulation. The underlying housewrap and window flashing should be checked for tears and gaps before new panels go up. On the older houses along Rockwood Road, vinyl changes the look of 19th-century clapboard walls and may not be the best fit.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Rockwood Road district is where Norfolk's 19th-century clapboarded houses are concentrated, and the Grange Hall there is a clapboarded example. Matching the original exposure, corner boards and window casings keeps those buildings consistent with their neighbors. For houses built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when old paint is disturbed. On newer houses, clapboard is mainly a choice of appearance and requires a painting schedule; factory-primed or pre-finished boards reduce that.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: For a Norfolk house built in the 1980s or 1990s, fiber cement provides a painted lap look with less upkeep than wood. Its weight means fastening into studs, and long walls need joint flashing behind each butt joint. Clearances at grade, decks and roof edges must follow the manufacturer's specifications. Pre-finished boards save painting time and keep the color consistent across the house.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit Norfolk houses near conservation land or wooded areas, where the natural finish blends with the surroundings. On shaded walls, shingles stay damp longer, so a ventilated backing and a breathable stain help prevent mildew and decay. Shingles take more time to install and more upkeep than lap siding, so they are often used on part of a house, such as gables, rather than all walls.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a Norfolk house from the 1980s or later is a chance to replace the original housewrap, improve window and door flashing, and add insulation under the siding. On older houses in Pondville, City Mills or along Rockwood Road, removing siding may reveal original clapboard or earlier layers, and rot at sills is common on houses of that age. EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply on pre-1978 houses when old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On Norfolk's 19th-century houses, trim such as quoined corners, like those on the Grange Hall, and cornices are part of the style and should be copied rather than replaced with generic boards. On newer houses, trim often fails first at window sills, garage door jambs and where decks meet the wall. Swapping just those pieces for a rot-proof material, and leaving the more decorative wood in place, is often the economical route.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Norfolk sits in the upper Charles River valley, with ponds such as Highland Lake and conservation areas like Leland Wild. Houses near wetlands or on low ground benefit from gutters and downspouts that carry water well away from foundations, and drywells can help on lots where water collects. Wooded lots fill gutters with leaves and needles, so guards suited to the trees are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many Norfolk houses built since the 1980s have complex roofs with dormers and valleys, which need careful flashing during a reroof. Ice dams start with heat loss into the attic, so insulation and venting deserve a look at the same time as the eave membrane. Houses near trees should have overhanging branches trimmed to reduce debris and moss. On older houses along Rockwood Road, the roof deck may be original boards that need new sheathing before new shingles.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Norfolk usually address storm damage, panels loosened by wind, and boards near decks or downspouts that have taken on water. Because vinyl fades unevenly, new panels rarely match old ones exactly; moving existing panels from a back wall to the front is one workaround. Wood boards on older houses can be replaced one at a time, and any bare end grain should be primed before the new piece goes in.

story: Franklin was carved from the western part of Wrentham and incorporated in 1778, and its oldest fabric still gathers around the triangular green that took shape in the mid-1700s. The Franklin Common Historic District, listed on the National Register in 2005, is mostly residential, with Federal and Greek Revival buildings around the green and along Main Street north to the Red Brick School at Lincoln Street. The 1895 Federated Church on the green is a Shingle-style building. Nineteenth-century industry added a second layer: straw hats were the most profitable business in the 1870s, and the Ray family ran woolen and shoddy operations in Unionville, the village that stretches roughly toward the Bellingham line.

Most of today's houses are far younger than that. Census figures put the median year built at about 1985, with only around 14 percent of homes dating from before 1940 and roughly 41 percent from before 1980. The population jumped from about 10,500 to about 17,800 between 1960 and 1970, and a Dean College history of the town ties the end of farming as the main economy to the construction of I-495 in the 1960s. Of roughly 13,000 housing units, about 78 percent are owner-occupied and fewer than one in ten sits in a two- to four-unit building.

For exterior work, that mix means two very different jobs. Older houses near the common and downtown call for careful matching of trim profiles and lap exposures. The larger share of homes from the last four decades often comes down to first-generation vinyl, builder-grade trim and original roofs reaching the end of their service life. The town also has a lot of water and woods, from Mine Brook's marshland to Franklin State Forest and the town forests, which matters for gutters and for siding near the ground.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With a median build year in the mid-1980s, much of Franklin's housing went up when vinyl was already a common choice, so many projects here are replacements of an earlier vinyl generation rather than first-time conversions. Removing the old panels is a good moment to look at the housewrap, flashing at windows and the condition of the sheathing before anything new goes on. Newer panels with thicker gauges and deeper profiles are worth comparing side by side, especially on large unbroken gable walls typical of subdivision houses.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Around the common, the historic district is made up mostly of Federal and Greek Revival buildings, where narrow wood clapboards and plain corner boards are part of the original look. On a house of that age, the exposure of the existing boards should be measured before ordering new material so the new courses line up with window casings and sills. Primed, back-sealed boards hold paint better, and any house built before 1978 falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules once old paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a practical option for the many Franklin houses built since the 1970s whose original siding is tired but whose walls are otherwise sound. It is heavier than vinyl and needs proper clearance above roofs, decks and grade, which is worth noting on lots near Mine Brook or other low, damp ground where splashback and standing snow keep the bottom courses wet. Factory-finished planks reduce repainting, and trim details at windows should be planned before installation begins.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can suit both older homes near the common and newer houses where a more natural surface is wanted. On wooded lots near the state forest or town forests, shingles stay damp longer in shade, so a breathable rainscreen or furring behind them helps them dry. Choosing between natural weathering and a factory stain is mostly a question of how uniform the color should look over time.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement makes the most sense when problems show up on several walls at once, which is common on houses from the 1960s and 1970s growth years that still carry their first cladding. Stripping to the sheathing lets rot, missing flashing and gaps in insulation be found and corrected before new siding covers them. It is also the point to decide on trim, soffit and window-wrap materials together, so the whole exterior ages at the same rate.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim is where Franklin's older and newer houses differ most. On Federal and Greek Revival homes near the common, cornice returns, wide corner boards and window casings carry the style, and replacements should copy the original dimensions. On houses from the 1970s onward, finger-jointed pine trim often fails first at the bottoms of casings and garage door jambs. Cellular PVC or properly primed wood can replace those pieces, with attention to how water sheds off each sill.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Much of Franklin drains toward the Charles River through brooks such as Mine, Shepard's, Miller and Uncas, and houses near wetlands or low ground benefit from gutters that carry water well away from foundations. Downspouts should discharge onto splash blocks or extensions, not into beds against the wall. Homes bordering Franklin State Forest or the town forests collect leaves and needles, so larger downspouts and guards that can be cleaned easily are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many of the roughly 13,000 homes in town were built between the 1970s and 1990s, and roofs from those decades are reaching or past the end of a typical asphalt shingle's life. A tear-off allows the decking, ice and water barrier at eaves and valleys, and attic ventilation to be checked. On older houses near the common, roof lines are simpler but framing can be irregular, so the decking should be inspected as soon as old shingles come off.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Small repairs are often enough: a cracked vinyl panel, a split clapboard or loose trim after a storm. Before ordering material, a sample of the existing siding should be matched for profile and color. If damage keeps recurring in the same spot, the cause is usually water behind the wall, and that should be traced before patching. On houses near the common, a repair on a front wall deserves the same care with exposure and nailing as a full restoration.

story: Webster grew around Samuel Slater's textile business. Slater moved his mills to the area in 1812, and the town was formed out of Dudley, Oxford and an unincorporated gore in 1832, named for his friend Daniel Webster. A 1978 survey by the Webster Historical Commission records that Slater's company began textile work at the East Village after buying land there in 1811 and 1812, woolens in the South Village from 1822 and cotton in the North Village from 1824. The town's own community overview notes that many downtown streets are still lined with housing built by mill owners for their workers, and that after the mills closed the town shifted from company village to privately owned homes.

The housing numbers reflect that history. The median year built is about 1962, close to 30 percent of homes predate 1940 and about two-thirds predate 1980. Roughly 31 percent of the town's 8,200 or so housing units are in buildings with two to four units, and about 60 percent are owner-occupied, so many exterior projects involve multi-unit buildings and owners who rent part of the house.

The other half of Webster is Lake Chaubunagungamaug, about 1,442 acres with a 17-mile shoreline divided into North, Middle and South Ponds. Long Island, Birch Island and Goat Island all have homes, and the community overview points to more upscale houses around the lake's perimeter. Lakefront and island homes face wind off open water, damp shade and harder access for materials, while the older mill neighborhoods near the French River and downtown are tightly spaced and often need careful staging between buildings.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: In the older mill-housing streets near downtown, vinyl is a common way to cover worn wood on multi-unit buildings, and with nearly a third of housing in two- to four-unit buildings the wall areas can be large. Before covering old clapboards, rotted sills and window trim should be repaired rather than buried. On lakefront homes facing open water, wind exposure is a reason to look at panels with stronger locking hems and fasteners spaced to the manufacturer's high-wind instructions.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: A few Federal-style mill houses survive near the former Cranston Print site in the East Village, according to accounts drawn from the 1978 town survey. On houses of that age, new clapboards should copy the original exposure and corner treatment so repaired walls do not look patched. Because about two-thirds of Webster homes are older than 1980, lead paint is likely on original wood, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply when that paint is scraped or removed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is worth considering on homes around the lake, where siding takes more sun, wind and moisture than in sheltered streets. It does not melt from reflected heat the way some vinyl can, and it holds paint well when factory-finished. Clearances at decks, porches and lower walls matter, since splashback and snow hold water at the bottom courses. Its weight means walls and sheathing should be in good shape before installation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles can suit lake and island homes, but damp shade near the water keeps them wet longer and invites moss on north walls. A ventilated backing and stainless or hot-dipped fasteners help them last. For island properties such as those on Long Island or Birch Island, material delivery and waste removal should be planned in advance, since access is more limited than on a mainland street.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Former mill housing that has been re-sided several times over the decades may carry several earlier layers of siding. A full replacement takes the walls back to sheathing so that rot around windows, missing flashing and old penetrations can be fixed. On multi-unit buildings, coordinating with tenants for access to windows and porches is part of planning the job, along with staging in tight side yards.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Porches, stair stringers and window trim on older two- and three-unit buildings take a lot of weather and often show rot first. Replacement pieces should match the original profiles when the building still has them. On lake homes, trim around sliding doors and decks faces the most water and is a good place for cellular PVC. Sills should slope outward and be flashed underneath so water cannot run back into the wall.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Close-set houses in the downtown mill neighborhoods often drain onto each other or onto narrow walkways, so downspout placement matters as much as gutter size. On lakefront lots, runoff should be directed away from foundations and, where possible, away from washing straight toward the shoreline. Wooded lots around the lake collect leaves and pine needles, which makes gutter guards and easy access for cleaning worth discussing.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With a median build year around 1962, many Webster houses are on their second or third roof, and older layers may still be in place. A full tear-off shows whether the decking is sound and lets ice and water barrier be installed at eaves and valleys. Lake homes see stronger wind across open water, so starter strips and fastening patterns should follow the shingle maker's high-wind requirements.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Many repairs here are local: a storm-damaged panel, a section of rotten trim near a porch, or a split board on an older wall. Matching profile and color is easier when a sample is taken from a hidden area. Repeated damage in one spot often points to a roof or gutter problem above it. On multi-unit buildings, damage on one tenant's side may be the first sign of a problem shared by the whole wall.

story: Bedford was formed in 1729 from parts of Concord and Billerica, and its colonial core runs along Great Road. The Bedford Center Historic District, listed in 1977 and enlarged in 2014, takes in the town common, the 1816 Federal-style First Parish Church and residential side streets, with buildings spanning more than two centuries; the Fitch Tavern dates to 1710. Nearby, the Job Lane House on North Road is an early eighteenth-century saltbox, and the Elijah Stearns Mansion at 4 Great Road is a Federal house from about 1800 with brick ends and four chimneys.

Most homes in town are much newer. Bedford's population more than doubled in the 1950s, to nearly 11,000, and reached about 13,500 by 1970 before leveling off. Census figures show a median build year of about 1976, with fewer than one in ten homes older than 1940 and a bit over half older than 1980. Roughly 69 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and only about 8 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings.

Water and open land shape a lot of the town. The Concord River forms part of the border, with the Great Meadows National Wildlife Refuge along its wetlands, and the Shawsheen River and Vine Brook run through town. Along Dudley Road, a narrow colonial-era road, the Two Brothers Rocks district is rural and residential with considerable conservation land. Hanscom Field and part of Hanscom Air Force Base sit in Bedford, and average snowfall is close to 59 inches a year, which is relevant to roof edges and gutters.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A large share of Bedford's homes date from the 1950s through the 1970s building surge, and many of them were sided in wood that has been painted many times. Vinyl over those walls can work, but the old siding and trim should be checked for soft spots and the window flashing redone rather than covered. On houses built before 1978, cutting or scraping painted wood falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules, which affects how the prep is done.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The historic center along Great Road and houses like the Stearns Mansion show how wood clapboards define Bedford's older streets. When clapboards are replaced on a house of that period, the existing exposure and the way boards meet corner boards and casings should be recorded first so the new work reads the same. Primed boards installed over a drainage gap or rainscreen give paint a better chance in a town with heavy snow and wet springs.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is an option for the many Bedford houses from the 1950s through the 1970s, provided the walls underneath are flat and sound. It resists rot and woodpeckers and holds paint, and it needs a two-inch gap above roofs and adequate clearance above grade. On lots near the Shawsheen River or Vine Brook, where the ground stays damp, keeping the bottom course well above soil is worth extra attention.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles fit both the town's older houses and some of its wooded, rural lots, such as those along Dudley Road. In shaded locations near conservation land, shingles dry slowly, so a ventilated backing and stainless fasteners help. Natural cedar weathers gray unevenly on walls with different sun exposure; a factory-applied stain or bleaching oil gives a more uniform result if that matters.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Homes from Bedford's 1950s and 1960s expansion are often at the point where siding, trim and sheathing problems show up on more than one wall. Taking everything down to the sheathing lets insulation gaps, rot and flashing at windows and doors be fixed in one pass. It is also the moment to coordinate siding with gutters and roof edges, since heavy snow loads and ice at eaves can push water behind cladding.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: In the Bedford Center Historic District, trim is part of what gives Federal and colonial houses their character: cornices, pilasters, door surrounds and window casings. Repairs there should follow the existing profiles closely. On later homes, the trouble spots are usually rotted sills, garage door jambs and fascia behind gutters. Each replacement piece should be primed on all sides or made from a rot-resistant material.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With roughly 59 inches of snow a year on average, gutters in Bedford take ice as well as water. Hangers should be spaced closely and fastened into rafter tails or solid fascia, not just thin trim. Downspouts should send water well away from foundations, especially on lower lots near the Concord or Shawsheen Rivers. Wooded properties near conservation land add leaf and needle loads, so cleanable guards are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Snowfall drives most roofing decisions here. Ice and water barrier at eaves and in valleys, along with balanced attic ventilation, reduces the ice dams that form when heat escapes into the roof. Many homes from the 1950s to 1970s have had at least one reroof; a full tear-off shows whether the original plank or plywood decking is still sound and whether earlier layers trapped moisture.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs often involve a few boards near the ground, a damaged corner or trim around a door. A sample of the existing siding helps match the profile and finish. If the same area keeps failing, the cause is usually water from a roof edge, gutter or missing flashing above. Ice that backs up behind gutters after a heavy snow is a common trigger worth ruling out.

story: Dudley's history starts on Dudley Hill, where a Nipmuc village stood before colonial settlement. The town was established in 1732, a meetinghouse went up on the hill in 1734, and Amasa Nichols founded Nichols Academy there in 1816, the institution that became Nichols College. The Dudley Hill Historic District runs along Center Street between Dudley Hill and Tanyard Roads; its houses are mostly Federal or Greek Revival, with two later Stick-style houses, plus the 1890 brick Conant Memorial Church and the Black Tavern from about 1803. The town lists the William Carter House of 1726 as its oldest standing building.

Down in the valleys, water power produced a string of mill villages. Merino, Chaseville and Perryville grew around textile mills and drew Irish, French Canadian and Polish workers; Perryville gained workers' tenements as its mill doubled, and Quinebaug, also called Dundee, was started near the Connecticut line in the early 1870s. The Stevens Linen Works in Merino, a five-story U-shaped granite mill with two seven-story towers, anchors a historic district listed in 2010. In the twentieth century, cottages went up around Pierpont Meadow Pond and Merino Pond, and residential building spread in Chaseville.

That range shows up in the census. The median house was built around 1967, about a quarter of homes date from before 1940 and roughly two-thirds from before 1980. About 21 percent of the roughly 4,500 housing units are in two- to four-unit buildings, a legacy of mill-era tenements, in a town whose mill villages included workers' tenements; about 73 percent of homes are owner-occupied. The French River marks the line with Webster, and the town sits at about 669 feet, higher than its eastern neighbor.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Multi-unit buildings in the old mill villages, such as the tenements built in Perryville, have large wall areas where vinyl keeps upkeep down. Before covering old wood, rotted sills, porch connections and window trim should be fixed, because vinyl hides rather than stops water. On pond-side cottages near Merino Pond or Pierpont Meadow Pond, shade and damp mean the drainage plane behind the siding matters more than the panel style.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Federal and Greek Revival houses along Center Street on Dudley Hill are the clearest examples of wood clapboard in town. When boards need replacing on a house of that age, the original exposure and corner details should be copied so new work blends in. Since most of Dudley's housing predates 1980, paint on original siding may contain lead, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when it is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable choice for homes from Dudley's mid-century and later growth, and for owners who want a painted look without the maintenance of wood. It needs sound sheathing and correct clearances above roofs and soil. On hillside lots, snow drifting against lower walls is a reason to keep the first course well above grade. Factory-finished planks cut down on repainting cycles.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles suit the cottages built around Merino Pond and Pierpont Meadow Pond, where a natural finish fits the setting. Near water and under trees, they stay wet longer, so a ventilated backing, good flashing and corrosion-resistant fasteners help. Owners should know that untreated cedar will weather unevenly on walls with different exposure; a pre-stained product gives more even color. Cottage lots are often small, so material staging should be planned with the neighbors in mind.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Older homes in Merino and Chaseville may carry several layers of siding added over a century or more. Removing everything down to the sheathing exposes rot at sills and around windows and lets insulation and flashing be brought up to date. On multi-unit buildings, the plan should include access for tenants and protection of porches and walkways during tear-off. Some buildings in these villages have stood for well over a century, so framing surprises should be expected in the budget.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim on Dudley Hill's Federal houses and on the two Stick-style houses in the historic district carries much of the architectural detail, so replacement should follow the originals. In the mill villages, porches and stair trim on tenements take hard wear. Cellular PVC works well for sills and lower trim that stay damp, while visible decorative pieces can be milled from wood and primed on all sides.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Dudley's hills and valleys mean water moves fast on many lots. Gutters should be sized for roof area and pitch, and downspouts should carry water past foundations, especially on houses near the French River or the ponds. Properties under mature trees collect leaves heavily in fall, so guards and an easy way to reach the gutters for cleaning are worth planning.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: At around 669 feet, Dudley gets weather that tests roof edges, and many homes from the 1960s and earlier have had several roofs. A tear-off lets the decking be checked and allows ice and water barrier at eaves and valleys. Older tenement roofs in the mill villages can have complex shapes and chimneys that need new flashing as part of the job.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Typical repairs include replacing a few damaged boards or panels, fixing trim around a door or patching storm damage. A sample of existing siding helps match the material. If the same spot keeps failing, the source is usually water from above, such as a gutter or roof edge. On older tenements, a small repair is also a good moment to check nearby trim and sills for hidden rot.

story: Chelmsford, incorporated in 1655, is really a set of villages: the Center, North, South, West and East Chelmsford, and the Westlands. The Chelmsford Center Historic District, listed in 1980, covers about 35 acres around the common and first burying ground, with Greek Revival and Italianate buildings. Local industry left its mark on building materials. A town bicentennial booklet records lime quarried west of the Center on Route 110, granite from South Chelmsford used in early nineteenth-century construction such as a Middlesex Canal arch, and Chelmsford brick from Brick Kiln Road in East Chelmsford used in the 1802 schoolhouse and many older houses.

The outlying villages grew around water power. In West Chelmsford, Deacon John Farwell dammed Stony Brook in the 1820s to make scythes, giving the place the name Scythe Factory Village until the railroad arrived in 1848 and the name changed; many later residents worked as stonecutters. North Chelmsford, along the Merrimack River and Stony Brook and centered on Vinal Square, is denser than the rest of town and still has mill buildings.

The biggest change came after 1950, when highway connections arrived; the population went from about 9,400 in 1950 to about 31,400 in 1970, and Route 3 and I-495 now meet in town. That timing is visible in the census: median year built around 1967, about 68 percent of homes older than 1980 and only about 15 percent older than 1940. Of about 13,900 housing units, roughly 82 percent are owner-occupied and only around 4 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so the typical project is a single-family house from the postwar decades.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Chelmsford's population more than tripled between 1950 and 1970, and many homes from those years have reached the point where the original siding, or an early layer of vinyl, needs replacing. Removing old material instead of layering over it allows flashing at windows and doors to be redone and rotted sheathing to be replaced. Since most of these houses predate 1978, any painted wood that gets cut or scraped falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The Greek Revival and Italianate houses around the Center common are where wood clapboards matter most. New boards should match the existing exposure and the way they meet corner boards and window casings. Back-priming and a drainage gap behind the boards help paint last. On houses in the older parts of North and West Chelmsford, it is worth checking whether earlier siding layers were added over the original clapboards.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: For single-family homes from the 1950s through the 1970s, fiber cement offers a painted-wood appearance with less upkeep. It is heavier than vinyl and should go over flat, sound sheathing with proper clearances above roofs, decks and soil. On lots in low areas near Stony Brook or Freeman Lake, keeping the bottom course well above grade reduces wicking and splashback damage.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingles are a good fit for wooded lots in South Chelmsford and for older houses where the owner wants a traditional surface. In shade, cedar stays damp longer, so a ventilated backing and stainless fasteners help it last. Natural cedar weathers to gray at different rates depending on sun exposure; pre-stained shingles give a more even appearance. Shingles also suit additions, where they can visually separate a new wing from the original house.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Houses from the 1950s and 1960s building surge often have thin sheathing, minimal insulation and siding that has been patched many times. A full replacement down to the sheathing lets all of that be addressed at once, along with trim and flashing. Planning siding, soffits and gutters together avoids mismatched materials that age at different rates. Window replacement, if it is coming soon, is easier to coordinate at the same time than after the new siding is in place.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: In the Center district, cornices, door surrounds and window casings on Greek Revival and Italianate houses carry much of the style, so replacement pieces should copy the originals. On postwar homes, rot typically starts at window sills, fascia boards behind gutters and garage door trim. Cellular PVC or primed, rot-resistant wood are both options, as long as each joint is sealed and sills shed water outward.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Chelmsford's position between the Merrimack and Concord Rivers and its many brooks, including Stony Brook and Beaver Brook, mean some lots sit low and stay wet. Downspouts should discharge well away from foundations, and on flat lots extensions or drainage lines may be needed. Mature trees on postwar lots drop heavy leaf loads, so guards that are easy to clean are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With so many homes built in the 1950s and 1960s, Chelmsford has plenty of roofs on their second or third replacement, sometimes over older layers. A full tear-off lets the original decking be checked and ice and water barrier be added at eaves and valleys. Attic ventilation in these older houses is often limited, and correcting it reduces ice dams and extends shingle life.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Many problems are small: a split board, a damaged vinyl panel or rotten trim near a door. Matching profile and color is easier with a sample from an inconspicuous spot. Where the same section keeps failing, the cause is usually water from above, which should be fixed first. On older houses in the Center or the mill villages, earlier layers under the damaged area may need attention too.

story: Belmont was assembled in 1859 from parts of Watertown, Waltham and West Cambridge and named for Bellmont, John Perkins Cushing's estate. It stayed largely agricultural until around 1900, when trolley service and better roads brought residential building; the population roughly doubled between 1920 and 1930, from about 10,700 to about 21,700. The town still calls itself the Town of Homes, and the Belmont Citizens Forum describes its historic houses as ranging from Georgian to Victorian to Craftsman and mid-century modern. The oldest surviving house, the John Chenery house on Washington Street, dates to 1654.

The housing is old by any standard. The census median year built is about 1938, about 57 percent of homes predate 1940 and roughly 87 percent predate 1980. About 38 percent of the roughly 10,900 units are in two- to four-unit buildings, and about 65 percent are owner-occupied. Most residents live in the lower, denser neighborhoods around Belmont Center, Cushing Square and Waverley Square, while Belmont Hill is known for large houses. The Pleasant Street Historic District, listed in 1979, follows Route 60 from Winn Street toward Concord Avenue with mid- to late-nineteenth-century single-family homes on large lots.

Terrain varies within a small area of 4.7 square miles. Wellington Hill rises to 295 feet, the Payson Park neighborhood was laid out on part of the Cushing estate near Pequossette Hill, and a 1940s planned community by architect Carl Koch was placed on the rocky ledges of Snake Hill. Close lot lines, multi-unit buildings and hillside sites all affect how scaffolding, ladders and material deliveries are handled.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Many of Belmont's multi-unit buildings and older single-family houses have already been re-sided at least once. Before a new layer goes on, the older material should usually be removed so window flashing and rotted sheathing can be dealt with. With nearly nine in ten homes older than 1980, original painted wood is likely underneath, and EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply once that paint is disturbed. Close side yards also make containment and cleanup a planning item.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Where a pre-war house still has wood clapboards, such as some of the nineteenth-century homes along Pleasant Street, replacement boards should match the existing exposure and the detailing at corners, windows and porches. Restoring clapboard on a few walls while keeping sound original boards elsewhere is often a sensible approach on houses of this age. With most homes predating 1940, original boards that are still sound are worth keeping and repairing rather than replacing.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement can give a multi-unit building or older house the look of painted clapboard with longer paint intervals. It is heavier than wood or vinyl, so the sheathing must be sound and fastened well. On tight lots where a neighbor's wall is only a few feet away, cutting should be done with dust control, and planks should be planned so each wall can be staged safely.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Where an older Belmont house was built with shingles, keeping them is usually part of keeping its style. Matching the original exposure and coursing, including any decorative patterns, is part of the job. On shaded walls between closely spaced houses, cedar dries slowly, so a ventilated backing and stainless fasteners are worth using. Pre-stained shingles reduce the amount of finishing work done on site, which helps where yards are small.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A complete residing on a house that is close to a century old often turns up surprises: earlier siding layers, missing sheathing, abandoned openings or hidden rot. Taking walls to the framing or sheathing allows those to be corrected and insulation to be improved. On multi-unit buildings, coordinating access with every unit and protecting porches, stairs and shared walkways should be planned in advance.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim carries much of the character on Belmont's older houses, from Victorian and Craftsman details to the nineteenth-century houses on Pleasant Street. Replacement pieces should be milled to match the originals rather than simplified. Porch railings, columns and stair stringers on multi-unit buildings take the most weather and are often the first trim to fail. Rot-resistant materials can be used for hidden or ground-contact parts while visible profiles stay in painted wood.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Hillside streets near Wellington Hill and Belmont Hill send water quickly to foundations, while the flatter neighborhoods around Cushing Square and Waverley Square have little space between houses for downspout runs. In both cases, discharge should be directed away from foundations and away from neighboring properties. Mature street trees in older neighborhoods mean frequent leaf cleanouts, so guards are worth considering.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: With a median build year in the late 1930s, many Belmont roofs have been replaced several times, and some still have older layers or original board sheathing. A full tear-off shows the condition of the decking and allows ice and water barrier at eaves and valleys. Complex rooflines with dormers and chimneys, common on houses from this period, need new step and counter flashing as part of the work.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Typical repairs include a few split clapboards, a damaged shingle section or rotted trim at a porch. A sample from a hidden area helps match profile and color. If damage keeps coming back in the same spot, water from a roof edge or gutter above is the most likely cause. On two- to four-unit buildings, repairs should be coordinated so that every affected unit's wall is checked.

story: Foxborough was settled in 1704 and incorporated in 1778, and until the early 1900s it was a set of small neighborhood communities rather than a single center. Names such as Foxvale (also called Paineburgh), Quaker Hill in South Foxborough and Lakeview in West Foxborough still mark those older pieces. The town's 19th-century industry was straw hats. Its hat factory, erected in 1886 and once described as the largest in the world, burned in 1936, and the post office now stands on the site.

The larger change came later. The population rose from about 10,100 in 1960 to about 14,200 in 1970, and Census estimates put the median year built of local housing at 1976. Only about 15 percent of homes date from before 1940, and a little over half from before 1980. Roughly three in four homes are owner-occupied, and about 11 percent of the town's roughly 7,400 housing units are in buildings with two to four units. Because so much of the housing went up within a few decades, original siding, trim and roofing on many houses are aging on a similar schedule.

Older buildings remain in the mix. The former Foxborough State Hospital at Chestnut and Main streets, built in 1889, was redeveloped after 2005, with some buildings converted to condominiums and to single- and multi-family housing. National Register listings include Memorial Hall and the Ezra Carpenter and Otis Cary houses on South Street and the Capt. Josiah Pratt House on East Street. The Neponset Reservoir, headwater of the Neponset River, and F. Gilbert Hills State Forest shape parts of town, which affects gutters and shaded walls.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: For houses built during the 1960s and 1970s growth years, vinyl is a practical replacement for worn original siding. Before new panels go up, old layers should come off where possible so the sheathing can be inspected; at that age, soft spots around windows and along the bottom of walls are worth looking for. Insulated vinyl or a foam underlayment can help panels lie flat on walls that are no longer perfectly straight. On lots near the reservoir or the state forest, pick a color that will tolerate occasional mildew cleaning.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard suits the town's older houses, such as the National Register houses along South Street and East Street. When replacing clapboard on a pre-1940 house, matching the original exposure (the visible width of each board) and the corner-board detail keeps the house looking like itself. Wood, fiber cement and engineered wood clapboard are all options, and wood will need repainting on a regular cycle. On any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices apply when existing paint is disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank is worth considering for the many homes built after 1960. It takes paint well, does not soften from reflected sunlight the way vinyl can, and resists insects and woodpeckers. It is heavier than vinyl and needs correct fastening, kick-out flashing where roofs meet walls, and clearance above grade. On houses close to the woods of F. Gilbert Hills State Forest, keeping the bottom course well above soil and leaf litter helps the boards last.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit the town's older houses and newer homes built with a traditional look. They need to dry from behind, so a rainscreen mat under the shingles is worth discussing. On lots shaded by tall trees near the state forest or the reservoir, north walls can stay damp and grow moss or mildew; trimming back branches and choosing factory-treated or pre-stained shingles helps. If a consistent color matters, plan on re-staining at intervals.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Since a large share of Foxborough's housing was built in a short span after 1960, many houses reach the point where patching no longer makes sense at about the same time. A full replacement allows the walls to be opened, damaged sheathing replaced, and house wrap and window flashing brought up to current practice. It is also the moment to consider insulation board behind the new siding. A written estimate should spell out how rot repairs will be priced, since hidden damage only shows once the old siding is off.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim on houses from the 1960s and 1970s was usually plain wood, and the bottoms of corner boards, window sills and door casings are where rot tends to start. Replacing those pieces with PVC or composite stock reduces repainting. On the older houses near the town center, trim profiles are part of the character, and matching existing moldings is worth the extra effort. Painted trim on pre-1978 houses falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when it is removed or sanded.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lots near F. Gilbert Hills State Forest and other wooded parts of town collect leaves and pine needles, which fill gutters quickly. Larger downspouts and guards designed for needles reduce clogging. Winters here are cold and snowy, so gutters should be hung with hidden hangers spaced closely enough to carry snow and ice, and downspouts should discharge well away from the foundation. Check that roof water does not land on walkways or driveways where it can freeze.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Winters in Foxborough are cold and snowy, and nor'easters pass through the region, so ice-and-water membrane along the eaves and in valleys is the main defense against ice dams on a new roof. Houses from the 1960s and 1970s were often built with limited attic ventilation; adding ridge and soffit venting during a reroof helps the shingles and reduces ice buildup. Ask for the roof deck to be inspected once the old shingles are removed, and for any soft boards to be priced in writing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A cracked panel, a loose corner or a short run of rotted clapboard can usually be repaired without residing a whole wall. The main limit is matching color and profile on older or discontinued siding. A free on-site assessment can show whether a repair makes sense or whether the damage points to a moisture problem behind the wall.

story: Somerville is one of the most densely built places in New England: about 4.1 square miles of houses on and around seven glacial drumlins, among them Spring Hill, Winter Hill, Prospect Hill and Clarendon Hill. Separated from Charlestown in 1842 and made a city in 1872, it grew with the railroads. The Fitchburg Railroad opened in 1841 and a line reached Davis Square in 1870. The population peaked at about 105,900 in 1940, and the tight residential fabric of the city largely dates from the building boom that ran up to that point.

Census figures reflect that history. The median home was built around 1938, about 59 percent of the city's roughly 37,800 housing units predate 1940, and about 80 percent predate 1980. Some 55 percent of units are in buildings with two to four units, and only about a third of homes are owner-occupied. A typical exterior project here is therefore a multi-unit building, often owned by someone who also lives in it or rents it out.

Spring Hill shows the range. Its National Register historic district holds Greek Revival houses from the 1840s, Italianate, Gothic Revival and Queen Anne houses, two-family homes, and triple-deckers that filled in the remaining land in the early 1900s, such as a 1910 Colonial Revival triple-decker on Preston Road. Other National Register districts cover Bow Street in Union Square and Mt. Vernon Street in East Somerville. On streets this tight, staging, ladder access and protecting the house next door take up a large part of the planning for any siding or roofing job.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: On a two- or three-unit building, vinyl keeps routine exterior upkeep down, which matters when the owner is also managing tenants. With about six in ten Somerville homes built before 1940, original details such as window hoods, cornices and bay window trim should be kept or carefully replicated rather than wrapped flat, or the building loses much of its character. Panels must be nailed loosely enough to move with temperature; on the tall walls of a triple-decker, siding nailed tight shows waviness quickly.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard fits the 19th-century houses that survive in neighborhoods like Spring Hill and along Bow Street. If a house sits in the Spring Hill, Bow Street or Mt. Vernon Street National Register districts, ask the city whether any local review applies before changing materials. Old painted clapboard on a pre-1978 building is likely to contain lead, so EPA lead-safe (RRP) practices apply, including containment that protects neighbors whose windows may be only a few feet away.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: On a three-story wall in a dense neighborhood, fiber cement plank gives a painted-wood look with less upkeep than wood and better fire resistance than vinyl, a point worth weighing where buildings sit close together. It is heavy, and cutting it requires dust control, which takes planning when the lot line is a few feet from the neighbor's house. Factory-finished boards reduce painting on staging and can shorten how long scaffolding has to stay up.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Spring Hill's historic district includes Shingle Style and Queen Anne houses, styles that often used wood shingles in gables or upper walls. Patching or replacing those sections with cedar keeps the detail intact instead of flattening it with a different material. Side walls between closely spaced buildings get little sun and dry slowly, so an air gap behind the shingles and working gutters above them make a real difference in how long cedar lasts.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Residing a triple-decker or two-family is a staging project as much as a siding project. Plan for scaffolding or lifts, protection of neighboring property, and any sidewalk or parking use the work requires. With the walls open, sheathing and framing around rear porches and bay windows deserve a close look. Owners with tenants should schedule around occupied units and ask for a written estimate that separates siding, trim and rot repair so the scope is clear.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Somerville's older houses carry a lot of trim: bay windows, porch posts and railings, cornices and window hoods. When pieces are replaced, matching the original profiles keeps the facade intact, and PVC or primed composite stock cuts down repainting on upper floors that are hard to reach. Painted trim on pre-1978 buildings falls under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when it is removed, scraped or sanded.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Tight lot lines mean roof water often lands next to a neighbor's foundation or a shared driveway. Gutters and downspouts should be routed so discharge stays on your own property and away from walkways. On a triple-decker, a long downspout run from a third-floor roof needs secure straps and a properly sized outlet. Houses on the slopes of Winter Hill, Spring Hill or Prospect Hill need extra thought about where water goes once it reaches the ground.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Roof work here is shaped by access: three stories of height, narrow side yards and neighbors close on both sides. Ask how materials will be lifted and debris removed, and how adjacent roofs and cars will be protected. Flashing at chimneys, dormers and the joints between attached buildings such as rowhouses deserves close inspection on century-old roofs. Ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys belongs in any reroof in this climate.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: On older Somerville buildings, a repair is often enough when one wall, a porch corner or a section of clapboard is damaged. The hard part is matching aged siding or old trim profiles. A free on-site assessment can determine whether a targeted repair will hold or whether moisture behind the siding calls for more work.

story: Medford grew along the Mystic River, which runs through the middle of the city, with the Middlesex Fells Reservation on its northern side. Its early economy included brickmaking, rum and shipbuilding. Thatcher Magoun opened a shipyard in 1803 that ran into the 1870s, and the Old Ship Street Historic District along Pleasant Street still holds a significant number of Federal and Greek Revival houses built between about 1803 and 1855. The city also contains the 1692 Royall House and the Peter Tufts House on Riverside Avenue, thought to be the oldest all-brick building in New England.

Railroads and streetcars turned Medford into a suburb. Population went from about 18,200 in 1900 to about 59,700 in 1930 and peaked in 1950. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1942, with nearly half of homes built before 1940 and about three-quarters before 1980. About a third of units are in buildings with two to four units, and a little over half of homes are owner-occupied.

Neighborhoods carry different layers. The Hillside Avenue Historic District near downtown is a late 19th-century subdivision built between 1875 and 1895, mostly Queen Anne, with Colonial Revival, Tudor Revival and Shingle style houses among them. West Medford, Fulton Heights, Wellington, South Medford, Lawrence Estates and Medford Hillside around Tufts University each have their own character. For exterior work, the age of the housing means lead paint, older framing and decorative trim come up regularly, and lots near the Fells add shade and falling leaves to the list.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: For houses from the city's growth years between 1900 and 1950, vinyl is a practical way to cut down painting, especially on two-family buildings where upkeep is shared. Keep or recreate window casings and corner boards rather than covering everything in aluminum coil; the result looks better and leaves fewer places for water to sit behind the trim. With nearly half of Medford's housing built before 1940, assume older paint is underneath and plan for lead-safe removal.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: In the Old Ship Street and Hillside Avenue districts, the siding and wood detailing are part of what defines the houses. Replacing in kind, with the same board width and corner treatment, is the safest approach for Federal, Greek Revival and Queen Anne houses. Ask the city whether any local review applies to the address before changing materials. Removing old painted boards from a pre-1978 house requires EPA lead-safe (RRP) work practices.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank suits the city's two-family homes and 20th-century houses where an owner wants a painted look without the repainting schedule of wood. Pre-finished boards come in narrow exposures that sit comfortably on older streets. The material needs clearance above roofs and decks and kick-out flashing where a roof meets a wall, details that matter on houses with porches and later additions.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Shingle style houses, such as the 1881-82 Bela Warner house on Hillside Avenue, were designed around wood shingles, so cedar is the natural material for repair or replacement on homes of that type. Queen Anne houses frequently mix shingled gables with clapboard below. On shaded lots near the Fells, a breathable underlayment and clean gutters help shingles dry out between storms and slow down moss and mildew.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: Residing a Medford house built a century ago often uncovers the history of every earlier repair. Budget for some sheathing replacement and for reflashing windows that were never properly flashed. On two-family homes, coordinate with both households, since scaffolding may be up for a while. A written estimate should break out siding, trim and unit pricing for rot repair so the final cost is predictable.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Porches, cornices and window trim on Queen Anne and Colonial Revival houses decay where water collects: sills, column bases and the undersides of porch roofs. Replacement pieces in rot-resistant PVC or treated wood, milled to match existing profiles, preserve the look. Along Pleasant Street, Riverside Avenue and Hillside Avenue, trim is part of the architectural record, so matching it closely is worth the effort.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Homes near the wooded parts of the Middlesex Fells sit under trees that drop leaves into gutters more than once a year. Guards, larger downspouts and cleanouts at the base reduce overflow that rots fascia and soaks foundations. Some older houses still have wood gutters or built-in box gutters; decide whether to restore or replace them, because a leaking box gutter can damage the cornice and wall framing below.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Queen Anne houses like those on Hillside Avenue tend to have complicated roofs with dormers, turrets and several valleys, while earlier Federal and Greek Revival houses have simpler, steeper planes. A reroof is the time to add ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, replace step flashing at walls and chimneys, and improve attic ventilation. Check whether multiple old roof layers need to come off, since extra layers add weight and hide deck damage.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A cracked panel, a loose stretch of clapboard or a rotted corner board can often be fixed without redoing a whole side of the house. On older homes, matching profiles and paint may take some searching. A free on-site assessment helps sort out whether the damage is isolated or a sign of a larger moisture issue.
