story: Canton sits at the foot of Great Blue Hill, with part of the Blue Hills Reservation inside its borders and the Neponset River along its boundary with Norwood, Westwood and Dedham. The Canton River runs through the center of town, linking Bolivar and Forge ponds before it reaches the Neponset. Incorporated from Stoughton in 1797, the town had early industry: Paul Revere built the nation's first copper rolling mill here in 1801, and the stone Canton Viaduct, built in 1835, is still in mainline railroad use.

The historic core is Canton Corner, centered on the junction of Pleasant and Washington streets. Its National Register district covers about 170 acres and more than 25 properties, with houses ranging from Georgian to Craftsman. The oldest is the c. 1725 David Tilden House on Pleasant Street, and one of the newest is the 1905 Bessie Estey House on Washington Street. Other local place names include Ponkapoag and Canton Junction.

Most of the town's housing is much newer. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1980, with only about 11 percent of homes built before 1940 and half before 1980. About three-quarters of homes are owner-occupied, and only around 6 percent of the roughly 9,900 units are in buildings with two to four units. In practice a large share of houses date from the 1970s onward, alongside a small group of much older houses near the Corner that need a more careful approach. Wetlands in the east along Route 138 and in the west along I-95 make drainage around foundations worth watching.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: With half of Canton's housing built since about 1980, many homes still have their first siding, and some of it has faded or cracked. Vinyl is a straightforward replacement. Remove the old layer rather than covering it, so the sheathing and window flashing can be inspected. Darker vinyl colors can fade or distort on south-facing walls in full sun, so color choice deserves some thought, particularly on open lots without shade.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Around Canton Corner, houses run from the Georgian period through Italianate to Craftsman, and clapboard is the expected look for many of them. Matching board exposure and trim depth keeps an old house consistent with its neighbors in the district. Ask the town whether any local review applies before changing siding there. For any house built before 1978, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement suits the town's many owner-occupied homes from the 1970s onward where owners want a painted look with less upkeep than wood. It holds up to sun and moisture and is available pre-painted. Near the wetlands along Route 138 and I-95, the bottom course should sit well above grade and mulch beds, and every cut edge should be sealed, since that is where fiber cement takes on water.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit owners who want a natural finish that weathers over time. On lots near the Blue Hills Reservation where trees shade the walls, factory-treated or pre-stained shingles with an air gap behind them resist mildew better. On the oldest houses in the Canton Corner district, find out what the original walls were clad in before choosing shingles over clapboard, so the house keeps its historic appearance.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: For a house built around 1980, a full siding replacement is the chance to add details that may be missing, such as a continuous weather barrier and properly lapped window flashing. Once the old siding is off, sheathing can be checked and replaced where it is soft. Rigid foam under the new siding can improve comfort in older walls. A written estimate should explain how any hidden damage will be handled and priced.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Plain wood trim on houses from the 1970s and 1980s tends to rot at the bottoms of corner boards, garage door jambs and window sills. Replacing those pieces with PVC or composite stock reduces repainting. On historic houses near the Corner, wood trim may be worth restoring rather than replacing, especially the cornices and door surrounds that define the oldest facades.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Trees on lots near the Blue Hills Reservation drop leaves into gutters each fall, and guards can cut down on cleaning. Parts of town include wetlands and low ground near the Neponset and Canton rivers, so directing downspout water well away from foundations matters; extensions or drainage connections help keep basements dry. Downspouts sized for heavy rain reduce overflow at the corners of the house.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On houses from the 1970s through 1990s, a first full tear-off often shows deck problems near the eaves and around skylights and chimneys. Ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys and balanced attic ventilation belong in any reroof here. On houses with complicated rooflines, step flashing at walls should be replaced rather than reused. For the older houses near Canton Corner, ask how the new roof will be detailed at cornices and chimneys.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A damaged section of siding, a few cracked panels or a rotted corner can often be repaired on its own. Matching older colors and profiles is the usual challenge. A free on-site assessment can show whether a repair is enough or whether moisture behind the siding needs a broader fix.

story: Malden lies on hilly ground north of the Mystic River, drained by the Malden River and bordered on the northwest by the cliffs of the Middlesex Fells, where Boojum Rock reaches about 275 feet. Settled in 1640 and incorporated in 1649, it became a city in 1882. Its fastest growth came between 1870 and 1900, when the population went from about 7,400 to about 33,700, and it kept growing until a peak in 1950. Industry included the Converse rubber factory in Edgeworth, at the bottom of Pearl Street.

Neighborhoods have distinct origins. Maplewood was laid out from 1847 by Joshua Webster, who planted hundreds of maple trees along wide streets. Bellrock, between Main Street, Charles Street and the Malden River, holds Bell Rock Memorial Park and a cemetery with graves dating to 1670. Edgeworth borders Everett and Medford, and other neighborhoods include Faulkner, the West End, Linden, Ferryway, Forestdale and Belmont Hill. Downtown landmarks include the public library designed by Henry Hobson Richardson and built in 1885.

Census estimates put the median year built around 1950, with about 45 percent of the city's roughly 28,000 housing units built before 1940 and about 71 percent before 1980. About a third of units are in buildings with two to four units, and most households rent. That mix means many exterior projects involve multi-unit buildings on tight lots, where staging, tenant access and protecting neighboring property matter as much as the material chosen.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: On a two- or three-unit building, vinyl siding removes painting cycles that are hard to manage with tenants in place. With nearly half of Malden's housing built before 1940, the existing walls may hide several layers, including painted wood; remove what is practical and check the sheathing before new panels go on. Choose panels thick enough to stay flat on tall walls, and leave window and door trim visible rather than burying it.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: For houses from Malden's 1870-1900 growth period, clapboard, in wood or fiber cement, keeps the traditional look of the street. Matching board width to what remains on the house and its neighbors helps a replacement blend in. Old paint on pre-1978 clapboard means EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply, with extra containment where houses stand close together and a neighbor's yard is only a few feet away.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank is a reasonable choice for owners of multi-unit buildings who want long repaint intervals and better fire resistance than vinyl between closely spaced houses. It is heavy and must be cut with dust control, which takes planning on narrow lots. Pre-finished boards reduce time spent on staging. Proper clearance at porch roofs and decks, and kick-out flashing where roofs meet walls, keep water from collecting at the board ends.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles can cover a whole house or be used for gables and dormers. Along Maplewood's tree-lined streets and on lots near the Fells, shaded walls dry slowly, so an air gap behind the shingles and clean gutters above them help. Pre-stained or treated shingles limit mildew and uneven color. Weathered shingles are hard to match, so replacing by full wall section usually looks better than patching.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on an older Malden house is the time to deal with problems that build up over decades: rot near the sills, missing flashing at windows, and gaps where additions meet the original walls. With most households renting, coordinate the schedule with tenants, and make sure the written estimate covers protection of neighboring property, debris removal and how rot repair is priced.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Porch posts, railings, window casings and cornices are where older houses usually show wear first. Replacing rotted pieces with PVC or composite stock lowers maintenance, while matching existing profiles keeps the facade consistent along the street. Trim on upper floors is hard to reach, so durability matters more there than on a one-story house. Painted trim on pre-1978 buildings must be handled under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Malden's hilly terrain sends roof runoff downhill toward neighbors and sidewalks. Downspouts should discharge where water flows away from the house without crossing walkways, where it can freeze in winter. Homes near the Fells and along Maplewood's maple-lined streets collect leaves, so guards and larger downspouts help. On tight lots, route water so it stays on your own property and does not soak a shared wall or driveway.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: On multi-unit buildings and closely spaced houses, access is the first question on any roof job. Ask how shingles will be delivered and debris removed without blocking neighbors or shared driveways. On older homes, ice-and-water membrane at eaves and valleys, new flashing at chimneys and walls, and improved attic ventilation are worth including, since many were built long before current ventilation practice.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A loose section, storm damage or a rotted board can often be repaired without residing the house. Matching older siding and paint colors is the main challenge. A free on-site assessment can show whether a repair will hold or whether the problem runs deeper.

story: Stoneham was part of Charlestown until 1725 and stayed small through the colonial era before becoming a major shoe-manufacturing center in the 19th century. That industry shaped the town center. John Hill's 1858 Italianate factory at 426 Main Street was the town's first major industrial building, and three Second Empire commercial blocks at the junction of Main and Center streets date from 1868 to 1890. The Central Square Historic District covers much of that business area along Main Street, the old Andover-Medford Turnpike.

A few blocks west, the Nobility Hill Historic District, bounded roughly by Chestnut and Maple streets and Cedar Avenue, holds houses built between about 1860 and 1920 in Italianate, Second Empire, Stick, Queen Anne and Colonial Revival styles, in an area once home to shoe factory and tannery owners. Stone walls and a gate from the Tidd estate now stand in front of mid-20th-century ranch houses there. In 1984, 63 Stoneham properties, most of them houses, were added to the National Register on a single day.

Even so, most of the housing is newer. Census estimates put the median year built at about 1964, with about a quarter of homes built before 1940 and about 70 percent before 1980. About 71 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and about 12 percent of units are in buildings with two to four units. Part of the Middlesex Fells Reservation lies in town, including Spot Pond, which is almost entirely within Stoneham, and the Stone Zoo, so homes near the reservation deal with shade and falling leaves.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical update for Stoneham's mid-20th-century houses, which make up much of the housing stock. Ask for the old siding to be removed so the sheathing and window flashing can be checked rather than covered over. Pick a profile that suits the street; on houses near Nobility Hill or Central Square, a narrow clapboard-style profile and visible trim sit better beside older neighbors than wide panels do.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The 19th-century houses around Nobility Hill and the many individually listed houses near Central Square are where clapboard work calls for the most care. Match board width, corner treatment and window trim to what is already there. With dozens of Stoneham properties on the National Register, check with the town about any local review before starting. For pre-1978 houses, EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply when painted surfaces are disturbed.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement plank works well on mid-century houses when owners want a painted look without frequent repainting. It resists moisture and insects, which helps on homes near Spot Pond and the Fells where shade keeps walls damp longer. It needs careful flashing at roof-to-wall joints, sealed cut ends and proper clearance above grade, and its weight calls for solid fastening into framing.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles suit Queen Anne and Colonial Revival houses that used shingled gables, as well as newer homes where owners want a natural finish. Near the Fells, shaded walls grow mildew easily; pre-treated shingles, a drainage mat behind them and trimming back overhanging branches all extend their life. Plan for periodic re-staining if a uniform color is wanted, or let untreated shingles weather naturally to gray.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: For a house built around the 1960s, a full replacement lets old layers come off, the sheathing be checked, and house wrap and window flashing be brought up to current practice. It is also a good time to add insulation board under the new siding. A written estimate should explain how hidden damage will be priced, since it only shows once the walls are open.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Second Empire and Queen Anne houses in the Nobility Hill area carry brackets, cornices and decorative porch work, while mid-century homes have simpler trim that tends to rot at sills and corner boards. In both cases PVC or composite replacements reduce repainting, and on historic houses matching original profiles keeps the facade intact. Paint on pre-1978 trim must be handled with lead-safe practices.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Homes close to the wooded parts of the Middlesex Fells Reservation and Spot Pond collect leaves and needles quickly. Guards and oversized downspouts reduce clogging and overflow. On sloped lots, such as those around Bear Hill, make sure downspout runoff is carried away from the foundation rather than pooling at the base of the wall or running across a driveway.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Reroofing a mid-century house may involve tearing off more than one old layer. Check the deck once the roof is stripped, install ice-and-water membrane along eaves and valleys, and add ridge and soffit ventilation if the attic lacks it. On older houses with mansard roofs or complex Queen Anne rooflines, flashing details and steep sections take extra time and should be priced clearly in writing.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: A cracked panel, a damaged corner or a short section of rotted board can often be repaired on its own. Matching older siding is the main difficulty. A free on-site assessment can show whether a repair will hold or whether the damage points to moisture behind the wall.

story: Quincy's housing history follows its industries. Granite quarrying was the city's main employer through the 19th century, and stone from the West Quincy quarries, hauled on the Granite Railway built in 1826, went into the Bunker Hill Monument; the old pits are now the Quincy Quarries Reservation. In the 20th century the Fore River Shipyard at Quincy Point took over as a major employer, and the city's population grew by more than half during the 1920s. Suburban building began earlier than that. After the Old Colony Railroad opened in 1845, Wollaston became one of the area's first commuter neighborhoods, and in 1896 the Quincy family's estate there was cut into house lots as Wollaston Park.

Census figures put the median year built at about 1958, with roughly 37 percent of homes built before 1940 and close to 70 percent before 1980. About one unit in five sits in a two- to four-unit building, and only about 45 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so an exterior project here can involve a landlord, several households or a condo association. Germantown, a planned manufacturing settlement of the 1750s, and Quincy Point are now densely built residential areas, while Marina Bay, developed in the 1980s on the former Squantum naval air station, is largely high-rise condominiums.

A large share of the city faces salt water. Squantum and Adams Shore started as summer resorts, and Houghs Neck, a one-square-mile peninsula between Quincy Bay and Hingham Bay, was a resort before it became a thickly settled year-round neighborhood. Inland, about 23 percent of Quincy's land lies in the Blue Hills Reservation. For exterior work that means two different settings: shoreline streets open to wind off the bay, and older, tighter neighborhoods where most houses predate 1978 and EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules apply whenever painted surfaces are disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Where a building holds two or three households, vinyl removes the repainting cycle from the owner's budget, which is why it is common on rental property. On the exposed ends of Squantum, Houghs Neck or Adams Shore, panel choice matters more than color: a thicker panel with a reinforced nail hem holds better in wind off the bay, and starter strips and corners need full fastening. On close-set lots in Quincy Point or Germantown, check how ladders and staging will fit before the job is scheduled.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Houses on Wollaston's commuter-era streets, built up from the 1870s and after the 1896 Wollaston Park subdivision, are old enough that original wood clapboard may survive, sometimes under later siding. Before replacing a wall, it is worth probing the boards: sound clapboard can often be kept and only damaged courses swapped, with the exposure matched so the repair disappears. New clapboard should be primed on all faces and installed over a drainage gap. Any scraping or removal on a pre-1978 wall falls under EPA RRP lead-safe practices.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives a painted-board look without wood's rot risk, which suits older Quincy houses where owners want to keep a traditional face. Near the shore, use the manufacturer's recommended fasteners for coastal exposure and keep the required clearance above roofs, decks and grade. The planks are heavy and long, so on narrow side yards in the denser neighborhoods, plan where material will be stacked and cut. Factory-finished boards cut down on field painting, but every cut end still needs sealing.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles fit the seaside history of Squantum, Houghs Neck and Adams Shore, which began as summer colonies. Salt air will turn untreated cedar gray within a few seasons; owners who want to hold a color should choose factory-stained or primed shingles. On walls facing open water, stainless steel nails avoid rust streaks, and a ventilated or drainage underlayment lets the back of the shingle dry. Corners can be woven or trimmed with boards, and the choice should match the rest of the street.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full strip on a Quincy two-family or a pre-1940 single often uncovers more than one earlier layer, along with patched sheathing around old window openings. Budget for carpentry that only shows up once the old siding is off. On owner-and-tenant buildings, agree in advance on access, parking for the dumpster and work hours. With close to 70 percent of the city's homes built before 1980, assume lead paint on any older painted layer and plan RRP containment. A written estimate should list siding, trim and contingency repairs separately.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Trim takes the brunt of weather on any house near Wollaston Beach or Quincy Bay: window sills, porch rails and the bottom edge of corner boards are where rot usually starts. Replacing those parts with cellular PVC or a primed, rot-resistant wood keeps the original profile without the same moisture problem. On older houses in Quincy Center or Wollaston, matching crown and casing widths matters more than any single material choice. Paint-disturbing trim work on pre-1978 houses is covered by RRP rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: The terrain splits the city. Houses on the slopes near the Blue Hills Reservation and Faxon Park see leaves and needles, so screened or covered gutters and larger downspouts make sense there. Along the shoreline, the concern is wind-driven rain and salt: aluminum or copper hold up better than steel, and hangers should be closely spaced. On multi-family buildings with long eaves, check that each downspout discharges away from the foundation and not onto a neighbor's driveway in a tight lot.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Shoreline neighborhoods such as Houghs Neck and Squantum are open to wind off Quincy Bay, so roof work there should follow the shingle maker's high-wind nailing pattern and use sealed starter courses at eaves and rakes. Ice and water membrane along eaves and in valleys is standard practice in this region. Where a two- or three-family building has a low-slope porch roof or rear addition, that section needs a membrane rather than shingles. On older houses, confirm the condition of the roof deck before a quote is final.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Repairs in Quincy often come down to a few damaged courses, a storm-loosened corner or a cracked panel on a rental building. The repair should match the existing profile and color as closely as possible and be fastened so it can move. On older painted walls, any scraping falls under RRP lead-safe practices. Near the water, check the sheathing behind a loose section for salt-driven moisture before closing it up.

story: Braintree was colonized in 1635 and incorporated in 1640, and its original territory was later split to form Quincy and Randolph. A few early houses survive. The Thayer house, a two-and-a-half-story saltbox built in 1720 and enlarged in the 1760s and again in the 19th century, stood on land bought by the Walworth company in 1958; rather than lose it, the house was taken apart and rebuilt about a mile down Washington Street, where it is now a museum. As late as 1888, Braintree and South Braintree were separate villages inside the town.

Early industry followed the water. The Monatiquot River, formed where the Farm and Cochato rivers meet, powered grist mills and a nail mill opened by Paul Revere before it empties into the tidal Weymouth Fore River. In East Braintree, Thomas A. Watson bought a house and about sixty acres along the Fore River in 1883 and started the engine works that grew into the Fore River Ship and Engine Company, which later moved to a larger yard at Quincy Point. After World War II, Irish American and Italian American families from Boston moved in, and the Census shows the result: a median year built of about 1957, about three-quarters of homes built before 1980, and only about 28 percent before 1940.

Most of the roughly 15,200 housing units are owned by the people living in them, about 78 percent, and only about 9 percent are in two- to four-unit buildings, so much of the exterior work here is on owner-occupied houses of mid-century age. Sunset Lake, Pond Meadow Park and a corner of the Blue Hills Reservation lie in town, and the town's coastal position brings nor'easters along with an average of about 61 inches of snow a season. Houses built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when old paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A house from Braintree's postwar building years may already be on its second cladding, so the first question is what is underneath. If original wood or an early asbestos-cement shingle is present, how it is handled affects both cost and schedule, and asbestos removal has its own regulations. New vinyl over a flat, sound wall with a weather-resistive barrier and properly lapped window flashing will perform far better than panels hung over a wavy older surface. Pick a panel profile with exposure that suits the proportions of a modest one- or two-story house.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Wood clapboard makes the most sense on Braintree's older houses, such as those along Washington Street or in East Braintree near the Fore River, where the original board width is part of the house's character. Matching the reveal of the existing boards keeps a repair or addition from standing out. New boards should be back-primed and nailed so they can move with the seasons. Removing or sanding painted clapboard on a house from before 1978 brings EPA RRP lead-safe practices into play.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: On a mid-century Braintree house, fiber cement is a way to get a painted-board look with less upkeep than wood. Weight is the main planning factor: fiber cement is heavier than vinyl, so the sheathing and framing should be checked before installation. Keep the manufacturer's clearances at the bottom course, especially where driveways or patios meet the wall and snow piles up through the winter. Factory-primed or factory-painted boards are available, and every cut edge needs to be sealed before it goes up.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles are a good match on houses where a natural or stained finish is wanted, and they suit older forms like the 1720 saltbox Thayer house on Washington Street. Shingles need a drainage layer behind them so they can dry from the back, and stainless or hot-dipped galvanized nails to avoid staining. Near Sunset Lake or wooded edges by the Blue Hills, mildew can build up on shaded walls, so plan for periodic cleaning or a factory-treated product.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With only about 9 percent of Braintree's housing in two- to four-unit buildings and a median year built around 1957, so a full replacement usually involves one owner making the decisions rather than a group of unit owners or tenants. The open wall is the time to fix flashing at windows and doors, add a weather-resistive barrier and look at insulation if the cavities are empty. Older layers may contain lead paint or asbestos-cement shingles, each with its own handling rules. Ask for a written estimate that separates removal, new cladding and trim.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Window sills, fascia and porch posts on mid-century houses are usually the first wood to soften, especially on the north side and under gutters that overflow. Replacing rotted sections with cellular PVC or primed, rot-resistant stock is often less disruptive than wrapping the whole house in aluminum, which can hide moisture. On older houses in East Braintree, cornices and window casings carry period detail worth copying rather than simplifying. Any trim work that disturbs pre-1978 paint is covered by RRP rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: With an average snowfall around 61 inches a season and frequent nor'easters, gutters in Braintree have to deal with heavy roof runoff and ice at the eaves. Hangers spaced closely and screwed into solid fascia hold up under snow load better than spikes. Lots near Pond Meadow Park, Sunset Lake or the Blue Hills Reservation tend to collect leaves, so a guard or wider downspout reduces clogging. Make sure each downspout carries water well clear of the foundation, especially on houses with basements.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Snow and coastal storms shape roofing decisions here. Ice and water membrane at the eaves and in valleys helps prevent ice-dam leaks, and attic ventilation should be checked during any reroof, because poor venting causes many dams in the first place. For a nor'easter, the shingle maker's high-wind nailing pattern is worth using. On a house built around 1957, the roof deck may be original board sheathing; inspect it once the old shingles are off before closing in.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Typical repairs on Braintree houses include storm-loosened panels, impact damage near driveways and rot at the bottom courses of wood siding. A repair should match the existing profile and finish, and be flashed properly where it meets windows or trim. On pre-1978 painted surfaces, follow RRP lead-safe practices. If several areas are failing at once on a mid-century house, compare the repair cost against partial or full re-siding before committing.

story: Settled around 1710 and incorporated in 1793 from the south precinct of Braintree, Randolph spent its first century as a shoemaking town. The trade grew out of farm households into the main local industry, and by 1850 Randolph was one of the country's leading boot producers. A handful of buildings from those years remain, among them the Jonathan Belcher House at 360 North Main Street, a Federal-style house built in 1806 and now home to the Randolph Women's Club, and Stetson Hall, built in 1842.

Most of today's houses came later. When the shoe industry declined in the early 1900s, Randolph turned into a suburban residential community, and the big change came after World War II: the population nearly doubled from 9,982 in 1950 to 18,900 in 1960, then reached 27,035 by 1970, as families from Boston were drawn by its transportation links. The Census reflects that wave. The median house was built around 1966, only about 14 percent of homes date from before 1940, and about 70 percent were built before 1980. Of roughly 13,100 housing units, about 71 percent are owner-occupied and only about 8 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings.

The town is drained by the Cochato and Blue Hill rivers, both flowing toward the Neponset, and Ponkapoag Pond, a 203-acre pond inside the Blue Hills Reservation, lies on the Canton line. For exterior work, this means many houses are now roughly 50 to 70 years old and may be on their second or third roof. Original materials from that era are worth identifying before tear-off, and houses built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules whenever paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: A house from Randolph's 1950s and 1960s building wave may still carry its original wood siding, or an older layer such as asbestos-cement shingles, so it pays to know what is on the wall before ordering vinyl. Covering over an old surface is sometimes possible, but only if it is flat and dry; soft sheathing behind a sagging course will show through new panels. Housewrap, flashing tape at every window and a proper starter strip at the base make more difference to the result than the brand of panel.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: Clapboard is the historic finish for Randolph's 19th-century buildings, including Federal-period houses like the 1806 Belcher House on North Main Street. On a house of that age, matching board width, reveal and corner treatment keeps the repair consistent with the rest of the facade. For new clapboard on a postwar house, pre-primed boards installed over a drainage gap hold paint longer. Removing old painted clapboard from a house built before 1978 requires EPA RRP lead-safe work practices.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement is a reasonable upgrade for a postwar Randolph house when the owner wants the look of painted boards without repainting wood every several years. Because the material is heavy, check that the walls are straight and the sheathing sound before installation begins. The product needs specific clearances above grade, decks and roof lines, and blind nailing or face nailing must follow the manufacturer's instructions. Pairing it with matching trim boards keeps the house from looking patched together.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: Cedar shingles bring texture to a simple postwar house and can be used on a whole wall or just in gables. On shaded lots, such as those bordering the Blue Hills Reservation, cedar can hold moisture and grow mildew, so a breathable underlayment and good airflow behind the shingles matter. Stainless or hot-dipped nails prevent black streaks. A factory stain or primer extends the time between refinishing.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: With about 70 percent of Randolph's homes built before 1980, a full replacement often means removing two layers: the original siding and something added later. Take the opportunity to check sheathing, flash every window and door correctly and seal air leaks while the walls are open. Assume lead paint is present on older painted layers and plan for RRP containment. A written estimate should break out removal, new cladding, trim and any sheathing repairs so bids can be compared fairly.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Postwar houses tend to have simple trim: fascia, rake boards, window casings and a few porch posts. These parts rot first where gutters overflow or where paint has failed. Replacing rotted lengths with cellular PVC or primed, rot-resistant wood keeps the clean lines of the original. Covering trim in aluminum coil hides the problem without fixing it, so inspect the wood first. Work that disturbs paint on pre-1978 trim falls under EPA RRP rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Lots bordering the Blue Hills Reservation or other wooded land collect leaves, seeds and needles into gutters each fall. Guards or screens and oversized downspouts reduce cleaning, and seamless aluminum avoids leaky joints. Hangers should be fastened into solid fascia, since fascia on a house from the 1950s or 1960s may be original and soft. Direct water away from the foundation with extensions or splash blocks, especially on lots that slope toward the house.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Many Randolph houses were built within a short span after 1950, so roofs on the same street can come due within a few years of each other. A new roof should include ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys and a check of attic ventilation, since poor venting shortens shingle life and contributes to ice dams. Removing the old layers lets the deck be inspected; boards from the 1950s and 1960s may need patching before new underlayment goes down.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Common repairs include replacing cracked or blown-off vinyl panels, rotted lower courses of wood siding and damage near driveways. Matching the existing profile and color keeps the repair from standing out. Older painted surfaces require RRP lead-safe practices when disturbed. When the siding on a 1960s house has faded, a new panel may not match exactly; using pieces from a hidden wall for the visible repair can help.

story: Few towns can point to a building as old as the Boardman House on Howard Street. Tree-ring dating puts its frame at 1692, and a rear lean-to added by 1696 gave it the saltbox outline it still has. The Saugus Iron Works, which began operating in 1646, was reconstructed in the 1940s and 1950s and is now a National Historic Site. In the 19th century the villages each had their own trade: shoes and woolen goods in Saugus Center, tobacco in Cliftondale and East Saugus. The town hall on Central Street dates from 1875.

Population rose from about 5,000 in 1900 to 14,700 in 1930, then from 17,162 in 1950 to 25,110 in 1970, and the housing stock carries both waves. Census figures give a median year built of about 1962, with roughly 29 percent of homes built before 1940 and about 72 percent before 1980. Of the town's roughly 11,400 housing units, about 72 percent are owner-occupied and about 12 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings. Most residents live in Lynnhurst, Pleasant Hills, Cliftondale, East Saugus and Saugus Center, while Oaklandvale and North Saugus are much less densely settled. Route 1, widened in 1933, became the commercial strip after businesses moved there in the 1950s.

The landscape is unusually mixed for a town this size. Rumney Marsh fills the southern end, crossed by the Pines River and Route 107, and the Saugus River runs through town toward the sea, which lies just past the Point of Pines section of Revere. Most of Breakheart Reservation and part of Lynn Woods also sit within town lines. A house by the marsh and a house backing onto Breakheart face different exterior problems, and in both cases homes built before 1978 fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Most Saugus homes were built in the decades around the 1950s and 1960s population surge, and vinyl is a common way to end the repainting cycle on houses of that age. Near Rumney Marsh and along the Saugus River, open ground lets wind reach the walls, so a panel with a reinforced nail hem and full fastening at corners and starter strips is worth the small extra cost. Check what lies under the existing siding before deciding whether to install over it or strip to the sheathing.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: About 29 percent of Saugus homes were built before 1940, many of them in the villages that grew around 19th-century shoe, woolen and tobacco work. On houses of that age, painted wood clapboard may still be on the walls or hidden under later siding. Matching the existing reveal and corner details lets a repair blend in, and back-primed boards over a drainage gap hold paint longer. Assume old paint contains lead and follow EPA RRP practices when scraping or removing boards.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement offers a painted-board finish with more resistance to rot and insects than wood, a useful trait for houses near the wet ground of Rumney Marsh and the Saugus River. It must stay clear of grade and roof surfaces by the distances the manufacturer specifies, and cut ends need sealing. The boards are heavy, so on a two- to four-unit building, which accounts for about one home in eight here, plan staging and material storage before starting. A factory finish reduces painting on site.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: The Boardman House shows how long timber construction has lasted in Saugus, and cedar shingles carry a traditional look onto a newer house. Lots that back onto Breakheart Reservation or Lynn Woods can be heavily shaded, and shade means slower drying and a higher chance of mildew, so a ventilated underlayment and stainless fasteners help. Untreated cedar weathers to gray; factory-stained shingles hold a color longer. Keep the bottom course well above soil and mulch beds.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a Saugus house built before 1980, which describes about 72 percent of the stock, can reveal multiple layers and water damage around windows and sills. Budget for sheathing repairs and new flashing once the walls are open. On two- to four-unit buildings, coordinate access and parking with tenants and neighbors. Pre-1978 painted surfaces require RRP containment. A written estimate that lists removal, siding, trim and possible carpentry separately makes comparison easier.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: On the older houses in Saugus Center and around Cliftondale, porch columns, cornices and window casings, where they survive, define the front of the building. Repairing or replacing rotted sections with matching profiles, in primed wood or cellular PVC, keeps that character. On mid-century houses, simpler fascia and rake boards usually fail first where gutters overflow. Wrapping wood in aluminum without fixing the rot underneath only delays the problem. Trim work that disturbs pre-1978 paint is covered by RRP rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Houses near Breakheart Reservation or Lynn Woods deal with leaves and needles every fall, so guards and wider downspouts are worth considering. In the low-lying areas near Rumney Marsh and the Saugus River, the bigger concern is moving water well away from the foundation, since the surrounding ground may already be wet. Seamless aluminum with closely spaced hangers handles snow and ice better than sectional gutters on spikes.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: The marsh in the south of town gives wind a long, open run, and roofs there should be nailed to the manufacturer's high-wind specification with sealed starter strips. Next to the reservations, shade keeps roofs damp longer, which encourages moss and algae; algae-resistant shingles help. Throughout town, ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys and balanced attic ventilation reduce ice-dam damage. On older homes, inspect the roof deck after tear-off before new underlayment goes on.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Typical repairs include panels loosened by wind, cracked vinyl and rotted wood near the ground. A good repair matches the existing profile and color and is flashed correctly at windows and trim. Pre-1978 painted surfaces call for RRP lead-safe practices. On houses near the marsh, look at the sheathing behind any damaged area, since trapped moisture there is easy to miss.

story: Weymouth dates its settlement to 1622, when the Wessagusset colony was founded, and a house at 84 Sea Street from about 1650 is counted as its oldest survivor. The town grew around four village centers: North Weymouth, East Weymouth, South Weymouth and Weymouth Landing. Next to the Landing, the Front Street Historic District holds nearly 150 resources across 77 acres, mostly houses, including a Cape at 160 Front Street from about 1720 and other 18th-century Cape and Georgian homes. Shoemaking was a local industry from the early 1700s until the Stetson Shoe Company closed in 1973, and a 19th-century shoemaker's shop at 99 Front Street is now a house.

Each village has its own character. East Weymouth has Victorian houses in the Queen Anne, Shingle and Colonial Revival styles, with restorations under way on Hillcrest Road. North Weymouth, the most densely populated part of town, has small waterfront cottages that are being bought and redone. In South Weymouth, the former naval air station is being redeveloped as Union Point. Population jumped from 32,690 in 1950 to 54,610 in 1970, and the Census shows it: median year built about 1964, about 22 percent of homes from before 1940 and about 71 percent from before 1980. Of roughly 26,700 housing units, about two-thirds are owner-occupied and about 7 percent sit in two- to four-unit buildings.

Water defines the edges. Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor lie to the north, the Fore River and Back River cut into town, and Whitman's Pond and Great Esker Park sit inland. Weymouth is considered especially vulnerable to sea level rise. For exterior work, that means salt and wind on the North Weymouth shore, older painted woodwork in the historic districts, and houses built before 1978 everywhere, which fall under EPA lead-safe (RRP) rules when paint is disturbed.

serviceNotes.vinyl-siding-installation: Vinyl is a practical choice for the postwar houses that make up most of Weymouth's stock and for North Weymouth cottages being redone. Near the water, choose a heavier panel with a reinforced nail hem, and fasten corners and starter strips fully to resist wind off Hingham Bay. On a Victorian house in East Weymouth, vinyl can bury the decorative detail that defines it, so decide first which trim and shingle areas should stay exposed or be copied in another material.
serviceNotes.clapboard-siding-installation: The 18th-century Cape and Georgian houses in the Front Street Historic District and the older homes around Weymouth Landing are where wood clapboard matters most. Matching board width, reveal and corner boards keeps a repair true to the building, and a converted shop like the one at 99 Front Street deserves the same care as the main houses. New clapboard should be primed on all sides and installed with a drainage gap. Before scraping or replacing boards on a pre-1978 house, plan for EPA RRP lead-safe containment.
serviceNotes.hardie-plank-siding-installation: Fiber cement gives a painted-board appearance with better resistance to rot than wood, which helps along the shoreline in North Weymouth and near the Fore and Back rivers. Use fasteners suited to coastal exposure and keep the required gaps above grade, decks and roofs. On a Colonial Revival or Queen Anne house in East Weymouth, the planks should be paired with trim sized to the original so the facade keeps its proportions. Seal every cut end before installation.
serviceNotes.cedar-shingle-siding: East Weymouth's Shingle-style and Queen Anne houses are the natural place for cedar shingles. Where a house has patterned shingles, such as fishscale or diamond cuts in a gable, a repair should copy the pattern and exposure so it reads as original. Near the shore, untreated cedar weathers to gray, and stainless nails prevent rust streaks. A drainage underlayment behind the shingles helps the wall dry between storms.
serviceNotes.full-siding-replacement: A full replacement on a 1950s or 1960s Weymouth house usually means removing one or two old layers, then installing a fresh weather barrier and window flashing before new siding. In North Weymouth, where small cottages are being redone, opening the walls may show framing or sheathing that needs work before anything new goes on. Pre-1978 painted surfaces require RRP containment. A written estimate should list removal, new siding, trim and contingency carpentry as separate items.
serviceNotes.exterior-trim-work: Victorian houses in East Weymouth carry the most trim, and saving original brackets, rails and cornice pieces where possible, then copying profiles in primed wood or cellular PVC where not, keeps the character intact. On the 18th-century houses along Front Street and Summer Street, simpler casings and cornices should match the period rather than be updated. In salt air, sills and lower trim are usually the first to go. Trim work that disturbs pre-1978 paint falls under RRP rules.
serviceNotes.gutter-installation: Along Hingham Bay and the river shores, wind-driven rain and salt wear on gutters, so aluminum or copper with closely spaced hangers is a better fit than steel. Trees near Great Esker Park, Whitman's Pond or any wooded lot fill gutters each fall, and guards with larger downspouts reduce clogging. Because the town is exposed to rising water, carrying roof runoff well away from foundations matters most on low-lying lots near the shore.
serviceNotes.roofing-installation: Shoreline houses in North Weymouth take wind straight off the harbor, so roofs there should follow the shingle maker's high-wind nailing pattern with sealed starter courses. Where an East Weymouth Victorian has dormers, towers or multiple gables, every intersection needs careful step and valley flashing. Throughout town, ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys and good attic ventilation help prevent ice dams. Check the deck after tear-off on any older house before new underlayment goes down.
serviceNotes.siding-repair-services: Common repairs include storm damage near the shore, rotted lower courses on older wood siding and cracked vinyl. The repair should match the existing profile and finish and be flashed correctly at openings. Pre-1978 painted surfaces require RRP lead-safe practices. On a Victorian house in East Weymouth, patterned shingles or trim pieces should be matched so the repair is not obvious.
